WArtvg. A BROKEN SWORD. The shopma,n shambled from the doorway out And reached it down— Snapped in the blade! 'Twas scarcely dear, I doubt, At half-a-crown. Useless enough! And yet may still be seen, In letters clear, Traced on the steel in rusty damaskeen— " Povr Paruenyr." Whose was it once ?—Who manned it once in hope His fate to gain? Inc. was it dreamed his oyster-world should opa To this—in vain?

Perchance with some stout Argonaut it sailed The Western Seas; Perchance but to some paltry Nym availed For toasting cheese! Or decked by Beauty on some morning lawn With silken knot, Perchance, ere night, for Church and King 'twas drawn— Perchance 'twas not. Who knows—or cares? To-day, 'mid foils and gloves Its hilt depends. Planked by the favours of forgotten loves— Remembered friends And oft its legend lends in hours of stress A word to aid; Or like a warning comes in Duffed success— Its broken blade. —The Magazine of Art
Ar STIN DOBSON.

_ Till the brightest hours vere gone. "Sometimes, though, I should be busy Making a marble roll; Or sitting, if I were hungry, To watch a mouse's hole.

"But if I were feeling lazy, I'd curl myself in a ball, : And lie all day by the fire, With nothing to do at all. Waiter (bawling to the cook) : "One roast goose and •one potato." Old gentleman: "No, no ! not se much .goose and more potatoes." None ara so seldom found alone, and are so soon tired of their own company, as those coxcombs who are on the best terms with themselves.—Caton. An attorney, about to furnish a bill of costs, was re- quested by his client, a baker, "to make it as light as possible." " Ahl" replied the attorney, "that's what you may say to your foreman, but it's not the way I make my bread." "James, do you love your sister ?" "Yes, sir." "Well, show me how you love her." The boy stood still, not knowing what to do. "James, how do I express my love for your mother ?" "Oh, you give her some bank notes, but I ain't got any." " Awl" exclaimed an English cockney to a Western traveller in England, speaking of the law of primogeni- ture, " 'ave you hentail in Amewica ?" " Hentail?" said the American, looking at his interrogator with curiosity. "No, sir. We have a cocktail in America, and a very popular drink it is." At Rotherham station, one day, a porter promptly offered the Bishop of Sodor and Man all possible assis- tance with his luggage. "How many articles, your lord- ship?" "Thirty-nine," said the bishop, with a sly twinkle in his eye. That's too many, I'm afraid," re- plied the man in good faith. " Ah," said the bishop, "I perceive you are a Dissenter. Englishman: "You Americans come over to Europe with your little hammers and hack away at every old ruin, getting 'specimens,' until there is scarcely any- thing left." American: "Well, why don't you retaliate ?" " Retaliate ! How? You have nothing in this country to hack at." "Oh, yes, we have." "What ?" "You can come over and take a hack at Niagara Falls." A great boy in school was so abusive to the younger ones that the teacher took the vote of the school whether he should be expelled. All the small boys voted to expel him except one, who was scarcely five years old. Yet he knew very well that the bad boy would probably con- tinue to abuse him. "Why, then, did you vote for him to stay?" said the teacher. "Because if he is expelled perhaps he will not learn any more about God, and so he will be more wicked still." "Do you forgive him, then?" said the teacher. Yes," said he, "papa and mamma and you all forgive me when I do wrong; God forgives me too, and I must do the same." THE SEASIDE PEA.—An old writer, speaking of the dearth which prevailed in England in 1555, .says : "At this time plenty of peas did grow on the seashore, near Dnnwich, in Suffolk, never set or sown by human in- dustry, which being gathered in full ripeness, much abated the high price of the market, and preserved many hungry families from perishing." The plant which thus appeared at so needful a season was the seaside pea (Pisum maritimum), which is a native of our shores, but not usually very common or abundant. It is a pretty wild pea, not unlike the sweet pea of our gardens. A BIT OF ADVICE FOR Boys.—" You are made to be kind," says Horace Mann, "generous and magnanimous. If there is a boy in the school who has a club foot don't let him know that you ever saw it. If there is a poor boy with ragged clothes, don't talk about rags when he is in hearing. If there is a lame boy, assign him some part of the game which does not require running. If there is a hungry one, give him a part of your dinner. If there is a dull one, help him to get his lesson. If th'ere is a bright one, be not envious of him; for if one boy is proud of his talents, and another is envious of them, there are two great wrongs, and no more talents than before. If a larger or stronger boy has injured you, and is sorry for it, forgive him and request the teacher not to punish him. All the school will show by their countenance how much better it is than to have a great fist. -

A FAMOUS BORDER KEEP.—The surroundings of the old keep of Thirlstane, in the adjoining dale, will appear familiar to those who know the Border landscape of the late George Harvey. There is the long shoulder of the pastoral hill, patched with heather and flecked with sun- shine'; the brawling mountain torrent hurrying down to meet the Leader and the Tweed; the strong square tower, with its immemorial ashes and knotted and twisted thorns, perched on the high table-land which rises steeply from the water-edge; the rounded backs of the Lammermuirs along the northern sky. Of a summer evening, when, though the sun has set behind -"Eildort's triple height," daylight still lingers in the west, and lipshes the zenith, it is difficult to imagine a scene more peaceful, or in some aspects more pathetic. Save for complaint of curlew and plover, the silence is unbroken, and the haunting fascination of the Border- land may then be felt at its best— The grace of forest charms decayed,

And pastoral melancholy. When we stood the other day within its crumbling walls the cuckoo and the corn-crake were calling. The corn- -crake and the cuckoo are not exactly modern inven- tions. They must have been vocal in the valleys when robber-chiefs dwelt here among armed retainers, and vigilantly watched the rough and dangerous track that led across the hills from the Scottish capital to the Northumbrian moors. We associate these sounds with utter peacefulness and the sweet amenities of the spring; what associations did they stir, what feelings did they rouse, in the breasts of the freebooters of the Border? The whole environment of our life has so completely changed, that it is wellnigh impossible to realise to our- selves, even imaginatively, the conditions, moral, intel- lectual, and physical, of that fierce and turbulent so- ciety.—" The Scotlazd of Mary Stuart" in Blackwood'' Mageeinek, )r HINTS ABOUT TITE HAIIL—It may seem strange, but it 'is a fact, that the peculiar constitution of the hair is in- herited. We notice that baldness--premature—runs in families, and so it is of the reverse condition, some men and women retaining quite a luxuriance of hair up to old -age. Still one ought to make the very best of the hair in one's possession. The weaker and softer the hair is, , the more carefully should it be treated. Children with ' soft, fine hair are probably more troubled with irritable scalps than others-, and I desire to impress upon mothers the fact that' if these are not treated immediatay on their appearance, weakness of the hair is to be looked for in the future, and even premature baldness. '7l But no great amount of hard brushing can be tolerateMby the scalps of young people. It ought to be better known that treatment on this rough principle though it :may stinaulate the skin and the consequent growth of hair for a time, soon does more harm than good, for the scalp be- comes weak, and the hair gets shorter, thinner, and falls off. Use, therefore, a soft brush, ladies, and youths of both sexes. But if you have very strong hair, then the brush may be correspondingly rougher.'a Should oil be used? Probably a waxy pomatum is best, but even this should be used most sparingly. Really, in my humble opinion, the hair, to be healthy, requires fresh lair and sunlight as much as does any growing plant, and all know what the result would be if a tree's bark were com- pletely coated with any stiff paste. When oils or barna- tums are used, care should be taken that they are quite fresh. Never make or buy any large quantities at a time therefore, and let the perfume with which it is mixed be of the simplest kind. Hair that is oiled must be more frequently washed—say, once a week. Use the best and mildest soap, or lukewarm water and yolks of new-laid Ptzg,,s, and dry carefully with a soft towel —Ca.uell's -Family Magazine.i.. _

You can get one passed on your ticket,and we'll,doi:them. See ?" ' "Yes, I see, but I haven't any ticket." ",Butll thought you were going by this train" "So I am; I'm the guard." WITH A PERAMBULATOR IN MID-ALPS.—When I resolved on a summer cool among the Alps, and wanted] a quiet restingVace for wife and five children, the youngest six months old, I fixed on the Montafun. Now, at the out- set,,let me protest that nothing is easier than to travel with a heap of women-kind, babies, and boxes. With a little intelligence and some experience it ileasily done. As so—on the thumb-nail write, as I did, "3," that stands for three women—wife governess, and nurse; on the forefinger write "5," that represents the children; on the middle-finger put " 6," that stands for boxes—all mind alike—iron] painted brown with brass mountings. Then on the ring-finger put the number of indiscriminate 'boxes, bundles, &c.; and on the little fingeenote the bundlestof umbrellas. Next,rtake for:the perambulator a separate luggage ticket 'and on reaching your:destina- I tion give that up only. Then you recovelthe perambu- lator, call over the live-stock, see to the items on the I ring-finger, and ignore the other two. Then plant the baby in the perambulator, and form in line of march, leading the way, or rather :going on before the body of the armya as an Chian or sharpshooter. Avoid every , large inn, enter and take stocka'of a small one, and secure it altogether. Thenceforth you are the sole guest. Everyone in the house is devoted to make you:comfort- able. At 4), large hotel children'are enuisance ; there is a difficulty about baths and milk, and pap, &c.; but in a little inn, which you occupy altogether, where there is no waiter with his napkin and black dress suit, but only simple girls and a host in his shirt-sleeves, you fare—to use a German expression—carried on hands. Moreover, thefamount of incense burned under the nose of the baby is enough to turn its head, were it at an age appreciative of worship and flattery: and secure the suffrages of the mother. On being settled into the rooms, and the perambulator under cover, and the baby engaged on fresh milk, give up your ticket to the host for the luggage, and he will see that it all comes right. That perambulator !—it had its history. To begin with: On reaching our destina- tion in Germany the autumn before, the first morning proved to be market day; and, on opening the window, I saw trains of perambulators going to market. In some were little pigs about to be sold; in others. baskets of eggs; in &hers vegetables. And, when market Was over, the villagers returned to their homes with their purchases in the perambulators—great loaves of bread, crockery, bonnets, gowns. That day only in the week were the babies not allowed rides in their perambulators —the vehicles went a-marketing. I rushed out and bought a perambulator, and it cost me under a pound; it was a basket on four wheels. In that same basket my baby began his voyage among the Alps. I will say nothip, about our journey to Bludenz, because that was done by rail and steamer; it was taken in instalments. We stopped where we liked, and whipped out our peram- bulator, and engaged an inn • no difficulty in the world —alLwent like clockwork—Front "The Nontafun," in the " Cornhill Magazine" for September. THE FUTURE OF THE NEGRO IN THE UNITED STATES.— Bishop Henry M. Turner, a coloured man, who was the first coloured chaplain in the United States Army, was afterwards the principal figure in the Republican party in Georgia, being twice elected a member of the Georgia Legislature, and finally became, first, the head of a Methodist "book-room," and next, Bishop of Kentucky and Tennessee, with his residence in Atalanta, Ga., was recently interviewed as to the future of the negro in the South. "Since the abolition of slavery (said the Bishop), the South has made remarkable progress, especially so in its industrial condition. Before the emancipation of the slaves, the whites were almost wholly dependent upon the negro traffic for their maintenance. Now everybody must depend on his own efforts. What was once con- sidered menial and degrading has assumed another and a higher aspect to the white population. You can readily perceive that this healthier and nobler view of labour is well calculated to work a vast improvement in the in- dustrial tone of the Southern States, and now, 20 years after the close of the war, the improvement is every- where apparent. The coloured people are chiefly engaged in agriculture, but the blacks, as well as the whites of the south, are being moved to the future importance of manufactures, and wherever possible engage in such business. Let me add right here that the coloured man is not the mean and degraded creature he is generally believed to be by the white people. There are some idlers, laggards, and loafers among the black people, but the majority are as diligent and industrious as most whites. As to the social condition of the Southern negro (continued Bishop Turner) I cannot say that there can be marked any im- provement in that. In every other respect the coloured man is infinitely better off than before the war, but there is now less social contact than then. The relations of the two races are not as intimate by virtue of the fact that while before the war black and white boys grew up in the same yard, played together, and respected and sympathised with each other, now they play apart. There is an alienation that did not formerly exist. We have to ride on separate cars, and the cars are much inferior. The negroes are mostly Republicans. The future of the negro is a very broad question. We have large schools in every Southern city and many colleges, and these are yearly turning out teachers for the lower classes. In this way education is being very generally disseminated. In no great time the black will refuse longer to concede superiority to the white. Both races must then occupy the same social plane, or one of them must quit the country. If the negro is not granted social equality he will tun to Liberia and establish a Government of his own there. He thus would become the agent of en- lightenment of the great African continent, and who knows but that this was God's design in enslaving the black race ?" EPPS'S COCOA. GRATEFUL AND COMFORTING. div.p: THE MANACTINENT OF POULTRY- THE MODERN POULTRY INTEREST.

In speaking of the modern poultry interest, the mind at once turns to the system of poultry shows as found in Great Britain, for whatever shows there are in other countries are to a very large extent a copy. We find that these shows flourish on every side, and in the course of each year there are some hundreds, in several of which the exhibits are not to be counted by the hundred 1 but by the thousand. In the northern districts of• En- ' I land almost every village has a show of its own, and the ' day on which it is held is made a great annual holiday.. Some of these, it is true, are in connection with a local agricultural or horticultural society, but the greater number of them are conducted independently, except that dogs and pigeons are usually associated with poul- try in the show. The competition is, as a rule, very severe, and the exhibitors give as much thought to the production of their specimens as if the whole fate of the enapire depended upon their success. We have known working men think of scarce anything else for months than how they can win at the next show. They have denied themselves and their families many things so that they could purchase a good breeding cock, and the infec- tion has spread to their wives and children, who have willingly given up many little things they would other- wise have enjoyed, so that there might be produced a I bird fit to win a first prize or a much-coveted cup. No one can have visited the shows in the north and midland counties of England, or in the east of Scotland, without being impressed with the intensity of feeling and wide- spread interest taken in the shows. And be it noted that these people are not mere novices at the business. They know a good bird when they see one, and a judge had better get out of the way as soon as posSible if he is not up to his work, for he will have to run a gauntlet of questions far more severe than ever a much-heckled can- didate for Parliamentary honours has had to undergo. We have sometimes stood at the entrance to a poultry tent and watched the exhibitors pouring in, noting the eager expressions of hope and fear on their countenances, the flush of pleasure, or the pallor of disappointment. And at other times we have stood near the pens, listening to the criticisms passed upon the specimens and the awards, surprised at the knowledge of breeding dis- played, and astonished at the practical opinions of both the exhibitors and their wives, who are just as eager as the men themselves. Be it beneficial or not, there is no question that "the fancy," as it is called, is a very widely spread factor in the lives of la,rge.numbers of our work- ing class population. It is very difficult, indeed, to estimate the number of those who are interested in this pursuit, but some years ago there was published a Fanciers' Directory, from which we find that there were then (1880) upwards of twelve thousand exhibitors, and we believe that since that time this number has been largely augmented, for shows have increased in number and size. Then there is also the fact that for everyone who exhibits there must be at least half a dozen who do not, for in many places the small breeders never think of sending their birds to shows unless they happen to breed one that is excep- tionally high in merit. It is, therefore, impossible to give any reliable figures as to the actual numbers of those who may be termed fanciers. The best proof that this is a strong interest may be found in the large num- ber of exhibitions scattered all over the country. At one of these—the Crystal Palace Show, held at Svdenham every November—the entries of poultry in 18-85 num- bered 3,474, or nearly 5,000 birds; and other exhibitions, such as Birmingham, the Dairy Show, Liverpool, and Edinburghltare also very large, indicating that there is a very widespread and strong interest taken in the breed- ing of poultry. Large businesses have sprung up to supply the needs of the exhibitions and their supporters; the railway companies derive an enormous revenue through the transit to and from the shows; several newspapers are run in the interest of fanciers; and during the show season there Is quite a little army of judges, reporters, and exhibitors always on the road, passing as rapidly as may be from one show to another. The show system is of very recent growth, and has really taken the place of the old cock-pit. It may be dated from the Cochin mania of thirty-five years ago, though there had been what were really shows on a small scale long before that time. The late Mr. Rd. Teebay, of Fulwood, Preston, once gave an interesting account of the competition in pre-exhibition days. Both in Lan- cashire and Yorkshire the breedinV of what we now call Hamburghs was -the chief recreation of the weavers of fifty years ago. In Lancashire it was the custom for the exhibitors to take their birds under their arms and show them on a table in a room, each exhibitor arguing for the good points of his specimen, whilst his rivals pointed out the bad points. The judge stood at one side of the table, and after lots had been drawn for the rotation in showing, Nos. 1 and 2 were put upon the table, and their merits decided upon, when the beaten bird was removed, and No. 3 brought forward, this being done until all were disposed of. Of course, the last one!was declared to be the winner. But with the advent of the Cochin mania the number of exhibitions increased, and the de- sire of the public to see the wonderful new fowls that were to be mines of wealth to every fortunate possessor was so great that shows were instituted. Though the system has been greatly modified, though the outside public do not patronise shows now as they did then. yet it is to the interest then engendered that we owe the present poultry system. The majority of the older generation of fanciers, the fathers of poultry breeding in this country, many of whom have, alas, passed away, first learnt to love fowls through buying a pair of Cochins. Some, it is true, were lovers of cock-pit, and when cock-fighting became illegal they followed the bent of their minds and took up the exhibition of fowls instead. There are yet many who can tell of their old conflicts in the cock-pit, and who, it may be, look long- ingly back on their older form of competition. But those who were the means of commencing the present show system little thought it would ever grow to its present dimensions. Much might be said about the early shows, and the story of the Cochin mania is a most interesting one, but it is not necessary that we should recount them more than to say that in the former there was very much less of the professional element than is to be found at the present time. The effect of this mania was to teach skilful breeders and sharp dealers that there was a very good living to be made out of the business, and then was established a class which have not tended to the eleva- tion of the pursuit. This, however, we will discuss later on; also the question as to the effect of exhibitions upon poultry, and whether they kave been beneficial in their effect influence. Nor has the fancy system been con- fined to Britain, for we find it has spread to America, to Denmark, to Germany, France, and to the Antipodes, where it is perhaps strongest of all outside England, most. nearly resembling the mother country. This is due to the fact that several very prominent breeders and exhibitors have emigrated to New Zealand and Aus- tralia, where they have carried their old ideas and tastes. Some of the shows in the southern hemisphere , are strong both in numbers and quality, and the breeders there have been most enterprising in securing first-class stock from the old country. In New Zealand especially, which is like the old country in many respects, is there a large poultry interest growing up, and we expect that it will do for the southern portion of the globe what Britain has for the northern, namely, be the great breed- ing ground for high-class stock. America also has done good service in that she has introduced several new breeds, and we believe that it is to the advantage of the pursuit that there should be fresh interest engendered, which can only be done by that which is novel. These breeds have a distinctive character of their own, and show that American breeders are determined to have

FOOT-ROT.— There are many remedies for foot-rot; the best I know is a mixture of sulphuric acid and lin- seed oil, equal parts. Pare the foot thoroughly and apply the dressing when the grass is dry, repeat at intervals of I two days till a cure is effected; two dressings will cure ordinary cases. Last year I carted some gas lime and put it in a heap on some clover eddish. I put 95 lambs into the field; they were nearly all lame, more or less. Of course they trampled the heap of lime; in a fortnight they were all cured.—Fox. TIIE HARVEST IN IRELAND.—The Farmers' Garette pub- lishes a very satisfactory report on harvest prospects in Ireland. "It has seldom," says our contemporary, "fallen to our lot to publish such a generally good re- port. Of 61 reports on the wheat crop 37 are average, 16 over average, and 6 under. Of 58 reports on the bar- ley crop 30 give it as average, 19 as over average, and 9 under. As regards oats there are 92 reports, of which 42 are average, 40 over average, and 10 under average. Of flax we have 23 reports, 12 average, 9 over average, and 7 under. Of 91 reports on potatoes, 53 are average, 34 over average, and 4 under. Of 92 reports of the tur- nip crop 34 mark it average, 40 over average, and 18 under. Of 87 reports on mangolds, 47 are average, 29 average, and 11 under. Of meadows—that is, the hay crop—as regards qulntity, 27 reports are average, 61 over average, and only 3 under average. Grass in pas- ture land seems equally plentiful, 35 reports being average, 52 over average, and 4 under. THE CHESHIRE DAIRY SCHOOL.—Since the opening of the Cheshire Dairy School, at Aston Hall, Worsleston, a good number of pupils have presented themselves for instruction in cheese and butter making, and already the project seems baring good fruit in the county. As proof of the value of the school, one or two instancf s are cited where persons, after taking lessons, have been :able to make several shillings per cwt. more of their cheese. The cheese-making department is under the direction of Mr. George Willis, secretary, Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association, whilst butter-making is carried on by Miss Mary Connell, of the Munster Dairy School. The demand for dairy produce from the school has increased to such an extent that it has been found necessary to obtain milk from a neighbouring farm in addition to that sup- plied by Mr. Jackson, the tenant. The cheese already sold has realised good prices, and this fact has caused confidence to be felt in the undertaking. Most of the landlords have visited the institute, and several are offering to pay all or a portion of the fees of those of their tenants who may wish to take lessons. A number of county ladies have given in their names to attend the school periodically as visitors to watch the dairy opera- tions. PLUM DRYING.—Mr. Roberts, of Ivinghoe, Tring, writes thus to the Standard :—ln contemplating the probable loss that many will sustain by the superabundant plum crop this year, it has occurred to me that something might be done in the way of artificially drying the fruit; and as I am living in the midst of a district in which a very large amount of damsons, of both the large :and small sorts (the former are called prunes), are grown, I intend practically to try the experiment, and shall be glad if any of your readers can give me any suggestions as to heat, Sec., and the mode of procedure adopted in France for drying the prune. Plums of the damson tribe contain many qualities that would tend to make artificialidrying practical—they contain a large amount of tannic acid, the skin is thick and tough, and the pulp of the plum is held together by a larger amount of fibre I than the earlier stone fruits possess. If one could only get the plums to shrivel to a small extent, they would be able to be held off the market until a more convenient season. I thought of stretching netting just above my maltkiln floor, placing the plums—having gathered them just before ripe—in a thin layer all over, and at short intervals slightly agitating the netting so as to alter the position of the fruit. Now, m the heat to start the at, and whether they should be allowed to cool several times during the process, and whether one could burn any substance upon the fire that would assist in shrivel- ling the skin (and not bursting it), are points upon which a little help would be worth no end of pity. THE WINTER DAIRY.—ON ERGOT AND ABORTION.— Among the advice given to farmers we find conspicu- ously the winter dairy, and no doubt the advice is good, but the cow due to calve in autumn has less chance of becoming the mother of a living calf than she whose time is arranged for spring. Ergot seems to be the cause of this. I have found the disease this year on nearly every grass on my farm, and my neighbours are, so far, ; not more fortunate; but as their cows are not yet in calf, or have only lately been served, they will not suffer except from such ergotted seed as will cling to the ; stalks for some months to come. I have reason to:be- ' lieve, however, that some of the graeses retain their ergot ! ! till March. There are two grasses on which I have not found this poison, viz., meadow foxtail and crested dog's-tail. Last year my hay and silage were ergotted, and about half my cows, out of a herd of 45, had dead I calves, and this autumn I have had two premature 'births, due, I believe, to ergotted grass. lam trying to , clear some land of the pest, and hope to save myself from I much further loss, but the subject is of such importance that I trust farmers will experiment with ergot on some 1 in-calf cows, so that we might get decided answers to th 3 following questions :-1. Does ergot produce abor- ! tion ? 2. How much ergot is required to produce abor- tion? 3. Is the effect of ergot greater or less as the time of prvnancy advances? 4. Does ergot affect a cow when given on a lull stomach? 5. Does ergot act im- mediately on the cow, or must she consume it for a length of time to make her abort? . Farmers also require some decided evidence as to sympathetic abortion I caused by ill-treatment, such as overdriving and other ! cruel treatment. If sympathetic abortion is a fact, no doubt cases can be quoted where many cows have I aborted on the same day in one herd, and where ergot , could not have been the cause. If abortion by over- driving is a fact, there should be many cases in fairs; land if violence isa cause, one would expect it to occur ! in cows given to jumping fences, as they frequently do in this country (Ireland). Bad smells, I have read, will , cause abortion. Can anyone produce evidence to that effect? I NORTH LANCASHIRE NOTES.—The weather continues , broken, fine one day, with hot sun, in a shade tempera- ture of 70 degrees—wet the next, with a drop of temper- ature ranging from 10 to 5 degrees. It is, lam afraid, just the weather to induce potato disease, although as ! yet there are few complaints. Grain is coming to the sickle, and a few early fields of oats were cut this week , and last. Grass lands are full of keep, but the after grass is not of the feeding nature we like to see, conse- quent upon so much wet, and it comes through the cattle like water. In the hill districts there is still a good deal of hay to save. Root crops are benefiting fast by the greater warmth and the showers, and they should make good crops. At the Barrow-in-Furness they Society's Show, on Saturday, there were some nice roots exhibited in swedes and mangolds but no mon- strosities such as we used to see at shows in former I years. During the past few years a change has come I over the opinions of farmers in this respect. Formerly, it was the practice to single the plants wide apart, and to use abnormally large quantities of superphosphate, guano, Etc., in order to produce the biggest roots. As time went on there grew the conviction that in the culti- vation of these giant roots the game was not worth the candle. They had not the same solidity, the same specific weight for size of the smaller roots, and it was found also that they had worse keeping qualities, and that the proportion of rotten roots grew year by year. more numerous, a result, we may take it, of unnatural culti- vation. Of recent years the tendency has been to single out the plants at shorter distance, with the result of producing a greater number of smaller roots, more solid, of higher nutritive value, and which keep better. At the same show on Saturday there were some large cabbages, but these showed an undue proportion of outer leaves to heart, a reflex of the showery season we have had. Last year our swede plants suffered from curl in the leaf, owing to a severe visitation of green fly, and I hear there are some crops now suffering from the same cause. This is somewhat singular. as there is no better preventive for the attack than showers of rain. The rains have saved the mangold crop from serious in- jury from maggot attack, experienced at an early stage of growth of the plant.—The following account of a farmer, who has died in America, has been sent Ito me, the subject of it having gone from this district, and it may be interesting to your North-country readers:— "There died at his residence, Lincoln Hill, Todd's Point, Shelley County, Illinois, U.S. North America, of consump- tion, on August 14th, 1886, Mr. John Turner, aged fifty- three years. He was a son of the late Mr. John Turner, formerly parish clerk of Lowick, North Lancashire, deceased. Emigrated to America in the spring of 1857 ; he married filen, third daughter of Mr. John Atkinson, of Howgill, Yorkshire, and leaves a widow, son, and daughter. He was well known in this and other States as one who took great interest in the raising of blood stock—Shorthorn cattle, Southdown, Shropshire, Cots- wold, and Merino sheep. His estate consisted of 500 acres, all in the highest state of cultivation, and noted for its shrubberies and choice fruits. Mr. Turner was at one time agent on the estate of the late Mr. Wei. Noble. of Beckfoot, Penrith, and also on the estate of Mr. Isaac Fleming, of Grasmere."—R.

div.head: NOTES ON A HOLIDAY IN WEST
div.p: NOTES ON A HOLIDAY IN WEST

WALES. BY W. A. ABRA.M, F. if, S. (From the Blackburn Times.) By way of redeeming a promise to one or two friends, I put down in writing for publication in the newspaper the following slight sketch of our peregrinations during a holiday spent on the western coast of Wales from which we returned home a fortnight since. Beyond perhaps furnishino•b a hint or two to readers who have not yet made the tour of that part of Wales, I do not expect that these paragraphs will prove to be of much practical use. With regard to scenes of natural beauty, the writer is one of those who consider that no effort in word-painting can convey to others even a faint phantasm of the impression the scenes themselves produced upon the mind of the beholder. Neither can one call back the glow of enthusiastic. admiration kindled in the breast at the instant of presentation of some of the grandest and most singular of terrestrial spectacles to the entranced gaze. Longfellow has dis- tinguished two human instincts, as —" The instinct that enjoys, And the more noble instinct that aspires." Of the "instinct that enjoys," I think I can claim possession of a proper share. The love of the sublime and beautiful in nature has been a lifelong passion, , which but intensifies as the years pass by. But I feel sadly deficient in that "more noble instinct that aspires" to translate one's holiday raptures posthu- mously into an epic, as, for instance, my friend and compagnon du voyage, Mr. Walker, can do and has done. . My emotions amid splendid scenery may be poetical, . but my description of it afterwards will be absolutely prosaic.

_ Wales is usually divided by geographers into North and South. But for purposes of touring, and con- venience of exploration of its beauties by those who visit the country for pleasure, it may be partitioned into quarters, answering to the points of the compass. North Wales embraces the scenery along the northern coast, from Flint to Holyhead, and the inland parts of Fiintshire, Denbighshire, and Carnarvonshire, along with the Isle of Anglesea. The tour of South Wales might comprise the southern coast, from Cardiff to St. David's,with the interior parts of the counties of Glam- organ, Caermarthen, and Pembroke, and the valleys of the Lower Wye and the Usk in the border county of Monmouth. To a journey through East Wales might be allotted the vales of Upper Wye and Usk in the counties of Radnor and Brecknock, the greater part of the county of Montgomery, containing the valley of. the Upper Severn and its tributary rivers, and the district of Llangollen at the south-east corner of Denbighshire. To the fourth division of West Wales would remain the 1 west coast from Bardsea Island to St. David's head, 1 and the counties of Cardigan and Merioneth, with 1 the peninsular portion of Carnarvonshire from Bedd- i gelert to its south-western extremity. In each of these ifour sections will be found ample ground for the most 1 enterprising tourist to cover, during a round extending i over two, three or four weeks according as the progress I is leisurely or rapid, and the mode of travel largely I pedestrian or altogether vehicular, and the study of 1 country thdrough or cursory. In whatever direction he , goes, the English tourist will find Wales a land of varied I attractions, affluent in every charm that nature can ' unfold, romantic in legendary lore, and rich in relics of , its heroic past, historic and prehistoric. i iOur holiday this summer was spent in West Wales, i but to reach that section from Lancashire, we had to I I cross in swift railway journey the whole width of Mont- , , gonteryshire, which we have suggested as an important ' I portion of a circuit in East Wales. It is one of the I most famous of Welsh counties, and every glimpse we I had of it, from the windows of the railway-carriage , going and returning, tended to stimulate the desire to 1 make a closer acquaintance. The route from Blackburn I is by the London and North-Western Railway to Whit- church in Shropshire, some seventeen miles beyond I Crewe, and by the Cambrian Railway from Whitchurch 'across Wales to the west coast at Aberystwith. Through , carriages are available from Crewe forward to our destination. The railway service on the main Cambrian line is good and expeditious. We pass through Elles- mere and Oswestry, and enter Wales by crossing the 1 river lryrnwy at Llanymynech, as the Welsh names of I villages at once betoken. The Tyrnwy unites with the 'Severn a little lower down, and the railway traverses the Severn valley hence for many miles, passing through 1 the towns of Welshpool, Montgomery, and Newtown. I The valley is fertile and highly-cultivated, sheltered by I hills whose shapely masses make a bold background to 1 the landscape, well-watered by the. numerous streams ' which pour into the central river, and studded with fine i trees that lend their peculiar grace and cool tone to the ' scenery. We descry the red walls of Powys Castle just 'beyond Welshpool, and the high rock upon which stands I the ruins of the Castle of Montgomery near the station 'at that town. Near Ca,ersws is the Moat-lane Junction I of the branch line to Llanidloes, and here we part com- pany with the Severn. Caersws is the site of an ancient 1 British stronghold, and also of a Roman station. 1 Ascending the pretty dale of the Came river, we pass the spots where two desperate and memorable battles , were fought, between tho forces of contending native ; chieftains, the first in 949, near the village of Came, and the second at Mynydd Carno in 1077, by the army of Gruffydd ap Cynan with that of Trahaiarn ap Caradoc. We are now upon the eastward slope of the range of mountains which extends northward and south- ward and constitutes the watershed of Central Wales. i The railway rises on a stiff gradient for several miles, and about two miles beyond Carno station attains its summit level, some 700 feet above the sea. By means 1 of deep cuttings tunneling has been avoided in con- structing the line, and it is a circumstance worth 1 nantin• g that in the whole distance from Blackburn to 1 Aberystwith, by the L. and /I.W. and Cambrian route, I 'about 170 miles, we do not notice a single tunnel. West Wales, our chosen bourne, may be said to be entered ' with the commencement of the descent of these uplands. Our train glides down the incline at high speed, and having passed Llanbrynmair and Cemmes Road, we are sooa at the important station of Machynlleth, surrounded by mountains, with Ceder Idris, the loftiest mountain of the group, eight or nine miles away on the north, and 1 Plinhnaraon about an equal distance on the south. The I journey is continued along the banks of the Dovey river, tthrough a charming valley, to Glandovey Junction, where the Cambrian line is continued in two branches, 1 the one running on the north shore of the Dovey estuary Ito Aberdovey, Towyn, Barmouth and the north coast of Cardigan Bay; the other proceeding by the south shore to Borth, and terminating at Aberystwith. We take the latter, and arrive at our destination in the late after- noon, after a rather long journey of seven hours or so from Blackburn including an hour's wait at Crewe; but so attractive had been the scenery throughout, gilded by the sunshine of a glorious summer day, that we had not felt the railway ride at all wearisome. Aberystwith, as a town, does not impress the visitor much at first glance, but it gains on acquaintance. We Lancashire folk, accixstomed to our own sea-side water- ing-places with promenades stretching 1.1. to 2 miles in an unbroken line, and their architectural embellishments concentrated upon the imposing line of buildings upon their sea-fronts, may, if we looked for the same features in this resort on the west coast of Wales, be rather dis- appointed. But we were prepared to find Aberystwith less pretentious and on a smaller scale than Blackpool or Southport, but we also anticipated full compensation for artificial deficiencies in superior natural environ- ments, and in this respect it fully answers to our con- ception. Aberystwith is a quaint old town, if not a handsome one. Its sea-frontage is limited, bounded by the projecting rocks of Craiglas (Constitution Hill) at the north end of the little bay in front of the town, and by the little promontory on which the old Castle was built, at the south end. Between these points the Marine terrace and promenade extend, crescent-shaped; but the front is less than half a mile, and there is no room for the erection of more lodging-houses upon it. Behind the Castle-rock there is another bit of smooth shore, frequented by bathers who dispense with the assistance of the owners of the bathing-vans, and beyond that is the entrance to the little port, where the two rivers Rheidol and Ystwith discharge their fresh waters into the sea, within a space of a few score yards. Interposed between the channels of these rivers is the hill Pen Dinas, abrupt on the shoreward face, on the summit of which is a column of simple design erected to commemorate the British victories in the campaign of 1815. Visitors to Aberystwith who want to have a sea view from their rooms are accommodated in the houses and hotels on the Marine Terrace; and the re- mainder of the eligible provision for visitors is situated chiefly between the North Parade and the promenade. The railway station is in the rear of the central part of the town. Aberystwith, it should be remembered, is a very old market-town, and was not founded merely as a watering-place within the century, like many of its competitors. Two hundred years ago it is spoken of as "the most populous town of the whole county" of Cardigan. Its Castle stood many a siege before it was finally dismantled and reduced to a heap of ruins by order of Cromwell, about the time that Clitheroe Castle, in our own neighbourhood, was shattered with gun- powder. The older streets are narrow and irregular. Of modern erections, the buildings near the Castle, appropriated for the Aberystwith. College, were much the most imposing, but they were destroyed by fire last year, and still stand roofless and ruined; they are, how- I ever, to be restored. Besides the old parochial chapel, a I new church has just been consecrated, and of Noncon- formist churches or chapels half a score or more are provided, nearly all of them new, and some of them large.

The Sea is the best of patrons to Aberystwith, whose presence brings all other patronage. The shore of fine shingle slopes quickly, and even at low water, the sea is not many yards away, whilst when the tide is in, it sweeps grandly up, with crested waves, which break into foam along the sea-wall of the promenade. When the wind is high, blowing from the south-west, and there is a high tide, the appearance of the sea at Aberystwith is awe-inspiring. For a couple of days whiLstowe were there, a very strong wind blew from seaward, and we realised the description of Mr. Thomas Roscoe, in his "Wanderings through South Wales" : " At Aberystwith, the ocean shows its grandest charac-

teristics. A stiff gale blew for some days after my arrival, and as I sat in my quiet study, on the Terrace, I could see the grand waves come rolling in, each like a huge living mountain, bending its prouti head over the cavernous depth below, before taking its last landward leap in scattered feathery foam; another and another close behind, in endless succession, seemed as if the ocean's boundaries had beim() too narrow for the world of waters they contain." Our little party, consisting of Mr. and Mrs. W., Mrs. A. and the writer, had very pleasant quarters at Aberystwith in the North Parade. There are obvious advantages in an arrangement which secures the com- panionship of a couple of friends on a holiday round. The honeymoon is an exception to that; but subse- quently it is usually found that for a lady, when from home, to have nobody to talk to of an evening, or indeed, at any hour of the day, except her own husband, is a terrible infliction. But when a party of four is made up, two wives and two husbands, there is not only all the pleasure of confidential confab, between the ladies whilst shopping or sauntering, but the further satisfac- tion for a lady of claiming the assistance of another gentleman in pointing her criticism upon any peccadillo or weak notion of her own liege lord. In the social circle, the witticisms are greatly stimulated by the presence of some good-natured fellow who will submit to be the butt. A good deal of fun and light raillery went on in our small party in West Wales, but at whose expense most of the jokes were cracked the writer does not deem it expedient to mention. Although the sea, in all its changeful moods, is always a conspicuous object, and an invigorating influence at Aberystwith, it is far from being the sole attraction. Compared with most other sea-side resorts, it offers an exceptional variety of delightful walks on the cliffs and inland excursions. The visitor's first impulse is to see the place near at hand from various points of view, and for this the walks laid out in the Castle grounds, over- looking the south end of the town and the little port, are well suited. Pen Dinas is easily scaled, and affords a wide and Most pleasing prospect all round, including the valleys of the Rheidol and the Ystwith between which it stands. At the back of the town on the other side of the Rheidol are smaller hills which give different aspects. The walks will soon extend to Constitution Hill, whose heights command the position of the town on the north-east. The hill is accessible by a convenient path, which skirts the scarped termination of the hill several hundred feet above the sea washing its base. This walk along the cliff, for a mile or so, to where the hill descends on the further side to a bit of level strand, is truly exhilarating. The morning on which we took this stroll, the weather was faultless; sea and 'sky were alike free from mist or cloud, and each a vast expanse of blue—the former a dark indigo tint on the horizon,, and the latter a gleaming. sapphire. The coast of Cardigan Bay from Bardsea Island to St. David's Head was dis- tinct in every feature; and the headlands and isolated rocks which break the line of the Carnarvonshire shore stood out as bold landmarks. But that which arrested the attention was the peak of Snowdon, nearly fifty miles away on the .north, clearly visible above the luminous haze which lay upon the land, and surrounding it some of the other mountains of Snowdonia. It is only when the atmospheric conditions are especially favourable that Snowdon is seen from the hills around Aberystwith as we saw it on Thursday, August 19th, 1886.

A short walk by the bank of the Rheidol in the rear of Aberystvrith brings us to Llanbadarn Bridge, whence to the village of Llanbadarn is another half mile. The village is of the ordinary Welsh type, but the Church has a peculiar interest. It is not only the parish church to Aberystvrith, but it is the mother church of all the churches in this part of the Principality. For a. Welsh church it is a large edifice, consisting of nave, deep transept a and chancel, and a very massive tower rising in the centre, terminated with a dwarf spire. The spacious churchyard, which is some feet above the road, is shaded by large old trees. We inspected the interior of the church, which has recently been handsomely restored. All the woodwork and the roof are new, but the ancient walls, arches, and narrow lancet windows remain. The fabric dates from about the 12th century, and has the simplicity of feature of the transi- tional period from Norman to Gothic. The tradition of Llanbadarn Church as told by the old chroniclers is as follows :—"Llan-Badarn-Vawr, that is, Great St. Patern's, who was an Armorican, and governed the church here by feeding, and fed it by governing. To whose memory a Church and Bishop's See were here consecrated, but the bishoprick (as Roger Hoveden writes) fell to decay long since, for that the people had most barbarously slain their pastor." We might deem this story mythical, but that there is standing witness to the extreme antiquity of this foundation. In the churchyard, opposite the south porch of the church, are to be seen two ancient stone Crosses, much battered and weather-worn, but still exhibiting the ornamentation of scrollwork which marks the Christian Crosses of the primitive age of English Church history. These Llan- badarn Crosses are, indeed, of the same type as the three Crosses in Whalley Churchyard, supposed to have been set up to signalise the foundation of the church there by Paulinus in the seventh century. All authorities agree that the Crosses ornamented in this fashion belong to the period named. St. Padarn lived in the sixth cen- tury, and he is supposed to have founded the monastery which subsequently existed here. Vestiges of the monastic buildings are yet to be seen. Llanbadarn ranked as a city in 987, and was destroyed by the Danes. Aberystvrith, castle and town, rose after Llan- badarn had been reduced to 'a small village, yet it has a record dating back to Norman times. The favourite excursion of tourists at Aberystvrith is the drive to the far-famed Devil's Bridge. Many thousand persons visit the spot every year. Our driver when we went there stated that he had himself taken nearly 900 visitors since May. The drive to Devil's Bridge and back, 27 miles, and the stoppage of two or three hours at the Bridge to explore the wonders of the place, and to dine, occupy a day, and, if the weather be propitious, it is a day of great enjoyment. The road taken in going to the Devil's Bridge gradually ascends the hilis on the left bank of the Rheidol, until, nine miles from Aberystwith, an elevation of about 900 feet is gained. At several points on the road, looking west,- ward, charming views are obtained .of the Rheid9l's serpentine course through the diluvlal flat, covering the middle of the vale, to the distant ocean. Further up, the valley narrows to a glen, between lofty heights almost too steep to climb. At one spot we alight, and walking a few yards from the road, stand on the edge of the steep, and look down at the river flowing far below, through the midst of a strip of cultivated land. This is a striking and singular picture. The road we taaverse now descends for a couple of miles,and we reach the hotel close by the Devil's Bridge; from the railed terrace in front of the inn we overlook the wooded gorge below the falls, and at the opposite side see the Rheidol dashing down its rocky channel, in a series of cascades, to the foot of the cliffs, where the nearer stream, the Mynach, unites with it. Both rivers are in volume after recent rain, and the scene is unimaginably grand. After luncheon we crossed the modern bridge which is flung across the chasm above the ancient Devil's Bridge, and descended by a path on the right• the position from which the two bridges, the deep cleft in the rock, and the stream at the bottom struggling through the narrow passage it has cut for itself, are best beheld. The spectacle differs little from the description written ninety years since by the author of a small volume I have,—the Rev. Richard Warner,. of Bath—whose "Walk through Wales" was accomplished in the year 1797. Mr. Warner wrote : " c. and I proceeded to explore the horrors of the Devil's Bridge. Our first observations were made from the bridge. This consists of a single arch, 29 feet in the span, thrown over the original one (which still remains) in the year 1753. The old arch was built [not by his Satanic Majesty, but) by the monks of Strata Florida Abbey, (a religious house ten miles from hence, the picturesque ruins of which still remain) about the end of the 11th century. It is called in Welsh Pont-ar- Mynach, the bridge Of the Mynach, and Pont-ar-Diawl, the bridge of the Devil, vulgar superstition asserting Satan to be the constructor of it. The chasm that yawns under these arches is so overhung with wood, that the eye with difficulty catches even a partial view of the gloomy abyss below." "In order to obtain a nearer and less interrupted view of this tremendous fissure, and the torrent that rushes through it, we proceeded over the bridge; and turning quickly round to the right hand, descended an abrupt and perilous path that conducted us to the base of the rocks on the eastern side of the arch. Language is but ill calculated to convey an accurate idea of the scene which is here presented to the eve. The awful height of thej fissure, which the bridge bestrides 120 feet above the observer, rendered doubly gloomy by its nar- rowness, and the wood which overhangs it; the stunning noise of the torrent thundering at his feet, ' and struggling through black, opposing rocks, which its ceasless impetuosity has worn into shapes strange and grotesque, fill the mind with a mingled but sublime emotion of astonishment, terror, and delight. Having gratified our curiosity here, we clambered up the per- pendicular path, and going in a left-hand direction from the 'bridge, about 200 yards, pursued a winding descent that leads to a rocky projection, which commands a view of the noble cataracts to the westward of the arch. Here the Mynach, bursting at once upon the eye in all its terrific majesty, is seen throwing itself down' rugged rocks at least 210 feet, in four separate, tremen- dous falls. The first is a leap of nearly 20 feet; after which it is received by a deep basin, out of which it pours with greater violence down a second fall of 60 feet. Its third attempt decreases again to 20 feet, and here it falls amongst broken rocks, which in vain pre- sent themselves as barriers to its passage. Then rushing over a projecting ledge with wonderful velocity, it tumbles headlong down a descent of 110 feet, and then hurries through a rocky channel to unite its waters with the Rheidol, which plunges from the oppo- site mountains with similar grandeur and impetuosity." Since Mr. Warner's visit paths .have been cut at no small expense, and a long wooden stair, nearly vertical, fixed on the precipitous rocks on the further side of the falls, which enable visitors who have the requisite nerve to descend to the very bottom of the chasm, to cross the. Mynach by a wooden bridge, and to ascend on the nearer side by similar zigzag paths and many flights of rock-hewn steps, with guarded projections for viewing the falls from every part of vantage, so that the inspection of this natural wonder may be most complete, and perfectly enjoyed. The charges for these

facilities and for admission to the grounds is a shilling, and there are few sights upon which that sum can be so worthily expended. We might mention that the Hafod estate, of 14,000 acres, in which the scenery above described is situated, for a short time belonged to the late Sir Henry de Hoghton of Hoghton Tower, who bought it from the Duke of Newcastle for £92,000, and sold it to Mr. Chambers, of Llanelly, for £102,000. Sir Henry de Hoghton was High Sheriff of Cardiganshire in 1849. The route in returning to Aberystwith is for two or three miles by a cross-road that winds round to the main road from Llanidloes to Aberystwith, passing over a bare plateau forming the base of Plinlimmou, which i 5 ascended from this side. At Pont Erwyd the road crosses the Rheidol river, and from the bridge and .the inn a' little further on the river is seen pursuing its course over a rocky bed between perpendicular cliffs, turning at a right angle where a stream pours into it in a fine water- fall. We next pass the Goginan lead mines, high in the moorlands, with their immense water-wheel, and begin to descend from this altitude, just then enshroudedlo mist, along a road out on the shoulder of the mountain,- gaining views, which become clearer as we emerge from the mist, of another glen-like valley, many hundred fee below. The scenery throughout the drive is remarkablY interesting. Halting at a wayside inn—l think it was at the village of Capelßangor,—our driver, a witty, good- natured young man, well up in the lore of the district, brought out of the house for our inspection a veritable relic of the British aborigines. It was a spade, rudely shaped out of a piece of hard oak-wood, which was one of several wooden spades and ancient implements found a few years ago by the miners in an old working, not far from the place we were passing through. These mines *were originally worked by the Romans and the native Britons, and there can be no doubt that these oaken spades were made and used by these early excavators, and were left in the mine when It was abandoned by them. The spade was much the same shape as a modern English one, but only about half the size. One fine sultry afternoon, Mr. W. and I set off to vi-91' the noted "Thunder Hole," or Monk's Cave, which ig five miles by the coast from Aberystwith. Most touristS drive to the vicinity of the cliff out of which the Cave has been scooped by the sea, but we preferred to walk the distance. The road is up the -istwith valley, branch' ing off by the Cardigan turnpike. We took a train on the Milford line to the first station out of Aberystwith, about two miles. It was quite as far as we should like to ride on that railroad, for the jolting in its carriageS is like that we remember when a boy, riding in a' springless cart on a rough moorland track. Aftebrwards we had several miles of a pleasant walk, the road ascending a hill, until we obtained a wonderful prospect, looking across the Ystwith valley—Plinlimmen rising centrally in the long range of mountains bounding the horizon and reaching from the south-eastern angle of Cardiganshire to the coast near Glandovey. Turnip& to the right by a bye-road, through farmyards ano fields fora mile or so, we strike the cliff at a point wheys it can be descended, and proceeding some distance en the shore, find first a minor cave, and then the great cavernous opening of the Monk's Cave. Its other name of "Thunder Hole" is suegestive of the loud thuhderous boom of the waves in tempestuous weather when the tide is high, as they sweep into the cave, and burst upwards through the opening to the level of the cliff. Of course at such seasons cave and shore are un- approachable ; the inrush of the mighty surgini ocean can only be witnessed from above, and the sounu will be more impressive than the sight. The sea was calm , and the tide down on our visit to the spot, so that Ws could safely enter the cave and mark the singular aspect of the cliff, which has been thus worn into holle° chambers, as well as the pillar of rock standing in front of the entrance, and the masses of flat rocks which forra a rude broken terrace between the sea at low water and the cliff. Having surveyed the place we started for home, intending to return along the shore. But the beach for miles here is strewn with splintered fragment of rock, large pebbles and larger boulders, beds of level rock • covered with a thick matting of sea-weed, with deep crevices filled with sea-water between, and reefs of slat/ istratum whose slippery shelves and sharp edges are bet° painful, and dangerous to walk upon. After doing a mile of this sort of road, and seeing nothing else as far as the eye could reach, the writer formed a sudden but definitive resolution to scale the cliff and make for Aberystwith by any circuitous path over the hills rather than encounter the risk of dislocated ankles and other painful effects to the feet which might mar the rest eg the holiday. This I did, and found a much more coin fortable, though less direct, line of travel by inland pathS and country roads, whereby, after seven mileg, ef walking, I got to what Lancashire folk call the" far-end." Friend W., more venturesome or heroic, declined to follow the writer up the cliff, and persevered in his grimage by the beach. He, however, found, like Noala'S dove, no rest for the sole of his foot," and his sorro'NS, surpassing those of Werter, have been described in gra- phic verse. He nevertheless had the satisfaction of coming in first by several minutes, having saved a couple of miles of distance at the expense of racked bones and strained sinews. The exhaustion of my alloted space compels the rapid summarising of the remainder of my Notes. Amongst other excursions we spent an afternoon at Towyn, a pretty village afid embryo watering-place, on the coast between Aberdovey and Barmouth. Another half day we devoted to exploring the Llyfnant valley, starting from Glandovey, whither we went by train. AS the upper end of this secluded glen is a waterfall. Aber. dovey, at the mouth of the Dovey estuary, and Borth, on the opposite shore, we cannot stay to notice, beyond remarking that both are pleasantly situated, and receive every year an increasing number of visitors. Upes another day we took the Cambrian train to Machyrillethp and went on by the" toy railway," as tourists call the little mineral Imes in these parts,-2ft. 3in. gauge—to Corns, five or six miles up a winding wooded vale, in which our miniature train traversed its narrow road 011 the brink of a beautiful river. We walked from the mining village of Corns to the foot of Ceder Idris, the craggy spur of which was a striking feature in ite cloud-capt altitude, and saw the lake of Tal-y-Llyn se• turning by the same way to our starting-point. 'ibe°' we went on to Barmouth, and spent several days in seeing the celebrated spots around that centre. The beauty of the walks and drives in the vicinity of Bar- mouth is known to many readers of ours. The "pane" rama" view of the Mawddach estuary, with the stir- • rounding mountains, from the hill a mile or so front Barmouth, is world-famed. Some hours of one of our happiest days were spent in going up this glorious val- ley of the Mawddach to Dolgelly, looking about the village, which has mighty Cader Idris for its majestie back-ground, and enjoying the shady loveliness of OW "Torrent Walk," watching at leisure from the manY points of view the fall of the crystal water of the river down its numberless succession of cascades. The day preceding our homeward journeY we took the train from Barmouth to Port Madoc, on the Carnarvonshirs coast, seeing as we passed the proud towers and massive walls of Harlech Castle on itS precipitous rock, and drove from there tor Bedd- gelert, through the magnificent pass of Aberglaslyn.. The weather on that day matched the scenery, and both were superb. The peak of Snowdon was conspicuous in our front for several miles after turning the corner of the round near Tramadoc, and was a sublime spectacle, flanked by other great mountains. Beddgelert has graces of its own which were not overlooked, and whilst two of our party strolled up to the cascades of Nant Colwyn on the Carnarvon road, the other two walked on up the valley to the right as far as Llyn-y-Ddinas. The drive back to Port Madoc in the afternoon was fully appreciated. The splendours of Snowdonia were never more richly displayed, nor beheld under more fortunate conditions. West Wales, in fact, is beautiful beyond the power of language to paint in whatever direction you traverse its vales of sweet waters, or gaze on its "delectable mountains," and those English people who neglect such scenery as exists in every part of the Principality, whilst spending their vacations in continental haunts, do 3 wrong to their native Isle, no less than to themselves.

THE SINGING FrNcisr.—All amateurs of song birds owe a debt of gratitude to Dr. Russ for having practically discovered the merits of this bird. Vieillot described 3 grey singing finch bred in captivity as long ago as 1790, but subsequently the bird seems to have disappeared from the market, and to some extent from the cognisance of subsequent authors. When the demand for foreign cage birds increased, about the years 1860 to 1865, dealer often mistook the grey singing finch for the female of the ultramarine finch or cornbasou. Few of these unpre- tending grey birds arrived, fewer still were sold; dealer; and amateurs left them unnoticed, and so they migbt have remained if Dr. Russ had not made this finch, like every other available foreign cage-bird a subject of care- ful study in his aviary. The rich music of the grey singiA finch's song, which would scarcely be uttered in a bi.ra dealers stare-cages, could not escape the doctor's :notice and the attention of amateurs was soon drawn to hinai with the result of, for a time, increasing the demand an price. When imported in larger numbers, the grey 51g- ing finches often arrived sickly, and many died during the voyage, or soon after, whereby the cost of the Sur," vivors becomes considerable. Brilliant and gaudy n°''' oured birds sell ra.pidl3, ; and dealers find that the sober" coloured little songsters are, after all, only known t° that minority of amateurs who' study books. Thus, a dealer who imports these songsters may sell a few at a remunerative price, and find the others dying in his hantlt The importation, therefore, decreased of late years tc extent much to be regretted. When once fairly reccv.er; ed from the fatigue of the voyage, the grey singina finches hire very well, in a moderate warm temperature, on a diet of millet and canary seed, with green-Milt:2i and a very little egg-food now and then. They br without difficulty, but best in a roomy cage, building an open nest much like that of a canary. The young bade are reared on scalded or soaked millet-seed and egg-fel or fresh ant's eggs, and the pairs live in great affectios for each other. The plumage of the female resemb.lee closely that of the male, but the brown marks are a triß.. less d/stinct.—From Canaries and Cage Birds, for Septa,' ber.
