div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. SECRET SERVICE 3,foNEv.—The Marquis of SALISBURY in moving the second reading of the Secret Service (Repeal) Bill, said the measure had for its object the repeal of the statute rejecting the regulations of the expenditure of secret service money, the amount fixed being £lO,OOO a year. A discussion had been raised in the other House in respect of the money, and it had been supposed that it bad been used for the purposes not suitable for the secret service. It was discovered that this supposition was incorrect, and that so far as the money could not be served for secret ser- vice it was. utilised in the payment of messengers, clerks, and so forth. On the whole it was thought desirable that this sum should be placed under the control of Parlisment. The bill was reed a second time. Their Lordships adjourned until Thursday. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. RUSSIAN APPROVAL OF THE REGENCY. SOFIA, SATUNDAY.—The Regency to-day issued a decree ordering the opening of the National Assembly on the 13th inst. The delay is due to the fact of the Regents and Ministers who accompanied Prince Alexander to the fron- tier not being able to return in time for the opening to-day, as originally fixed. To-day being the feast of St. Alexan- der Vevski, and the fife day of the Czar, a Te Deum was sung in the Cathedral. The following coneatulatory tele- gram was subsequently despatched by the Deputies to Prince Alexander at Darmstadt :—" The National Deputies assembled here on the occasion of the lite of your Highness offer up hearty prayers to almighty tied for the preserva- tion of your health, and wish yen long life. We are deeply grieved at your absence from your beloved coantry Bul- garia, and earnestly desire to see among us our hero and Prince, the defender of our national liberty and indepen- dence. Long live your Highness for the glorv, honour, and greatnese of Bulgaria." The telegram was signed by 200 Deputies. Similar messages have been sent to the Prince from other parts of the country, and the officers of all the garrisons have also telegraphed congratulations to his Highness on the part of the Bulgarian army. Monsignor Clement and M. Zankoff are detained in their houses, but are permitted to see their friends. Solna, MONDAY.—It is stated that the Russian Diplo- matic Agent leas resolved an answer to the propositions of the Bulgarian Government. It is to the effect that Russia will recognise the Regency and assist in consolidating the union of Bulgaria and Rournelia on condition that no acts of violence are committed. The Busier' Government fur- ther advises that public opinion should be allowed te calm down before the election of a new Prince is proceeded with. This reply, however, has not been communicated to the Bulgarian Government, as the relati•ne between the Ministers and the Russian Agents are very strained. In the preliminary sittings of the Chamber yesterday several deputies proposed to send a despatch to the Czar requesting a reply from his Mtjesty, and not through the medium of the Diplomatic Agent. The session of the kobranje was opened this morning by the Regents. A deputy rose and exclaimed 'Long live Prince Alexaader," the Prince's name being received with prolonged cheering. VIENNA, Morentor.—Aceording to a rumour circulated in diplomatic circles in Vienna, the negotiations of the three Imperial Cahinets have yielded a favourable result, and there are now prospects of an agreement being shortly ar- rived at relative 110 the common attitude in the Bulgarian question, at least with regard to the measures to be next adopted. The Russian Cabinet, it is said, has resolved to give up the plan of procedure by itself in Bulgaria, and in- tends to meat the whole question on the basis of the Treaty of Berlin, and to sabmit it to the consideration of Eurepe. With regard to the despatch of a Russian special cemmis- eery to Bulgaria, it is assorted that the mission will be carried out in an undemonstrative fashion. On the one hand regard will be had to the greater intereette of Russia in Bulgaria, while, on the other hand, the susceptibilities of the interested Cabinets and of the Bulgarian people will be spe red.—" Times." CONSTANTINOPLE. TTIBSDAY.—The representatives of the Powers have presented the reply of their respective Powers to the last Circular Note of the Porte. The terms are identieal, and it sets forth that the departure of Prince Alexander does not change the political sitaation in Bul- garia, nor does it constitute any infringement of existing international engagomente. The Parte is assured that no foreign military intervention will take place in Bulgaria, the Powers haying received gaaranteee and assurances from Russia to that dire. The Porte has not yet taken any ac- tion in respect to a new raler for Bulgarkt, preferring to let the Powers act in concert for the choice of a prince. Sorel, MONDAY. —ll O-day, after the opening speech of the Council of gee Regency had been read, the Sobranje elected M. Givkoff president, and it was decided to proceed to-morrow to the appointment of a committee to draft the reply to the address. Sores, TrasDas. Prince Alexander replied to-day to the telegram sent to him by the deputies congratulating him on the oceasion of his name day, and also to that of the officers begging hire to return. The Prince thanks the de- duties and officers alike for the mark of devotion. which has deeply touched him. THE CHOLERA. ROME, TUESDAY. The cholera returns for the last 24 hours are :—Torre Dell Annunziate, 13 cases, 3 deaths ; Castellamare, 1 and 1; Santagnello, 1 and 1; San Marco in Lamis, 12 and ; Putignano' 12 and 6; Venice, 2 and 1; Ferrara. 11 and 5; Copparo,l2 and 4; Ravenna, 12 arid 6; Padua, 4 and 1. THE CAMPAIGN IN BURMAH. RANGOON, MONDAY.—A reconnoitring party from Tan- tabin, north of Mlevraybo, recently surprised an encampment of daHite, and in the skirmish that ensued six of the instil*. gents were killed. General Sir Herbert Macpherson has started for Mandalay, but Sir Charles Bernard did pot ac- company him. ENGLAND AND EGYPT. CAIRO, MONDAY.—During the Feast of Bairam large quantities of seditious proclamations, specially directed against the English, were circulated among the natives, with the result that many assaults upon Europeans took place. Nnkhtar Pasha, for alleged political reasons, declines pro- ceeding to Port Said to meet the Duke of Connaught on his arrival there on his way to India. CONSTAMTINOPLE, SATURDAY.—Rnmours are current to- night in official ciroleathat within the last few days re- newed attention has been directed to the Egyptian question, and there is revived irritation at the prolonged British occu- pation. GERMANY AND RUSSIA.

The Lord Chancellor took tbe chair at 4-0. EXCISE OFFICEES.—Mr. W. L. JACKSON, in reply to Mr. Tomlinson's question as to the grievances of the excise officers, said the case of these officers bad been fully con- sidered by the present Chancellor of the Exclnquer and himself, and they had come to the conclusion that the ser- vice had received fair and liberal consideration and that no substantial grounds for complaint existed. CIVIL SERvICE INQUIRY.—Tbe CHANCELLOR Of the Ex. CHEQUER, in reply to Mr. Puleston, said :—Tbe operation of the Playfair scheme has long been a subject of controversy, and the Government are of opinion that it, operation may be usefully inquired into as part of the general inquiry ' into the Civil Service establishment, which they have de- cided immediatiely to initiate. The Government have de- termined to appoint a Royal Commission to investigate the public departments of the State—(a laugh)—more particu- larly with regard to their clerical establishment. The Commission will inquire into the numbers, hours of labour, superannuation, cost of the staff, and the administration, regulation, and organisation of the offices. They will state whether the werk of the different offices is effectually and economically performed ; whether it may be simplified ; whether the method of procedure can be improved ; and , whether the system of control is deficient or unnezeesarily elaborate. As ten years have now elapsed since the adop- tion of the Playfair scheme the time has come when the working of that pheme may with advantage be reviewed. The Commission will therefore report whether the scheme has been fairly tried ; whether its provisions have met the requirements of the service and deserve confirmation ; and whether any modifications are needed to give it com- plete development. Lastly, they will examine the non- effective charge of the Civil Service, and advise whether the present pension scheme regulations are equitable alike to the State and to its servants. The names of the Commissioners were—Sir Matthew White Ridley, chairman—(hear, hear); —Lords Brownlow, Lingen, and Rothschild; Messrs. G. Scleter-Booth, Henry Fowler, C. Lewis. A. O'Connor, P. Rylands, Sir E. Guinnesa ; Messrs. Cleghorn (director North-Eastern Railway), Harvey (secretary Messrs. Glynn, Mills, and Co.), and Mitford (late Assistant-Commis- sioner of Public Works) : and Mr. Walpole, Permanent Assistant Secretary to the India Office, secretary. (Hear, hear). FACTORY INsPgcTorts.—ln answer to Mr. Byron Reesl, Mr. Mirranws said that no official report had been made to the Factory Department of the Homo Office that the number of factory inspectors was inadequate to the per- formance of their duties, although various trades councils had requested that the number of inspectors should be in- creased. INDIAN CIVIL SERVICE INQUIRY.—Sir Joint GORET, in reply to Sir Roper Lethbridge, stated that the inquiry in India into the civil services would be conducted by a Com- mission. No information as to the actual composition of the Commission had been received by the Secretary of State. it was intended that some of the members should be natives, and that the Commission should extend the in- , quiry over various parts of India and amongst all classes of the people.
SUPPLY.

The House having gone into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, On the vote of £30,000 for foreign and other secret set, vice, Mr. BRADLAUGH asked for some statement as to the amonnts of secret service money expended in the different departments of the State.—The CMANCELLOR of the Ex- CHEQUER said he could not give the information asked for, for the reason that it would be against the principle of abso- lute secrecy. He did not think the protection of life and property could be provided for unless Parliament voted the money.—Sir G. CAMPBELL held that it would be impossible to carry on a great Empire without secret service money.— On a division the vote was carried by 159 to 54. After discussion, the vote of £12,780 for the Scotch Fishery Board was agreed to; as were also the votes of £2400 for the Lunacy Commissioners in Scotland, £3089 for the registrar of births, deaths, and marriagesin Scotland, and £3340 for the Scotch Board of Supervision. On the vote of £7560 for the Household of the Lord Lieutenant ef Ireland, Mr. T. W. RUSSELL moved the reduction of the vote by £1,563, the item for Queen's Plates in Ireland.—Col. Noaite opposed the reduction, declaring that if carried it would have an Injuribus effect upon the breed of horses in Ireland. —Mr. Laßoucamen, in supporting the amendment, submit- ted that tie encouragement of racing was only calculated to develop a weedy race of horses, and that it would be far more useful to lend State aid in the breeding of sowed animals for the cart and for the road.—Sir G. CAMPBELL looked upon the vote as an attempt to corrupt Ireland wholesale.—On a division the amendment was rejected by 178 to 36. Dr. TANNER moved to reduce the vote by £789 for the office of chaplain to the Lord Lieutenant.—Negatived by 179 to 55. Mr. CLANCY moved to reduce the vote by £1,079, the cost of the Ulster King of Arms, which he regarded as a piece of mediaval mummery.—Mr. CONYBEARE was re- ceived with groans and spoke amidst continuous cries of “Divide."—The House divided at midnight, and rejected the amendment by 172 aajtinst 62. Mr. DILLON moved the reduction of the vote by £6O, for insignia and banners of the Order of St. Patrick. He said the people of Ireland objected to Ray this money, and characterised the Order as a monstrous fraud. (Irish cheers.)—The amendment was rejected by 156 votes to 65, andlthe vote was agreed to. Mr. SaaTole observed that the next vote was for the office of Chief Setretary to the Lord Lientenent, and as an Irish member proposed on that vote to raise the question of the Barbavilla murders, he hoped, considering the late hour of the evening, that the Government would allow that vote to be postponed.—Sir M. H. BEACH agreed, on condition that certain other Irish votes of a non-contentious character were taken. (Hear, hear.)—Several other Irish votes having been passed, The Chairman proceeded with the English votes. Ma Deame protested, stating that many English members had been informed that the Irish votes would occupy the whole of tbe evening, and had left the kouse.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER did not think such a slight con- sideration ought to be allowed to impede business. .(Minis- terial cheers.)—Mr. Cone-names moved to report progreere remarking that the noble lord was fall of serprisee.—Mr. J. Mr. Maws de- fended the action taken by Irish members. Mr. T. P. O'Coermon taunted Lord R. Churehill with having, by his discourtesy that night, taught the Irish members the spirit in which to conduct business. The Committee divided For the motion, 46; against, 148. Mr. DILLIVIN moved the Chairman do now leave the chair.—Mr.LalagYestrongly condemned the course taken by the tSiovernment. Lord R. ST. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY.—Prince William of Prussia, on his arrival at Brest, Litoe sk, was received by the Em- peror, the Czarewitch, and the other Grand Dukes at the station, where a guard of honour was drawn up. The Prince, accompanied by the Emperor, afterwards drove to the fortress to salute the Czarina. At the gala dinner which followed, Prince William occupied the place at the right hand of ber Majesty. GERMAN COLONIAL ENTERPRISE. BERLIN, MONDAY.—The German General Congress for the promotion of the interests of Germany across the ocean was opened to-day by Herr Peters. Dr. Jammaseh said the object of the Congress was to form a strong political party, resolved to support the colonial alms of the Imperial Go- vernment. Four sections were formed to discuss (1), prac- tical colonisation ; (2), German emigration; (3), German missions; and (4). the preservation of the German language and customs in foreign regions. ILLNESS OF PRINCE BISMARCK. BERLIN, SUNDAY.—Prince Bismarck's health has im- proved but slightly. He is able to rise from his sofa and walk about, but for a few minutes only. This delay in his convaleecence has made his intended departure from Varzin qaite uncertain. Nor will he be able to attend the opening of the Reichstag next Thursday. THE LABOUR QUESTION IN CANADA. PHILADELPHIA, MONDAY.—The Provincial Government and the Montreal Colonisatian Society have made arrange- ments for the return to Canada of 105 French Canadian families frcm Massachusetts. Fifty thousand acres have been secured in the Lievre and La Rouge valleys, in the Ottawa district. FAILURE OF THE LABRADOR FISHERIES. GREAT DESTITUTION. HALIFAX, SUNDAY.—The" Halifax Herald" states that information received from Newfoundland confirms the re- ports of the utter failure of the Labrador and shore fisheries. The Labrador catch is one third of the average, and not enough to cover the transport and the supplies advanced to the fishermen. Sixty-five thousand people. who are depen- dent on the Labrador fisheries, stretching over 3,000 miles of coast, are in actual destitution, and looking to Govern- ment aid from starvation during the coming autumn and winter. It is asserted that the sNewfoundland shore fisher- men will be almost as destitute as those engaged in Labra- dor, and accordisg to a reliable estimate, a hundred thousand persons will be partially or wholly dependent on Govern- ment Support during the winter. TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN NEW YORK STATE. SIXTEEN EXCURSIONISTS KILLED. NEW YORE, TI;TESDAY.—An excursion train on the New York, Chicago, and St. Louis Railway, while proceeding to- day from Erie to Niagara Falls, came into collision with a freight train near Silver Creek, New York State. The smok- ing car was completely telescoped, and thirteen of the excur- sionists were killed and many others injured. NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY.—The accident to the excursion train at Silver Creek yesterday occurred through the engine ariver disregarding his instructions as to shunting. The last reports state that sixteen of the unfortunate passengers were killed. COLLAPSE OF A BRIDGE: SEVEN LIVES LOST. VIENNA, VVEDN)3SDAY.—A. telegram from Ostran. in Moravia states, that a suspension bride over the Os- travitza there gave way suddenly just as a squadron of Uhlans was about to cross. A considerable number of peo- ple were on the bridge when it collapsed. and they were hurled into the river. Up to the time of telegraphing seven persons had been taken out of the water dead, and eight more had been rescued in an injured condition. One of the Uhlans was drowned. THE CATHOLICS IN CHINA. ROME, THURSDA.T.—Acting upon instructions from the Vatican, Monsignor Agliardi has suspended the arrange- ments for his departure to Pekin. Meanwhile the Vatican awaits further communications from the French Govern- ment explaining the steps which it purposes to take in pm- suance af the understanding recently arrived at. MR. GLADSTONE'S RETURN. VIENNA, THURSDAY.—The " Fremdenblatt " announces that Mr. Gladstone, while visiting the Monastery at Reich- ersburg, in the Inn district, stated that the impending de- bate in the British Parliament on Mr. Parnell's Tenants' Relief Bill compelled him to hasten his return to London.

PRINCE ALEXANDER.—RepIving to a question from Sir Henry Tyler' Sir JAMES FERGIISSON said: Her Majesty's Government have no official information that would justify them in stating that the Emperor or Government of Russia have compelled Prince Alexander to abdicate the Throne of Bulgaria. They therefore cannot make the assumption on what the hon. 'umbel's question rested. Prince Alexander was seized and carried out of the country by an act of mutiny and treachery on the part of a portion of his army. He returned to Bulgaria, and thereafter abdicated for reasons which he stated in a public document. lam unable to undertake at any definite date to lay before the House the communications that have already passed on this subject; I have already submitted to the House that in the opinion of her Majesty's Goverment no good purpose, but probably the reverse, would be served thereby. We know that the constitutional forms proper to the occasion are being fol- lowed by the Regency, and that all the different parties in Bulgaria appear to be determined to co-operate for the maintenance of peace.
ENGLISH FISEINO BOATS DETAINED IN FRAKCE.—II answer to Mr. Round, Sir J. Funoussorr said he had reeeived a telegram to the effeet that the fishermen and boats detained at Havre had been released.
Tan ADDREES.—The Comptroller of the Household (Lord Arthur Hill) presented her Majesty's gracious reply to the Address.

SUPPLY.—IRISH ESTIMATES. The House having gone into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, upon the vote to complete the sum of £40,866 for the office of the Chief Secretary to the Lord- Lieutenant of Ireland, Mr. TIIITE called attention to the Barbavilla case, complaining that the juries before whom the prisoners had been tried were packed by the officers of She Crown, and convicted at a time of panic on evidence of the most untrustworthy ebaracter.—Mr. J. F. O'BRIEN also urged the necessity of further inquiry into this case.—Mr. DONALD Streavaei likewise appealed to the Government to permit an independent investigation into the cases that had been referred to.—Mr. SEXTON, in supporting the request for inquiry, asked for any report Sir Redvers Buller may have submitted as to the payment of rent in the district to which he had been sent.—The CHAIRMAN here interposed, and ruled that the hon. member was not in order in canvass- ing the mission of Sir. R. Bailer on this vote. Several other members were called to order in the debate which en- sued, the Hesse sitting till a late hour. The discussion on the vote for the Office of the Chief Secretary was kept up till the rising of the House, when the vote was passed. That single rote was all that the Govern- ment obtained as the result of Tuesday's work—from five o'clock till half-past two in the morning. , HOUSE OF COMMOIIB.—WEDNESDAY. . The Speaker took the chair at 12-15. SIIPPLY.—The Government, having only secured one vote in the whole of Tuesday's sitting, were naturally impatient to make more progress with the Estimates in the House of Commons on Wednesday. The ingenuity and detail, how- ever, with which the Parnellites, in spite of many checks from the Chair, managed to defeat the Ministerialist wishes evoked an emphatic protest from Sir M. H. Beach, who complained that during three hours there had been a con- stant iteration of the same points and continuous attempts to enlarge the scope of the discussion beyond the limits laid down by the Chairman. After this the vote for Irish Local Government was agreed to. One English member, Mr. Cossham. participated in the Parnellite experience of re- straint from the Chair, and was, in fact, obliged to resume his seat under the rule forbidding irrelevance and tedious repetition. On a second vote for Public Works in llreland, the Chancellor of the Exchequer interposed with another protest against the discussion in "immense detail and with incessant repetition of every imaginable griev- ance that any member could have to complain of." This proceeding he complained of as calculated to cripple the power of the Government, and their physical and mental energy to deal with these Irish Questions, which he assured tqe hon. members the Government seriously intended to pla sithin the control of the Irish people themselves next ' year, so far as they considered themselves entitled to so under the mandate of the country at the last election. The Ministerial appeal was made in vain to the Parnellit,es, who questioned the noble lord's interpretation of the country's verdict, declined to assume that his measures next session would satisfy them, and maintained their right in the mean- time to bring forward their grievances in detail. "You must have patience," said Mr. Molloy. The vote for Public Works, however, was agreed to shortly afterwards. On the vote of £5,126 for the Irish Registrar-General's Department, Mr. A. O'Coxxou complained that the way in which the money voted to this department was distributed amounted to a most flagrant and disgraceful job, the distri- bution being altogether in the interests of some senior offi- cials, and detrimental to the whole body of the clerks. The hon. member was speaking at a quarter to six, when, according to rule, the discussion was suspended. The report of Tuesday's Committee ef Supply was agreed to. THE. BELFAST RIOTS.—The amendments to the Disturb- ances at Belfast Inquiry Bill having been considered and agreed to, the measure was read a third time. EXPIRING Lews CorrrixueNcs BlLL.—This Bill passed through Committee without amendment, and was read a third time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THUESDAY.

-- - Bums Anvexcxn.--Severat local bills were advanced a stage, the following being amongst the number read a third time :—The Halifax High Level and North and South Junction Railway, the Mersey Railway, and the Manches, ter, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. The Electric Lighting (Provisional Order Bill) passed through all its remaining stages. The Secret Service (Repeal) Bill passed through Committee. The Submarine Telegraph Act Amend- ment Bill, the Disturbances (Belfast) Inquiry Bill, and the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill were brought up from the House of Commons and read a first time. Their lordships adjourned until Monday. HOUSE OF COMMONS—THURSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. LAND PURCHASR.—Sir M. HICRS•BEACII, in reply to Mr. Hunter, said down to the 13th inst. the loans applied for , under the Land Purchase Act amounted to £1,778,858, of which £1,163,400 had been sanctioned and £513,000 issued. He did net gather from these circumstances that there would be any necessity in the meantime to increase the sum of five millions sterling already provided for. THE EXPLOSION AT LEIGH.—Mr. BURT asked the Home Secretary if he had received a communication from thelLan- casbire Miners' Federation expressing dissatisfaction that no legal gentleman had been appointed to attend the adjourned inquest connected with the explosion at Leigh Colliery, and whether he would, in accordance with custom, send such a representative.—Mr. Merrnnws said he had received such a communication, but had also received a subsequent letter in which the Federation expressed full cenfidence in the ability of the gentlemen who were conducting the inquiry —a confidence which he fully shared; but if the inquiry should set satisfactorily dispose of all the questions on which information was desired he would direct an indepen- dent inquiry to be made. WAR DEPARTMENT DEFICIENCIES—Mr. W. H. SMITH, in answer to Colonel Duncan, said the following would consti- tute the Commission to inquire into the complaints made as to the military stores and equipments:—Sir James Fitz- james Stephen, Lieutenant General Sir A. Alison, Vice Ad- miral Sir ^Noel Lalmond, Sir Walter Barttelot, M.P., and Dr. Pierey, F.R.S. SUPPLY.—RENEWED SCENES.

The House went into Committee of Supply a few minutes before five o'clock, and resumed the consideration of the Civil Service Estimates. For a while the prospects were of the brightest, and one vote—that for the Irish Registrar General's office—was actually passed in less than fifteen minutes. But excited controversies unfortunately arose upon the vote for criminal prosecutions, the Parnellites de- manding the release from gaol of the Galway priest Father Fairy, who had refused to enter into securities to keep the peace towards a landlord whom Sir Joseph INPKenna des- criued as a rather " peppery " gentleman. Mr. Holmes was left to defend the conduct of the magistrates in the matter as best he could, and after a long series of harangues had been inflicted upon him by the indignant Irish- men below the gangway, Sir Wm. Harcourt urged I the Government to offer fuller explanations. Speaking:frotn his own experience as Home Secretary, be stated that there was one practical objection to putting clergymen in prison, because it was always "very difficult to got them out again." —The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND cheerfully respon- ded to his appeal. which had greatly delighted the Irish party. but Mr. Holmes threw no fresh light on the subject, and the Parnellites renewed their clamorous championship of the incarcerated priest's cause. Strong surprise was aroused by the intervention of Mr. BRADLAIMR, who by ob- serving that in the course of a troubled life he had often come into collision with the authorities exposed himself to the ridicule of the Tories, upon whom he retorted with the remark that under similar difficulties they probably would not have " got off " as well as himself. The • point of his short speech was that nobody had ever questioned the impartiality of English administration of the law except Lord R. Churchill, who at one time had declared that the Government could get whatever decision it pleased from any of the judges. The Chancellor of the Exchequer had been absent some time, but he happened to return at this moment, and being informed by Mr. Balfour of what had been said he immediately arose and with unwonted courtesy repudiated Mr. Bradlaueh's accusation. With equal polite- ness Mr. Bradlaugh accepted his .assurance on the spot, and then ran out of the riouse to refer to "Hansard." He soon came back, and then admitted that his memory must have entirely deceived him, adding, amidst hearty plaudits from the Ministerialists that he tbrught it "only loyal " to say so. This curious incident over, the membere renewed their complaints about Father Fahy, and evinced their zeal lon his behalf by moving to report progress and by compel- ling a count for the special behoof of Mr. Matthew Har- ris. Indications of an approaching storm grew apace. One of the irritated Parnellites, Mr. Jeremiah Jordan, was four ' times called to order. Mr. Henry Campbell, in utter 1 ignorance of the facts, declaimed fiercely against the tyrants who would not allow a poor priest to come out of prison when he was anxious to do so, and Mr. J. F. X. O'Brien, raising commotion by his own calm, deliberate style of delivery, turned to the Chairman with the air of a victim of persecution, and in soft accents said : " Really, Mr. Courtney, I do wish you would kindly preserve order." Ever( when at last the case of Father Fahy had been dis- posed of, fresh grievances were forthcoming, and apprehen- sions still prevailed of unmitigated obstruction; but at eleven o'clock the second vote of the evening was allowed . to pass. Several others were afterwards agreed to. Sub- sequently there was more discussion upon the rumours that
General Sir R. Buller had reported that the people in Kerry were unable to pay their rents. The House continued t,ittiug until a late hour.

RUGBY RULES. THE SANKEY RANGERS opened their football season on Saturday last, by making a draw with Friar's Green. Score :—Sankey Rangers, 1 try, 5 minors; Friar's Green, 1 try, 3 minors. RUNCORN RECREATION v. WARRINGTON RANGERS.—The opening match of the Recreation fixtures was played at Runcorn on Saturday against the above team. The " Rees" kicked off against the wind, and a tight game resulted, not a point being scored on either side up to half time. On change of ends the Recreation had it a little more in their favour, soon scoring a couple of minor points, and just before the call of time S. Abrams got over the line near to touch, the kick at goal failing, the Recreation thus winning by a try and three minor points to Rangers nil. THE WIDNES INTER-WORKS FOOTBALL COMPETITION.— The second match in connection with this competition was I played on Monday evening between teams representing the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and those of Messrs. Muspratt. Play commenced shortly after six o'clock, two twenty-fives being the time allotted. Hutchineons' team bad the best of the play throughout, E. Broome, J. Smith, and F. Smith es- pecially distinguishing themselves by their capital runs. The result of the match was illutchinsons' team, one goal, two tries and two minors, to Muepratt's one try and one minor. The following were the teams :—Hutchinsons' : Full back, W. Bingham; three-quarter bac*, E. Broome, J. H. Smith, and J. Roscoe; half-backs, W. Bradshaw and G. Evans ; forwards' fleMason, M. Whelan. J. Tonkies, A. Wright, F. Smith, J. Devine, J. Taylor, W. Norris, and J. Evans. Umpire, Mr. Kiddy. Musoratt's team: Fall back, Cooper; three-quarter backs, J. Hodgkins, W. Ratcliffe, and J. F. Burdoe ; half-backs, Tickle and E. S. Rimrner ; for- wards, H. Bingham, D. Gargban, J. Atherton, A. Parkinson, P. Boardman, T. Dolan, G Burgess, J. Smith, and W. Lo- max. Umpire, P. Corns. Referee, Mr. W. E. Oakden. RIIIICORZT Y. MANCHESTER RANGERS (2ND TEAMS).— This match was played at Rusholme on Saturday, when a good game was played, resulting in an easy win for Run- corn by one goal, one try, and eleven minor points, to one try ani a minor. Riley and Whitby got the tries for the visitors. Wilson, the three-quarter batik, obtained the try for the Rangers. The game was chiefly confined to the for- wards, who completely ran round their opponents. Runcorn kicked off against a stiff breeze, when P. Riley sent the ball towards the home line. The ball was not returned, and 'Cawley picked up and further pregress was made towards the home quarters, and for a considerable time the Runcorn team were in the Rangers' half. During some pick ex- changes W. Riley got hold and smartly scored the firat try, Seddon very nicely kicking a goal. On the *me being re- started the play assumed the same aggressive character,when the Rangers, being pressed by Whitby, touched down. A little later, capital chances of scoring were lost by the visit- ors' forwards, who, when near the line, kicked too hard and so lost possession of the ball. Wilson the home three-quar- ter back, made acted* and a try at goal was made, bet the result was simply a deed ball, the enly minor scored by the home team. A little later Wilson again got hold of the ball, and rovnding his opponents got over the has close to touch. No goal resulted trom the place. This brought half tinae. After change of ends Graham started the ball from centre, when the new rule was enforced. The home team being off side at the kick off a scrimmage was formed in centre. Caw- ley was the first to move towards the home goal, and owing to'the strong wind and long kicking of the kuneorn team, a number of touchdowns were scored. Soon after Whitby formed a scrimmage near the line an scored the second try, Sed- don, however, failing at goal. Nothing further of moment was scored. Runcorn had by far the best of the game, and by a little more judicious play will do well in the future. Teams :—Runcorn: Seddon, back; Cawley, Mather, and Riley, three-quarter backs; Whitby and Clare, half backs; Dnnbavand, Cox, Stubbs, P. Riley, Hancock, R.affe, Dobson, Orme, and Gittene, forwards. Rangers : Parkinson, beck; Wilson, Graham, and Donaldson, three- quarter backs; Parlain and J. Parlain, half backs; Dawson, Kinder, Goldsehmidt,Varley,Violet,Hooke, Mildant,Caven- dish, and Breen, forwards. RUNCORN V. MANCHESTER RANGERS. The Runcorn team played their first match at home on Saturday, when they met the Manehetter Rangers' team, and recorded a win to the first match of a strong and lengthy list. With one or two exceptions, all the first fif- teen will again play. Woods will again fill the position of full back, E. Lunt, H. C. Speakman, and T. Davies occupy- ing the post of three-quarter backs, H. Hughes (captain) and H. G. Andrews their usual places at half-back, and the usual team of forwards will again den the "myrtle green," viz., W. Wright, W. Hughey, J. Lewis, J. Dean. J. Barns, G. Wainwright, J. Gattley, W. Faulkner, and F. G. Joule. With the excellent reserve men the strength ef the team will again be fully maintained. The match on Saturday was not a display of very good football; there was a lack of that,pombination necessary to make a game brilliant and the frequency of packed scrimmages marred the game con- siderably. The major points scored were pieces of very quick play ; the two tries by Wainwright were the result of being always on the alert for chances, and Lunt's try was the result of some passing which. if practised more frequently, would add to the pleasure of the spectators, and stand the team in better stead. Speakman's try was also a well-merited one. In the Rangers' team there were some good men, and some excellent passing was at times shown, H. Haselman scoring the tries. The visitore commenced by playing a strong for- ward game. They were well combined, and their passing I was sure. In the back division a good deal of skill was dis- played, with the result that the Rangers drew the first blood in the shape of a minor point. The Rangers made admira- ble attacks on the home lines; and at the close of the first half of the game they seemed to have every chance of win- ning. Hughes's lads, however, pulled themselves together, and let loose the energy which they had been reserving. Notwithstanding the stubborn defence of the Rangers, who throughout played a most gentlemanly game, they could not withstand the vigorous attacke of the home team, who afterwards did all the scoring. The game ended in Runcorn scoring one goal, four tries, four minor points, to two tries and four minor points. The teams were :—Runcorn :—W. Faulkner, back; E. Lunt, H. C. Speakman, and T. Davies, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes (captain) and H. Andrews, half-backs; W. Wright, W. Hughes, J. Lewis, J. Dean, J. Barns, Gatlev, R. Dolan, G. Wainwright, and E. Andrews, forwards. Manchester Rangers :—W. G. Sabin, back ; H. Hasleman, H. Radcliff, and F. Radcliff, three-quarter backs; S. S. Taylor and F. Radcliff, half-backs; Herbert Hasleman, E. Mee, J. Jones. J. Pollard, F. Galley, W. Bain., \Tickers, Scholes, and Abrams, forwards. Referee, Mr. Roger Wil- cock, Liverpool.
WARRINGTON v. SWINTON.

The opening match of the season of the Warrington Football Chap was played on Saturday on the ground off Wilderspool Causeway, and it was in every resnect a sue- cesefulevent. The opposing team was that of Swinton, i which s correctly described as " famous " in the football world, and in decisively beating opponents of this calibre at the very opening of the season the Warrington men have, to say the least, "begun well." There was a very large at- tendance of spectotors, there being about 3,000 persons present, and throughout the keenest interest was taken in the game. The home captain having won the toss. Swin- ton kicked off against the wind. For a minute or two it seemed as though the visitors were going to have the best of it as they followed up the will with great dash, but Gra- ham effectually returned, and, playing well together, the home team carried the oval into the visitors' 25. Several scrimmages here took place in wbich Swinton had slightly the advantage, but so admirably combined was the play of Ashton's men that their opponents gained no ground. Val- entine, getting hold of the ball put in a nice kick ; but Brixton returned one equally as good, and scrimmages were the or- der of the Ray, until Barnes excited the admiration of the spectators by a splendid screw-kick. The Swinton forwards then broke through, but Speakman and Graham were equal to the occasion and checked the rush. Bumby put in a nice kick, and following ep again obtained possession, only to be brought down by Gilbert. The Swinton forwards, step by step, took the ball to the home 25; but it was not allowed to remain in that position, as Rigby, Turner, and Ashton, by a combined dribble, brought it to the centre. Fair. Turner, at this period of play, rendered himself con- ppicuous by a splendid rush; but he was cleverly stopped by Murray. Graham shortly afterwards gained a lot of ground by having a free kick accorded to him for a very clever catch, but Valentine equalised matters by a tremen- dous punt into touch. The visitors' forwards again broke through and came down with a rush; but Jolley saved, and came through with a nice dribble, Speakman seconding his efforts by taking the ball still further. Speakman sent the ball across the field, intending it for Graham, but as he did not allow for the wind, it went into the hands of Murray, who put in a good run, being eventually stopped by Barnes. The ball afterwards got into Graham's hands, and that player put in a short run, and passed nicely to Jolley, who gained grounsl. Fair. Turner sulssequently distin- guished hirnself by smartly collaring Valentine when he had thrown off several of the Warringtonians, and Graham aided still further by a well-judged kick to touch. The Warrington forwards then made a determined rush, and confined the play for some time to the visitors' 25. A touch-down shortly afterwards resulted in favour of tee home team, and from a kick out Speakman obtained the ball, and put in an excellent pass to Jolley, who, however, did not gain much ground. Valentine and Moore took the ball up the field, but Gilbert put an end to further progress, , and replied by punting the ball to touch. Some severe scrimmages then took place, and some excellent passing was witnessed on the part of the Warringtonians. In a scrim- mage which took place near the visitors' 25 flag the Swm i - tonians heeled the ball out, Bumby receiving t and passing it to Valentine. Gilbert, who was on the alert, smartly rusticl at him, and secured the sphere, made a dodgy run, and unselfishly passed to Barnes, who secured a try amidst tremendous applause. Ashton called Speakman to kick at goal, the ball being piloted safely between the uprights. Again ringing cheers were given. The .ball was afterwards taken to the centre, and Barnes returned it. Frank Turner then gained a lot of ground, and Sam Hough coming to his assistance with a dribble, a minor resulted. A series of scrimmages took place, the home team having slightly the best of them, and shortly afterwards half-time was called with the ball in the visitors' quarters. On the resumption of play, Frank Turner kicked or , and Jolley dribbled, to the

full back, who replied with a kick, the ball falling into the hands of Graham, who executed a clever run. Almost im- mediately afterwards J. Rigby got over, but to the surprise of the players the ball was ruled back. For a time play was very even. Valentine secured the ball in the home team's 25, and made a capital run; but he was splendidly collared by Graham and Buxton, who brought him down within a foot of the home team's lines. A close scrimmage ensued, but the home team were determined that their op- ponents should not score, and by irresistible force they car- ried the ball by scrimmage and dribble to the 25 flag. The visitors gave evidence of flagging in their efforts, whilst Warrington on the other hand played with greater dash. Bumby and Banks made repeated efforts to get away, only to be collared with the ball in their possession by the War- rington forwards. Play was confined for some time to cen- tre; but eventually Bumby obtained possession again. The Warrington forwards, headed by Ashton, came through, and the captain picking up smartly, brought Bumby down with- in a yard of the visitors' line, but the ,ball was ruled back to centre. Excellent play was next observed on the part of Beswick and Bumby on the one side, and of Graham and Barnes on the other, the advantage, however, falling to the lot of the home team. The Swinton forwards tried hard to score, and took the ball with a rush to the home 25; but Barnes put in a running kick. Bumby followed suit and the ball travelled over the Warrington line. Buxton, with clear perception, however, called into requisition the saving clause, thus reranting Bwinton their only point during the game. Barnes showed up prominently with a good kick, and gaided ground. ,d during the rest of the game it took the united efforts of t s bwintonians to prevent the cupholders from further seork Warrington won by a goal and three minors to one mino..

The style of play through which Warrington won the match left little to be desired. All the players appeared at their best, and one of the features of the game was the judicious passing that was indulged in, and which in no slight degree contributed to the success. Barnes delighted his admirers by several of his dodgy runs and clever kicks, and Graham, by first-olass play, quickly installed himself a popular favourite. Jolley likewise did some good work. The half-lsaeks, Gilbert and Speakman, as usual played a fearlese and steady game, and certainly did not lose by comparison with Banks and Bumby. Among the forwards Ashton and Fair Turner were seen at their best. The for- mer on several occasions was the means cf gaining a lot of ground, while the collaring of the latter was more than I could be struggled against, and as the game wore on the ' Swinton men, learning by experience, when once fairly held by their powerful opponent yielded quietly to the inevit- table. In the play of the rest of the forwards it was not easy to detect a flaw. The Swinton men played a very de- termined game, but towards the end of the first half seemed somewhat disconcerted by the goal that was obtained by the home team, as the ball had barely been re-started when the latter rushed through and won another minor. In the second part of the game, however, the visitors struggled hard to equalise matters. Valentine, Cook, Murray and Bumby did well for their side, while the forwards were par- ticularly strong in the scrimmages. The following were the teams :—Warrington: Full back, Buxton; three-quarter-backs, Graham, Barnes, and Jolley; half-backs, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, H. Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Haves, Povey, E. Dillon, T. Davies, Sam Hough, and Rigby. Swinton: Full back, Cook ; three-quarter-backs, Valentine, Murray, and Beswiek; half-backs, Banks and Bumby ; forwards, Hotch- kiss, Marsh, Honey, Follett, Seddon, Kenyon, Harris, and the brothers Hope. Umpires, Messrs. Barnes and Seddon; referee, Mr. Jones, Broughton Rangers. . ASSOCIATION ttULES. RUNCORN ASSOCLATION v. LITTLE LEIGIL—A match be- tween these two clubs was played at Runcorn on Saturday, the visitors winning by four goals to mine.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The draws for the first round of the Lancashire Cups, which were made at Fleetwood on Saturday, have not caused anything like the same amount of interest and anxiety as accompanied the draw of the parent association at the beginning of last week. In the draw for the Senior Cup the most interesting game will undoubtedly be that between the North End and Boyers. The news of these clubs being drawn together has caused much comment and invariably lovers of the game expressed pleasure and confidence in the victory of the North End, The other leading clubs in the competition have easy things en, but a few interesting games will take place between the second- rate clubs in the competition. The season commenced well at Warrington, on Saturday, when the local players gained a sound victory over Swinton. They met with a well-received ovation afterwards. The season opened at Bradford, on Saturday, with a match between the Yorkshire cupholders and Halifax. Winning the toss, Halifax played with the wind in their favour, and at half-tiale crossed over with three minor points in their favour. After changing ends Bradford had con- siderably the beat of the game, and P. Robertshaw, by a fine ran, got a try, but Haigh failed at goal. Afterwards F. Bonsor crossed the line, and Haigh this time registered the major point, Bradford thus winning by a goal and a try to three minors.

The following Association matches were played on Satur- day :—Derby County 4, Everton 0; Asten Villa 4, Lincoln City 1; Small Heath Alliance 3, Halliwell 1; Balton Wan- derers 7, Druids 1; West Bromwich Albion 4, Stoke-on- Trent 1; Crewe Alexandra 4, -Stafford Rovers 0; Long Eaton Rangers 1, Wolverhampton Wanderers 3; Norwich Victoria 2, Davenham 2; Walaall Swifts, 3, Mitchell's St. Georze's 1; Echington 2, Staveley 1. Among Rugby matches were :—Bilnighton Rangers v. Ashton, on the ground of the latter, the Rangers winning by two goals, five tries, and one minor to one minor. Wer- Beth v. Rochdale Hornets, on the ground of the former; Werneth one try and four miners, Hornets one try and three minors. Aspull v. Mr. Sutton's team, at Aspull, the home team winning by one goal, five tries, and seven minor points to one goal.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of Guar- dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. The chair was occupied by Mr.J.Lowe, and there were also present the Rev. Thomas Chambers, Messrs. W. Birchall, Wm. Middlehursr, James Birchall, Jas. Ranson, William Gerrard, James Fisher, Charles B. John- son, Richard Tuson, Thos. Hill, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). ) OFFICIAL RED TAREISII.—At the last meeting of the Guardians it was decided to meet half an hour earlier to I give the members an opportunity of attending the Farn- worth Agricultural Show, but it was found the alteration in commencement of the business could not be legally done without the sanction of the Local Government Bard. The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board sanc- tioning the proposal that the meeting should commence at ten o'clock instead of 10-30. The reading of the letter created some amusement, and the Rev. T. Chambers re- marked that the Guardians might be considered to be a lot of schoolboys. _

RELIEF STATISTICS.—The Workhouse Mister reported there were 474 inmates this week, 456 last week, and 409 in the correspondiag week of last year. The vagrants re- lieved were 49, against 62 in the corresponding period last year. THE MILK CONTRACT.—The Local Government Board wrote consenting to the proposal of the Guardians to deter- mine the contract for the supply of milk and butter to the Workhouse, entered into by the Guardians with Mr. 0. Ward, farmer, Whiston. THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR ECCLESTON AND KNOWS- LEY.—The Local Government Board transmitted a copy of correspondence relating to the alleged non-performance of duties by Mr. Thomas Parkinson, assistant overseer for the townships of Eccleston and Knowsley, and asked for the observations of the Guardians thereon. The District audi-

_ tor had reported that a rate was made on the 16th June, , 1885, amounting to £5,506 188 2d, but only £379 5s lid was collected at Michaelmas, 1885. Of a special sanitary rate for Knowsley, made at Lady Day, 1835, £137 183 remained uncollected. Of £47 Os 5d in respect of toe ' Knowsley rate recoverable arrears at Lady Day, 1835, only £1 6s 9d was collected daring the half-year ended Micimel- mite, 1885. A new rate was made on the Ist December, 1885, and at the audit about £5OO of the sum bad been col- lected, but no entries appeared in the rate-book in respect of such collection. Mr. Parkinson bad replied at length, the principal points being that be was only promoted to the position of assistant overseer on the 11th June, 1885, and he bad immediately to proceed with an extraor- dinary amount of work under the Registration Act, 1885, in the preparation of lists of voters, attend- ing revision courts, oic. After that was over all his energies were devoted to the collection of the Eccleston rates, which were then largely in arrears. As to the £5OO collected but not entered, he said he had received it from one person, and did not think it right to enter it into the rate-Dook hefore the completion of the audit of the 29th September.—The Clerk said the correspon- dence had been before the Finance Committee, who had resolved that Mr. Parkinson's explanation was not satisfac- tory, but, with the view of affording him another oppor- tunity of amendment, they recommended the Guardians to postpone any decision that would jeopardise his position. Another audit was close at hand, and the Guardians would see if be passed favourably and was doing his work fairly well.—On the motion of the R-v. Thomas Chambers, the clerk was instructed to send a copy of the resolution to the Local Government Board. APPOINTMENT OF NunsE.—Mrs Ann Barrett, nurse at the Worksop Union Workhouse, was appointed nurse, at a sal- ary of £3O per annum.

FOUR COLLIERS SUFFOCATED.—Four colliers, named James Moore, Job Riddle, Elizih' Hardina, and Ernest Emery, were killed by afterdamp at BraysLwn affery, near Radstock, on Tuesday night. They went into the pit at seven o'clock, and three hours afterwards were found dead. Late on Tuesday afternoon the manager pagsed the spot where the men were suffocated, but did not notice the presence of foul air. The beat from the boiler tire is sup- posed to have generated the gas. THE DISASTROUS COLLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR BRISTOL.-- The inquest on the bodies of the ten men killed on Friday last in the Dean Lane colliery explosion, near Bristol, was resumed on Wednesday afternoon, and further adjourned till Monday, when two of the injured men will, it is ex- pected, be able to attend. The Coroner cautioned the jury not to be influenced by the statements reported to have been made by some of the men as to the management of the mine. On Monday the Government inspector who examined the mine will be present, and the inquiry will be continued from day to day until finished.

div.head: TRADES UNION CONGRESS.
div.p: TRADES UNION CONGRESS.

The Congress met at Hull on Saturday, and there being 21 resolutions on the agenda paper the speak- ing was brief and to the point. The Congress passed resolutions in favour of free elementary schools, immediate legislation on the subject of un- employed workmen, the stoppage of unnecessary Sunday labour, and the abolition of property quali- fications for magistrates, guardians, and other pub- lic positions. The repeal of all laws affecting Trades Unions was called for on the ground that the common law is sufficient. Systematic working of overtime was condemned as an injustice to unem- ployed, and inspection of railways by practical men was demanded. The business was completed about noon, and a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Mad- dison for his able occupation of the chair. In returning thanks, Mr. Maddison alluded to the strictures which the newspapers had passed upon his opening address. He denied that he had inten- tionally said anything hard about employers. In- deed, his remarks had been intended to apply solely to the unfair employer of labour.—The Congress then broke up.

div.head: SUICIDE AT SA IN KEY BRIDGES.
div.p: SUICIDE AT SA IN KEY BRIDGES.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, respecting the death of Elizabeth • Barker (21), wife of William Edward Barker, a wiredrawer's apprentice, who lives at 66, Haydock- street, Warrington. On Friday evening deceased was seen to jump into the Sankey canal, and her dead body was removed to the Black Horse to await an inquest. Mr. W. Summersgill was foreman of the jury. The evidence appended was taken. Martha Ratcliffe, mother of the deceased, who was the first witness called, said that her daughter was the wife of William Edward Barker, a wire- drawer's apprentice, who lodged with witness and Iher husband at 66, Haydock-street, Warrington. Deceased was 21 years of age, and she and her hus- band were about 19 years old when they married. Witness last saw her daughter alive at about 1-15 on Friday afternoon, when she left home, apparent- ly in her usual health. Witness saw the dead body of the deceased next morning at the Black Horse Inn, Great Sankey. Dr. Fox had attended deceased before and after her marriage, and she had also been attended by another doctor.. She had been, subject to fits, and both doctors said that she was rather weak in her mind. Deceased had complained very much about her head, and had many a time &rid that she wished she could give it away. De- ceased had been employed under witness's husband, who was an overlooker at Cockhedge Factory. Mary Ann Balshaw, a weaver employed at Cock- hedge factory, who lives at 69, Dallam-lane, War- rington, said that she was a companion of the de- ceased. Deceased, when leaving work at about 5-40 on Friday night, told witness that she (deceased) had spoilt a cut of velvet cloth, and had been before Mr. Lingard, cut-looker. Deceased did not mention to her what Mr. Lingard said, but cried very much. She afterwards became more cheerful. When she left work witness did not think that deceased was about to harm herself. It was an ordinary occur- rence for weavers to spoils cut of cloth. Different penalties were attached, from a small fine of 3d. to stoppage of work. The deceased spoke to witness about purchasing some furniture for a house she and her husband were going to live in. Witness had known her for five years. She (deceased) had been very weak, and had had a great deal of sickness. In answer to questions, witness said that deceased told her that she was going into a house of her own, but she did not know what she was going for. Deceased asked witneSs to help her, and she replied that she would. She had seen deceased have twenty fits in one night. She was not aware that deceased ever threatened to commit suicide. She remembered deceased having a fit while in a boat at the fair, and on one occasion deceased had to be taken out of the factory in a fit. Deceased lost her child about three months age, but witness had not seen much change in her since. Deceased would sometimes be upset, by very little things. George Potter, 48, Howard-street, deposed that at about seven o'clock on Friday evening he was on the bank of the canal at Sankey, near the Cheshire Lines railway bridge. He saw a woman about 400 yards distant, nearer Sankey Bridges, throw up her arms and jump into the canal. Witness went at once to offer assistance, but could not discover the woman. She was sinking as he approached, and did not rise again.—The Coroner: Did you know who the woman was when the body was recovered? —No, sir; she was a complete stranger to me. lam quite cert airishe jumped in herself. Thomas Such, mill furnaceman, Priestley-street, Warrington, said that he recovered the body of the deceased from the canal at about 7-30 on Friday evening. It was cOnveyed to the Black Horse Inn. The last witness told him that he had seen a woman jump into the water, and witness and some others , procured a rake, with which witness recovered the body.--The Coroner; Was her body visible then ?--- No, we had to rake her from the bottom; she was quite dead.

John Lingard, cutlooker employed at Messrs. Armitage and Rigby's factory at Cockhedge, said that his duty was to see whether the pieces were good or bad. He remembered examining a piece woven by the deceased. It was a very bad piece. He showed it to her, and then to her father, who also said it was a very bad piece. The work was so imperfect that deceased had nothing for weaving it. —How long would it in the ordinary- couse take to weave that piece? Perhaps two days. They have the option either to buy the piece or have nothing for that would be going out of the frying pan into the fire? Some buy and then sell them, and some would rather pay extra than be fined.— You told her she would receive nothing for weav- ing? Yes, and she did not say a word.—By a jury- man: It is a daily occurrence to have pieces spoiled. We have them in daily for making mistakes, and not minding their work. Witness added that he did not sauce the deceased, and said that she bad not seemed right since she was confined. After a short conversation the jury uns.mMoy.try- came to the conclusion that the de3Lasedcoratiptted. suicide whilst temporarily insane.
F ARLESTUWN. Tun Dnirroars CLUB—The memb,ms of the Earles- town District Draughts Club held a special meting at the Welcome Coffee Palace en Thursday evening. Mr. John

Makin (captain) occispied the chair. The principal business was the consideration of rules for the ensuing w:nter sea- son. There are at present about 40 itereber, and a con- siderable addition is expected daring the winter season. GOLBORNE WESLEYAN BAZA.A.U. —The Wesleyan bazaar opened at Golharne last week has Ipen concluded. The total receipts amount to upwards of £l3O, and there are goods left sufficient to make up another stall or an ex- cellent Christmas tree. With the donations received and the sale of goods it is expected the bazaar will net about £l5O. The proceeds are in aid of a much-needed Sunday school, estimated to cost £4OO. . DISORDERLY CONDUCT AT .THE WELLINGTON HOTEL. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, C. Filkington, and W. F. Gooch, Richard Flan- nag,an and James Flannagan, brothers, were summoned for being disorderly, and refusing to leave the Wellington Inn,. Earle-street, Earlestown. when requested on the 25th Aug. Mr. J. W. Thorp stated that the defendants were in his house between half-past nine and ten o'clock, and wera creating a disturbance. They were very disorderly, and re- fused to go out when requested. He went for a policeman, and when he returned the defendant Richard had left bat James had not gone. This statement was corroborated by Mr. D. Cullen, manager for Mr. Tnorp. and P.C. Lloyd.— The defendants pleaded not guilty, and alleged that they did not create any disturbance and that they left the house when they were ask-ed.—The Bench inflieed a fine of 5s and costs upon each defendant. ANTI- VACCINATION.—At the Newton Petty Sessions. on Saturday, before Messrs. Houghton and W. F. Gooch, Edward Dickens, of Earlestown, was summoned for failing to have his child vaccinated.—Mrs. Dickens appeared in answer to the summons.—Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer, said the case had been adjourned for proof that he had de- livered a notice upon the parents requiring the child to be vaccinated. He now contended that according to the Art It was not necessary to prove that a defendant had received notice. At the last hearing Mrs. Dickens said that they bad not received any notice for the child in question, but for another child. The Clerk (Mr. Buckton): Is the child vac- cinated ?—Mrs. Dickens : No, sir. I have not had a notice for his child.—Mr. Cooper said he bad given notice to Mrs. Dickens on the 9th July, 1865, and he also sent a notice by post. On the 22nd June he saw Mr. Dickens, who said the child was all right, and he had no intention of having it vaccinated. On the 24th he saw Mrs. Dickens, who said the child was quite well and it was not going to be vaccineted.—The Chairman (Mr. Hoag,liton): Are you still of the opinion that you will not have this child vaccinated ?—Mrs. Dickens: Yes, I don't intend to have the child vaccinated. I would like to explain the reason why we have not had it done. I have had to suffer a great deal through having two vaccinated, and I think it is very bard to be brought up here after having suffered so much. It is a very great an- noyance.—The Chairman: The law says children must be vaccinated, and we are here to try to carry out the law. WS make an order for the child to be vaccinated within 21 days.—There was an adjourned summons against Michael Connell, of Earlestown, for a like offence.—Mr. Cooper stated that since the last court he had received notice that the child had been vaccinated, and the summons would be withdrawn on the payment of costs.—The Bench ordered the defendaut to pay the coote.

RUNCORN UNION.—CONTRACTS for PROVISIONS and SUPPLIES for the half-year ending 30th March, 1887.—The GUARDIANS Of the POOR of the Rimanur Union are desirous wf receiving TENDERS from parties willing to CONTRACT for the supply of Flour and Oatmeal, Groceries, Peas, Cheese, Salt Butter ; Cod Liver and Paraffia Oil; Quinine; good Beef, to consist of vein and brisket pieces, the price to include about 301bs. per week of the best butcher's meat for the officers, and sides of Mutton; nest Brand (Ists ) American or English Bacon; Pota- toes; Wheat Straw; Drapery and Clothing; Men's, Women's, Boys' and Girls' Shoes, of various sizes, as per samples to be seen at the Workhouse, Dutton; House Coal (colliery to be named); good Deal Coffins, specifying size, and including plate with name, age and date of death, to be de- livered in the Union when and where required ; Cart- ing at per mile, and Funerals at per funeral. Parties tendering for the supply of the aboye-mentioned goods will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples (except drapery goods) as far as Practicable, The Guardians do not bind themselves to ac- cept the lowest or any tender. Persons desirous of tendering must apply by letter to my office, in Frodsham, for a printed Form of Tender (and none other can be entertained), where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars can be obtained. Sealed Tenders, addressed to the Guardians, to be forwatcled to the Clerk's office, Frodsham, on or before Monday, the 27th day of September, 1886, endorsed "Tender for ." The tenders will be opened and considered at a meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board Room, Dutton, on the 28th Septemb?r, 1886, at Two p.m. Parties whose tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if re- quired by the Guardians. By order of the Board. H. LINAKER, Frodsharn, 10th Sept., 1835. Clerk to the Guardians.

div.head: . THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1886.
div.p: . THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 18, 1886.

MR. PARNELL'S Land Bill, notwithstanding that it is a measure.of a temporary character, introduces an element which is of a disturb- ing and unsatisfactory character, and that is the idea that Irish tenants are entitled to look to Parliament as a sort of special Pro- vidence to help them out of their financial difficulties. It is true that, having once admitted the principle that rent is a matter, so far as Ireland is concerned, which may be determined by Act of Parliament, we have opened the door to its being re-determined, though as to that the impression was that the rent, once fixed, was fixed for fifteen years. It may be that we shall find as we progress towards Uome Rule that it will become unnecessary for Parliament to have anything to do with the fixing of rent; that the tenant, protected in various ways as he requires to be, will be strong enough to make a fair bargain for himself. We cannot think that, in the long run, Parliamentary interference as to rent will be beneficial either to tenant or landlord ; but we are in a transitional stage as to the Irish land ques- tion, and having set up a Land Court Mr. PARNELL is certainly within his rights as a leader in asking Parliament to consider whether, in bringing into operation such a measure as he proposes, the Court would not be usefully employed during the coming winter. Ur. PARNELL'S Bill has the merit of simplicity and clearness; it is what it pur- poses to be—a measure "for the temporary relief of agricultural tenants in Ireland." The Government by instituting an inquiry admit that, on the face of it, something requires to be done; but they propose to leave it till next February before they express an opinion as to what that something should be. The leader of the Irish Nationalists says in effect: —" This matter is urgent; we cannot wait until next year; whilst the inquiry proceeds the tenant starves; he will be rendered miserable and desperate by evictions; and, unless something is at once done, there will be civil war in the country." To prevent the terrible evils which he believes he foresees, if affairs in Ireland are allowed to drift, Mr. PARNELL proposes to put a stop immediately to evictions, under certain con- ditions which he specifies; and at the same time ease the way for the Irish tenant for this year and the next by granting, where it is deemed "just and expedient," certain abate- ments of rent and arrears. The Bill, if it became law, would give the tenant power to apply to the Land Court to protect him as against his landlord, but not before he wa. s in a Position to show that he had Paid at least "half the rent ordinarily payable in the year 1886 in respect of such holding, and half of any antecedent arrears." It w!ll thus be seen that the landlord could not in

AnY Case lose anything under a judicial de- cision until one half of what was owing to him had become so much cash in hand. it is not unlikely, therefore, that the bill Would in many cases ensure the landlord a substantial sum when, if there were not such bill, he would get little or nothing ex- cept by the dangerous and cruel process of , eviction. More than this, the tenant, before he could make good his claim to abatement, Would be required to show that he was "un- able to discharge the remainder of such rent, or arrears, without *loss of his holding, or depreciation of the means necessary for the cultivation and stocking thereof." Even then it would not follow that he would be relieved of the payment of half the rent, or of the arrears; he would get a n abatement; but it would be for the Court to say what abate- tnent of. rent and arrears would be "just or expedient" as applying to antecedent arrears, to current rent, " and to the rent which would have been payable in the following year." Let us take the case of a tenant whose rent is £3O per year, and let it it be supposed that he is one year in arrear, and that he has paid nothing towards the rent for the cur- rent year. Before he could come into court to ask for an abatement, he would have to pay his landlord at least [30—that is clear off half the arrears, and pay half the current rent. The Court might say, after investigat- ing the case, that there should be an abate- rnent of 20 per cent ; and this would mean £6 from the arrears, £6 from the current rent, and £6 from the rent of the following year; while as to the rest the landlord would have his usual ' title to recover, including, in the ordinary course, the power of eviction. Another clause of Mr. PARNELL'S Bill gives leaseholders of a certain class the benefit of the Land Act of 1881; and, as to this, it may be said that there are not a few of thse Ulster-men who are in favour of this being done. It will thus be seen that there is nothing either extravagant or unreasonable in Mr. PARNELL'S proposals; and, assuming that he can make out a good case for intervention, it would seem that the intervention which he suggests is of the right kind. The Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union argue, however, that although there has been a fall in the price of produce it is not such a fall as would justify the Legislature in Stepping in Land taking something from the landlord's rent. They have published some Notes in which they institute a comparison between prices obtained in the first six Months of 1885, and those of the first six Months of 1886. But this, unfortunately for the purposes of their argument, does not cover the whole of the ground. Mr. PAR- NELL'S Bill would give relief to tenants whose rents were fixed by the Land Courts prior to the close of 1884, his contention being that prices have been falling for several years. And that this is so is proved by the figures Which the Unionists Themselves furnish. They give the price ofi beef from rBBe to iBB4 as 675. per hundred-weight, and admit that the price for the present year is 545. 2d. This, roundly speaking, indicates a decline in this respect of zo per cent; and if tenants could have an equivalent reduction from their rents they would have little cause to Complain. Some Irish landlords have already made reductions to this extent, and some, like Lord FITZWILLIAM, have reduced their rents from forty to fifty per cent. Each case re- quires, of course, to be determined on its merits; and it is to ensure that this shall be done' and done in time, that Mr. PARNELL has brought in his Tenants' Relief Bill. Frankly speaking, we do not like the idea of the Land Court being set to work to revise rents; but we do not, at the same time, like to think of tenants being evicted because of their failure to pay impossible rents. It is a choice of two evils, and Mr. PARNELL'S Land Bill would seem to be the least of the two.

The Trades Union Congress held its last Sitting on Saturday, and passed several im- portant resolutions. Amongst other _ques- tions raised was that of Free Education, and after some discugsion, the opinion of the Congress being tested by an amendment, the following motion was adopted by an over- whelming majority :—" That. ita the opinion of this congress, the public elementary schools of this country should be placed under the control of duly elected representa- tives of the people during the hours in which - secular instruction is given, and that the ad- mission to such schools should be free of charge." Mr. R. KNIGHT, who.. moved the resolution, stood upon the solid ground that, as large sums were paid from the public ex- chequer in support of denominational and Board schools, the *managers of both classes of schools should be alike responsible to the public. There is a disposition in some quar- ters to complain that denominational schools are at a disadvantage, seeing that Board Schools are in part sustained by the rates ; but on the other hand it must not he forgot- ten that Board Schools are responsible to the ratepayers for every penny which they expend of the ratepayers' money. Let the denomi- nationalists who ask for aid from the rates say whether, as a condition of their acceptance of it, they will submit, as the managers of Board Schools must submit, to the con- trol of the public. They surely cannot ex- pect that if they are put on a footing of equality with Board Schools in obtaining support from the rates that they will be on a different footing as to their responsibility to the ratepayers. If they do count upon such a thing, they are most certainly delud- ing themselves; the ratepayers will never consent to voting sums of money either for schools, or baths, or libraries, to bodies of men who are not amenable to their control. The grants of the Education Department al- ready go too far in this direction, and the tendency of opinion is undoubtedly in the healthy direction of making bodies or com- mittees that expend public money more imme- diately responsible to the public. As to the need for schools being made free, it was urged at the Congress that it was a great in- justice when parents were struggling with po- verty to compel them, because they wete unable to pay school fees, to reveal the depths of ' their poverty to School Committees. And then in case of parents who are not doing ' their duty, is it prudent, is it right, that , children should be left to acquire evil habits in the streets because school fees are not put I in their hands? There was a ease, pitiful I enough in all its details, before the Warring- ton magistrates the other day ; a wretched woman sacrificed herself to drink, and the children were being sacrificed, too, because she spent in intoxicating liquor the money which should have gone towards paying the schoolmaster. It is not asking mnch, after all, to make our elementary schools free; two-thirds of the cost of national education are already met by the State: and, as the , members of the Trades Union Congress I perceive, it would be taking a wise course, and involve no sperifice of principle, if the cost of the other third were also paid out of the public purse.

"TOUCH AND GO." At Birmingham, Wm. Nokes, a captain of the Salvation Army, has been deserting his wife and family in order, as he put it, to " serve the Lord." The magistrates thought he would be better employed in serving a month in gaol; it is the best place for sanc- timonious vagabonds.

There has been another drowning case in the canal near Sankey Bridges—the third in three weeks. "One woe doth tread upon another's heel, so fast they follow." The body of the last victim—that of a joiner named George Unsworth—has been removed to the Black Horse Inn, where no less than four inquests have been held within four weeks.

More records of violence and brutality; at S. Helens a young man brought before the Bench for kicking a man whilst he is down, and thereby cutting his lip through; at Earlestown another young man fighting with his father, and following this up by throwing a brick which strikes a woman, who is thereby injured and dies within a week!

It is too much to expect that the brute shall be eradicated from society ; but surely by taking him in hand early he can be kept better under control. Why should not the schoolmaster operate on him be- fore he is in his teens ? If violence of all kinds, and especially kicking, were put dawn in the boy there would be less of it in the man.

Sir W. Cunliffe Brooks, M.P., who has paired for the remainder of the session with Mr. Channing, has been entertaining Lord Cranbrook in Scotland. His lordship, on leaving Balmoral, where he had been act- ing as minister in attendance on the Queen, went on a visit to Sir William at Glen-Tana, near Aboyne Castle. Lord Cranbrook has this week, however, returned to London.

A contemporary says :--" At the Accring- ton Police Court, on Wednesday, several gentlemen concerned in a bazaar held in the Town Hall in aid of the Church Conservative Club, were summoned for permitting lotteries at the bazaar. The Bench deferred their decision for a fortnight." This is as it should be; it is time that " gentlemen" were made to feel that the law may apply to them as well as to publicans and other sinners.

A special committee at St. Helens has re- ported in favour of a Branch Free Library for that portion of the borough known as East Sutton. From certain figures that were taken into consideration, there is reason to believe that the increased facilities for obtaining books would treble the number of readers. This is a point which the Warrington Library Committee would do well to consider; they have not yet come to the conclusion that one Free Lending Library, is necessary in the town—to say nothing of two. Poor War- rington I

Lord Randolph Churchill is redeeming one of his pledges in overhauling the De- partments. Speaking at Blackpool some two years ago, he said :—" The first and most vital business of a natinn is finance ;" and then he added, "I should like to turn the members of the House of Commons loose into our public departments on a voyage of dis- covery." He has got his opportunity as Chancellor of the Exchequer and leader of the House of Commons, and he is having his way; he has let the members loose "on a voyage of discovery."

It is a fitting thing that Mr. Peter Rylands has been appointed a member of the Com- mittee of inquiry into the national expendi- ture and the working of the various depart- ments of the public service. He has often fought the battle of economy when there were few to. stand beside him; and it is to be hoped he will be the means, under im- proved arrangements, of helping to check extravagance in high places. If Governments had less money to spend, there would be less mischief done and there would be a reduction of the income tar.

It transpired at an inquest in Liverpool, on the body of a farmer who had been drowned in a pit, that about a dozen people had seen the body without making an effort to remove it. The impression was that it would be il- legal to touch it until seen by a policeman. The same ignorance, or fear, has been shown in cases of suicide by hanging. Is it not time that schoolmasters labouring amongst the bucolics dealt with matters of this kind. Restoration is out of the question where a victim is left lying in a pit for three hours after he is first seen.
