div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

THE BAPTIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—The Baptist Chapel, Bridge-street, Runcorn, which was recently offered for sale but found no purchaser, is being fitted up as a room for pub- lic meetings. The building has been rented by Mr. Richard, Moore, stationer, Church-street, who intends, after the al- terations to let it for any public purpose. Bony 'WASHED ASHORE AT tiALE.—The body of an ap- 'meetly new horn female child was found lying on the shore at Hale, on Saturday morning, by two boys. The body was very much decomposed, and had evidently been in the water for some time. An inquest was held re- specting it by Mr. J. R. Buckton, coroner for Hale, the same day, when a verdict of "Found drowned" was re- turned. WIDNES CHURCH PAY SCHOOLS.—The annual sermons in aid of these school's were preached. on Sunday. The Rev. John White, vicar of Deere, occupied the pulpit at St. Mary's in the morning, and the Rev. J. Roger Jones in the evening. The preachers at St. Paul's were the vicar of Widnes and the Rev. Jelan White. At each service there were good congregations. In the afternoon a special ser- vice was also held in St. Paul's, when a sermon was preached by the Rev. J. White. FARNWORTII CHURCH OP ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—A. demonstration in connection with the Farn- worth Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held at Farnworth on Saturday afternoon. About 206 members met at the schools at two o'clock and having Paraded the parish, headed by the Widnes C.E.T.S. brass band, proceeded to the church, where a sermon was preached by the Rev. Richard Postance, jun., MA., of Liverpool. A collection was made in aid of the expenses, which realised the sum of 18s. A tea party was afterwards held in the pelage's, and subsequently an entertainment, under the presi- dency of the Rev. R. Potence, was held in the same place. Selections of music were given by members of the society, and an address WAS delivered by Mr.W. Touchstone, of Manchester. Amongst those present were the Rev. George Bond, Vicar of Farnwortb ; the Rev. J. Lawton, of Gars- ton; and Mr. J. W. Davies. RuNcoRN RURAL SANITARY AUTITORITY.—The ordinary fortnightly meeting of this body was held at the Board- room at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. The chair was occupied by Lieut.-Colonel Ashton, and there were also present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood, Messrs. Stokee, Aaron Weir, Knowles Mclntyre, Hadfield, Whitlow, Brandreth, 'Wallington, and Lewis; 11. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—An estimate of general expenses for Lady Day half-year 1887 was read by the deputy clerk, and adopted without discussion.—Mr. John Derbyshire wrote to the chairman of the Authority complaining of the manhole covers of the main sewer at Stockton Heath, several of which, he said, stood so high above the surface of the road as to make it dangerous to horses and conveyances. The inspector (Mr. Farrington) was directed to attend to the matter.—A nuisance was re- ported as existing at Halton station by the almost daily arrival of bones, which were saidby the medical officeri(Dr. Adams) to smell abominably. It was resolved to serve notice on the railway company to abate the nuisance.—This I was all the business of public interest. BUY YOUR GROCERIES from LAWLESS BROS., 5, Market- place, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: TEE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER, 18. 1886.
div.p: TEE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER, 18. 1886.

THEFT• OF POTATOES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, yesterday, Henry Randles, a young tramp, was con- victed of stealing a quantity of potatoes, the property ot Mr. Clarke, farmer, Upton Rocks, and he was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. THE REVISION AT RuNnonx.—The annual court for the revision of Parliamentary voters 10 the Runcorn Polling District will be held on Saturday next at the Sessions House, Runcorn. The claims are considerably more numer- ous than last year, and it is expected that one or two inter- , esting cases will be tried. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES NEW PUBLIC OFFICES.—John Brownball, of Victoria-place, Present, was seriously injured whilst following his employment as a joiner at the New Public Offices on Wednesday. A beam that had just been placed in position fell upon him and fractured his left leg and otherwise seriously injured him. THE INTER-WORKS FOOTBALL COMPETITION, WIDNES.— Last night the Widnes Alkali Company's numuer one team met a team representing the works of Nlessrs. Mathieson in the first round of the competition. The alkali, which in- cluded "Curley" Farrel and " Harry" Speakman, the Cheshire county three-quarter beck, had an easy victory. They scored 2 goals, 3 tries, and several minor points, to nil.

GOOD TEMPLARY AT RUNCORN.—The members of the Prosperity of Runcorn Lodge (No. T. 20), commenced their winter session on Wednesday evening by a tea party and entertainment. There was a good attendance. Mr. F. J. Norman occupied the chair after tea, and delivered a spesch. Addresses were also given by Sergeant-Major George Meads, P.G.W.C.. and Quarter-master Peter Hawthorn, G.W.S . of the United Service Grand Lodge, London. Songs and reci- tations were given by s:Neral brethren. SMUGGLING AT RUNCORN. Yesterday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, Janice Watizfisson, master of the schooner Mary Watkinson, was charged with smuggling three bottles of sweetened cor- dial spirits. Officer Goodall found the bottles concealed in the bunk in the captain's cabin. The prisoner said he had committed the offence in ignorance. Under these circum- stances the magistrates only fined him the single duty and the value of the spirits, 18s 10d, with 5s costs. ROBBING A RUNCORN DRAPER —At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Mary Ellis, a married woman, who lit-co in a house off Penketh-lane, was charged with stealing a number of pieces of oilcloth, worth ss, the property of Geo. Joseph King, draper, Bridge-street, Runcorn. It appeared that the oilcloth had been placed at the back of the business premises for the purpose of being painted, and pieces were missed from time to time. The prisoner stated that Mr. I King's servant, a girl named Edwards, gave her the cloth. I She called her son, who said the servant brought a piece of 1 the cloth and placed it behind the door. The Bench altered the charge to one of receiving stolen property, and fined the prisoner 20s. FAREWELL DINNER TO Mn. Jent BRIGGS.—A meeting of Widnes cricketers, and personal fliende of Mr. Jack Briggs, the Lancashire ceunty cricketer, was held at the Alexandra Hotel, qtrWeciriesday evening for the purpose of bidding that sterling player farewell previous to his departure to Australia with the English team. About sixty persons sat down to the tea provided by Mr. Gerrard, and subsequently an appropriate toast lie, interspersed with numerous songs, was gone through. Mr. William Moreland was in the chair.l The principal toast was, of course, "SuccePs to Mr. John Briggs," and it was proposed by Mr. S. Upward and drunk with musical honours. Mr Briggs suitably reeDonded. Yesterday morning the Lancashire professional cricketers, R. G. Barlow and J. Briggs, left Manchester to join Messrs. Shaw and Shrewsbury's team for Australia. DEATH FROM SHOCK AT RUNCORN.—At the Navigation Inn, Canal-street, on Monday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Sarah Heyes, aged 37, wife of a boatman named Thomas Heyes, in the employ of Mr. S. Taylor, boatownee. The evidence showed that the woman had been in delicate health for many months. On Friday night a constable served !a summons at the house I charging her husband with cruelty to a horse, and this "up- set" her very much. On Saturday morning she gave birth to a female child, and she received every attention from Mrs. Barrow, 3, Hope-street, Mrs. Ellen Brown, 45, Marson- street, and Sarah Houghton, 39 Mason-street. The deceased told Mrs. Barrow that she had not tasted food since Thurs- day, and she was very weak. On Saturday afternoon her condition was such that Dr. Robinson was sent for, but she expired before his arrival. The doctor was of opinion the woman had died from shock.—ln charging the jury, the ; deputy coroner complimented the neighbours of the de- ceased for the care they had bestowed upon her. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased died from the ' anxiety caused to the deceased from the probable conse- quences of the summons, such anxiety operating upon a weak constitution. THE APPROACHING WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION. —The triennial election of 11 members of the Widnes School Board will take place in November next, and it is considered probable that on the present occasien there will be an election. Last year the Church people, the Catholics, and the Nonconformists agreed upon the representation they desired, and thus avoided the expense and trouble of a contest. Dissatisfaction is said to reign in certain quarters, but as the time draws near an amicable settlement may be arrived at. On Monday evening a meeting of Churchmen was held in Page-lane Mission-room, under the presidency of the Rev S A Spooner. There was a good attendance, amonest those present being the Rev George Bond, the Rev A P Hamilton Wilson, Messrs E Carey, J Valentine, w Tracey, senr, W S Callander, J Williams, H Marcer, and J C Crawford (sec.) The United Church Council of St. Mary'r, St Ambrose's, and St Luke's had decided to submit the following names as candidates :—Mr T S Timmis, Mr H Wade Deacon, Mr J B Imison, and Mr J W Wareing. Mr John Brock, J.P., who had been selected as a candidate, has declined to stand in consequence of the pressure of busi- ness. The Rev J Wright was selected as a reserve candi- date, in case one of the gentlemen mentioned should fail to accede to the wishes of the councils, or it should, be neces- sary to run a fifth candidate. The Rev George Bond, who is of opinion that Farnworth does not receive the attention it merits, announced that he should appear as an independ- ent candidate. It was resolved that the secretary should ' write to the Catholic and Nonconformist parties, asking if , they were satisfied with the present relative strength of parties on the Board, and to state that if so, the Church ' party were also agreed. There are 4 Churchmen, 4 Catho- lic. and 3 Nonconformists on the Board. 1 PENKETH FOOTBALL CLITB.—On Monday night last the members ot the above club held their an- nual meeting, at their room at the Liberal Club when the following officers were elected to the various offices ;—Captain, Mr. James Dumbill, sub- ! captain, Mr. A. Greenhalsh ; treasurer, Mr. J.Foden; ! secretary, Mr. A. J. Pownall. PENKETH CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. Onl Saturday, the Conservatives of Penketh had a suc- cessful trip to the Liverpool Exhibition. About GO ! persons availed themselves of the opportunity. The busses, three in number, left the club-room at 7-30 a.m., and arrived back at Penketh at 11 p.m. THE LIBERAL CLUB FOR RuNconN.—From an ad- vertisement which appears in our advertising• columns it will be seen that a meeting of Liberals is called for Tuesday evening, to further discuss ! the important questions of forming a Liberal Club ' for the Runcorn district. We understand that the Committee appointed to draw up a scheme will re- port favourably, and in a matter of so vital import- ance to the party locally, it behoves all Liberals to .put in an- appearance at the meeting, and give the project their aid. THEFT BY A LODGER AT BI7RTONWOOD.—At War- rington County Petty • Sessions, on Wednesday, a young woman named Catherine Maher was brought up in custody on a charge of stealing a number of articles of clothing, valued in all at £3 ss, the pro- perty of Samuel Lloyd, teamsman, Burtonwood. From a statement made by Superintendent Weir, and evidence adduced, it appeared that prisoner in March last went to live at the house of' the prose- cutor as a lodger, and remained there until the 30th of last month, when she left. Mrs. Lloyd, early in the afternoon, went out to work, and on her return prisoner had left the house. From what sloe was told by her son, Mrs. Lloyd made a search of the house, and then missed the articles enumerated in the charge It afterwards transpired that prisoner had taken Mrs. Lloyd's little boy to Warrington, where she pawned some of the: articles, giving the tickets to the boy to take home. Other things she pawned at St. llelens. Afterwards she returned to the prosecutor's house, wearing a'stolen shawl, and having Mrs. Lloyd's hat under it, and said that she had come to give herself up. Mrs. Lloyd sent for P.C. Grundy, into whose charge she gave prisoner. Prisoner,who put no questions to the witnesses,was committed for trial. _ -

_ THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—Mr. Digby Sey- mour, Q.C., attended a gathering of the workpeople of Messrs. Daniel Adamson and Co. at Hyde, .on Aturday, and made some practical suggestions with regard to raising the capital necessary for the con- struction of the Manchester Ship Canal. He be- lieved that if five millions were raised the remain- ing three millions would be taken up at a handsome premium. As to raising the five millions, he had the assurance of leading financial men in London, that if the public could be relied on for half the amount " they,would undertake in the course of a day or two to underwrite and provide the rest."— Consequent upon Mr. Seymour's address, a deputa- tion from the men waited upon Mr. Adamson at his works at noon on Monday, and informed him that they had arranged to work at least two hours extra per week, ,the amount earned during that time to be deducted by the firm and invested for , ' the men in the capital of the Ship Canal. Taking a moderate estimate of the annual amount to be raised for the Ship Company from this source, the minimum will be £l,OOO, and it may run up to £3,000, depending on the state of trade. If the em- ployes of a thousand other firms of equal magnitude could be induced to follow this example, hardly any other subscriptions, it is stated, would be wanted. It only remains for the workmen of industrial establishments to organise a system on the same basis and communicate with the Directors of the Ship Canal Company. The whole matter may then be got into working order.

I A LONG RUN WITH HOUNDS. - The Cheshire ;Hounds met at Ridley Toll Barr for cub hunting on Monday, and had a remarkable run of 55 miles after a smart young fox. It was noted as a singular occurrence that during the whole of this long course the hunters.never came across a corn- field.

RELIEF FOR CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS.—The Cheshire dairy farmers, through the action of the County Dairy Farmer' Association, have just re- ceived communications from both the London and North-Western and Great Western Railway Com- panies announcing that a reduction of freights will be made on Cheshire cheese to London of 5s per ton. This relief will greatly affect dairy farmers, and the cheese trade with the metropolis will be largely tuagmented. A WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION has been started in the Crewe Division of Cheshire, with Mrs. Latham as first president. Mrs. M`Laren, wife of the representative of the division, met a large num- ber of intending members on Wednesday, and urged them to unite in assisting the Liberal party, which was seeking to bring about several reforms inti- mately concerning women. The new Asociation has already a large membership. VALUATIONS AND DEBTS OF LOCAL U•Nioxs.—A return just issued gives the gross estimated rental and rateable value as last received from the various Unions in Lancashire and Cheshire, and also the amount of loans owing by the Guardians. The fol- lowing are particulars in regard to local Unions : Warrington: rental £357,985, value £305,747, loans £14,782; Runcorn: rental £238,993, value -.q12,071, loans £2,708; Prescot : rental £772,574, value £636,594. loans £14,608. THE REVISION OF NEWTON DIVISION VOTERS.— The revision of voters for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire commences next Monday. The Revising Barrister will be Mr. James Thomas Foard. The first court will be held at Warrington on Monday, and on the following Monday the Re- vising Barrister will sit at the Newton Town Hall, on Tuesday at Ashton, Wednesday at St. Helens, Thursday at Golborne and Billinge, Friday at Pen- keth, and Saturday at Rainhill. COMMERCIAL DECADENCE AND . THE DRINK TRAFFlC.—Cardinal Manning visited Blackburn .on Wednesday evening, and, after administrating pledges to nearly a thousand children in St. Anne's Church, addressed a' great temperance meeting in the Exchange Hall. He declared that the drink traffic was the worm gnawing at the root of our Commercial prosperity, and a great cause of trade depression. He argued strongly in favour of local option and Sunday closing. Parliament should un- do what it had done by passing licensing laws ; and as members in favour of local option increased in number with each extension of the franchise, he was hopeful of legislative action. Much could be done by personal effort.
FATALItY .THROUGH CARELESSNESS AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Saturday held an inquest, at Widnes Accident Hospital concerning the death of Elias Robinson, aged 32 years. who bad lived at 3, Travis-street, Widaes. The deceased was a brick- layer employed at the works of the Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Company, Limited. Ditton-road. On Tuesday, the 31st August, whilst he was erecting a brick wall round a stone bin, a derrick pole fell upon him and indicted such in- juries that he died on Wednesday last week. From the evidence of Thomas Stanton, of thanville-street, Runcoru, It appeared that the derrick was erected near to where the deceased was at work. At the time the inclination of the poll was being altered, avid one of the chains btoke whilst the witness and two other men were pulling at it. In reply to Mr. W. J. Swift (who represented the relatives of the de- ceased), witness said the chain lied been broken and linked with an "S " link. It was the "S " link that broke. On Sunday a tank of 14 or 15 cwt. had been lifted with the chain.—By the Deputy Coroner: He did not warn the deceased to get out of the way whilst the job was being altered.—Mr. Leith (who reliresented the firm with Mr. E. J. H. Synge), said the chain was a quarter of an inch thick.—Miss Downie, matron of the hospital, deposed that the deceased suffered from injuries to the head, shoulders, and chest-. He was attended by Dr. O'Keeffe, and everything possible was 'done for him. The deceased spoke to her about the acci- dent. He told her that Stanten was a careless man, and that he had often warned him about his carelessness.—John Conway, 31, Milton-street, Widnes, said he was a labourer at the works, and gave evidence similar to Stanton. Stan- ton. he stated, was not a careless man. He had no doubt about the chain. He was a bit doubtful about the "S " hook, and showed it to Stant di, who said it was good enough. There was no other chain they could use —Mr. E. J. li. Synge was called, and said he was the sub-manager at the works. It was not correct that there was no other chain to be got. There was a lot of spare chains lying where the accident occurred. The blacksmith had no right to do anything without his orders, anti he had no authority to put on the "S" link. In his opinion the link broke in consequence of the shape of the bend. 1n his opinion Stan- ton was quite competent for the work, but he should not have let the" S" link have been used had he known.—Stanton recalled, denied that the deceased had ever told him he was a careless man, anal warned him. He considered the chain strong enough, and when Conway said he was doubtful, he did not see the blacksmith. He acted on his own responsi- bility.—The Deputy Coroner, in addressing the jury, said the question they had to decide was whether Stanton was so far criminally responsible for the death of Robinson that they coald send him to the Assizes for trial. The least bit of forethought would have prevented• the accident. It would have been avoided if the men had simply warned Robinson to get out of the way while the derrick was tieing altered. That Stanton deserved a severe reprimand he had not the slightest hesitation in saying.—After 15 minutes' deliberation the jury, through the foreman (Mr. B. Dutton) stated that they considered the managers of the firm were almost culpably neglectful in not seeing that the work was in order before it came into the hands of Stanton. They found further that the derrick was being moved apparently without anyone being in charge who understood the work. The jury had seriously considered whether they ouvilt not to find Stanton criminally responsible for the accident, and they recommended, after viewing the whole of the circumstances, that he should be strongly censured for his conduct in the matter. Thy considered that Stanton was morally responsible for Robinson's death. —The Coroner said bad he been a juryman he, should cer- tainly have been of opinion that Stanton should have been sent for trial. He severely censured Stanton, who said he would be more careful in the future.—The foreman said the jury also recommended that the firm should in future use six guy chains to a derrick instead of four. The verdict was ".Accidental death."
UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.
OPENING OF NEW SCHOOLS.

A very pleasant gathering took place on Monday evening in connection with the Zion United Methodist Free Church, Widnes. Its purpose was three-fold. The chief object was, perhaps, the opening of the new schools, in which the meet- ing was held, secondly, the reception of the Rev. E. Hall, the recently appointed pastor, and then the presentation of a timepiece to the Rev. W. Vause, of Blackburn, who until a few months ago was the minister of the Runcorn circuit, of which Widnes forms a part. The school, it may be stated, has been erected by Mr. T. Sadler, builder and con- tractor, at a cost of nearly £5OO. In its exterior the build- ing harmonises with the chapel adjoining, and has a good appearance. The dimensioes of the interior are 53 feet by 311 feet, and sitting accommodation is provided for about 400 persous. The room is well lighted, well ventilated, will be heated by the hot water system, and is altogether well adapted for the purpose intended. The furniture has been made by several members of the congregation, and their handiwork does them great credit. The gas fittings were fixed free of charge by Messrs. Myers, Hartland, and Case, and they were heartily thanked for their generosity. The proceedings commenced on Monday evening with a tea party, at which there was a good company present. Subse- quently, a public meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. Greig, and there was a large audience. After devotional exercises the report of the secretary (Mr. John Betney, jute.) was read. It stated that some 13 years ago the adjoining building was erected to serve the purpose of both school and. chapel. Daring this period the school had made consider- able progress, end the scholars became so numerous that the chapel did not afford sufficient accommodation. At present there were on the books 134 males and 138 females, with 35 teachers, making a total of 307. It was thought desirable for the g ,od of the school and the neighbourhood generally, that a new building should be erected to serve as a Sunday school, and the result ot their efforts was the building in which they were assembled. Towards the.cost about £l7O had been raised by means of a bazaar, harvest festival, &c. By hard work and economy they hoped to liquidate the debt in a few years. (Applause.)—The Chairman, in the name of the church, then gave the Rev. E. Hall a cordial welcome, and expressed the hope that his ministry amongst them would be a success. (Applause.)—The rev, gentleman, who had a most enthusiastic reception, promised that no effort should be wanting on his part to give every satisfaction. In a brief though eloquent address he dealt with the question of Sunday school work, and gave the parents and teachers some advice which was attentively listened to.—Mr. John Betney, sen., now presented the Rev. W. Vause with a beautiful timepiece, as a memento of his three years' labours in Widnes. During that period, he said, they had had abundant opportunities of knowing Mr. Vause thoroughly. They learned to admire his good quali- ties of hand and heart, and recognised that his desire and aim was to elevate his fellow man, both morally, spiritually, and socially. He was what many were fond of terming a political parson—(applause)—lant his politics never inter- fered with his religion, and he was ever ready to identify himself with the pleasures and sorrows, the trials and vicisi- tudes and troubles of the people. He could assure Mr. Vause that be had left many frieads behind him in Widnes and Runcorn, and it was the earnest hope of all that not only at Blackburn, but throughout his future career, he might be attended with every success. (Applause )—Mr. Lock also spoke. He thoroughly endorsed all their worthy chairman had said with regard to Mr. Vanse's 'ministrations. They felt better for his labours amongst them, and they thanked bim for the interest he took in them. (Applause.) With

irespect to Mr. Hall, they promised to do all they could to make their c,intring together of advantage to ' all of them. (Applanse.)—The Chairman said they bad to thank Mr. Vanse in a great measure for , their Sunday school. (Hear, hear.) He worked mors eareestly than he had seen any man .work in the caus?!. ..(Applause.) —Mr. Vause, wh4 wig cordially greeted, said be received many kindnesses at their , hands whilst he was amongst them, and now that he had left be was again indebted to them. .He should ever look U-ck upon Widnes as the sp.)t that be loved, and he should remember the people of Widnes because of the help they gave hitn in the irork of the Lord, and of the solid progress they made whilst they were associated together. There were churches in the coorn,ction that had made greater progress, but when be thought of al they had done togetljer during the past three years, he doubted whether there had been any chuiches that had made more centinuoris and solid progress during that palod. (Hear, hear.) From the spirit which he knew anirated the Widnes Mende, and from the good accounts he had heard of Mr: Hall bad doubt that toe three years which were n., . he now before them would be more successful than the three years that were passed. (Applause.) That beautiful timepiece ,epuld remiod him again and again of the Widnes friends. , When be thought OA they bad raised so much money durng the 'past year, arid although anxions to clear off the debt on the school, were willing to make an extra:et-Tort in the midst «f so many efforts. his sense of gratitude to them was inCreased. He Omni,' always remember the With ' nes friends w 1.1) the greatest, affection and. love. ( A pp'a use.) The proceedings were enlivened by Abe following items : —Song' Our PulAv Cat," Alfred Voyd ; Lancashire read- reading. Mr. T. Riley (Runcorn); song, "Thy voice is near," Miss E. Rutuns.in ; sueg, " fire musical gent," Miss A. Benney ; pianoforte sulo, Mr. A. Ogden ; song, "The right man in the right place." Mr. W. A. Price; song," The fickle man," Mr. A. Price; song, "He wipes the tear from every eye," Mrs Locke; sung, Bertha Lloyd; recitation, Mr. Riley. Mr. A. Ogden officiated at the pianoforte, and Mr. J. Betney, senr., conducted the choir. The meeting concluded with singing the doxology.

Lieutenant Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present—Mr. Weir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. Lock- wood and J. W. N. Tanner. Messrs. Aaron, Mclntyre, Stokes,. SpQakmari. Had fleld, Wallington, Brandre:h, Knowles, Whitlow, Lewis, Warburton, 'Fisher, H. Liaaker (clerk), and W.- H. Linaker (&pury clf-rk). - - - THE MaerEaaND Misraes,.— It was reported Via: the c-erneni`tee" appe,sited wirn ref.-renc-s to the ressenitien of the MstAer and Matson of the •Workhou-e bed new] ved that successors be advertised for, the salary for the master to be £7O, and for the tnAtron £3O, a year. Tbe present master had been eeceiving £BO, and the matron £55 a year. The report was adopted. RELIEF SUPERVIL,ION.—The report of the Relief Super- , vision Committee was adopted on the motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood. - It was not of public interest. Ts s CALLS—The Clerk reported that the calls due from several townships were as yet unpaid. The total . amount not paid was £647. It was resolved to take meaus to recover the money befo4 the 23rd instant. THE Foca Law CONFERENCE—Mr. Speakman drew the attention of the Board to the Poor Low Conference about to take place at Uverpool, and asked if it was the custom of the Board to send a deputation to such conferences. It was stated that it had not been customary, and, after a little discussion, it was decided not to appoint a deputation.. Fueelecs Commerrsa—The Rev. J. Lockwood proposed the adoption of the report of the Finance Committee, which included a report and estimate of the probable balance in favour of or against each township in the, Runcorn Poor Law Union, at the end of Current half-year ending Michael- mas 1886, and amount of con•ributions required from the overseers of the.respective townships in the Union, to meet the expenditure of ensuing half-year ending Lady Day, 1837. The report statA that the basis of lontributions re- (paired from the overseers for the ensuing half-year, ending Lady Day, 1887, was submitted for consideration, being calculated on rateable value as per valua- tion lists in force. The total capital for the cur- rent half-year ending Michaelmas, 1886, amounted to £3,425, and the net probable expenditure was estimated at £8,454, which showed a probable balanca in favour of the Union at Michaelmas, 1886, of £1,971. The , probable expenditure during the ensuing half-year ending Lady Day, 1886, was the school fees of non-pauper chil- dren £l2, county rate £1,590, net common fund charges £3,740, balance and contingency fund £2,000, total £7,342. The total amount required as above for ensuing half-year ending Lady Day, 1877, was £7,342, and after taking credit for the probable balance at Michaelmas, .1886, the amount required by contribution orders from the overseers is £5,371. The rateable value of the Union, as per valuation lists im force, was £213.517, being a'decrease of £B2O, as compued with the corresponding period of laet year. A rate of 6d in the £ would produce the sum of £5,337 18s 6d, being an in- crease of din the £, as compared with the corresponding period of last year, and a decrease of id in the £ as com- pared with rate for current half-year ending Michaelmas, 1888. These calculations, the report added, were subject to alterations which might be made in valuation lists previous themontribution orders being signed, the following im- portant matters being included :—lncreased assessment of Bridgewater Naviestion Company's property, assessment of Mersey Salt and Brine Company's property, sundry valua- tion and supplemental valuation lists. The county rate precept amounting to £1,154 7s Bd, the preceptfor constabu- lary general expenditure £ll5 7e Bd, and that for constabu- lary local expenditure £230 16s 10d, making a total of £1,500 12s 21. The total last year was £1,319 7e 11d.— The 'report Was adopted without discussion. The Board then proceeded with relief business.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly Ineeting was held on Tuesday, under .the presidency of Mr. F. H. Gossagi. J. P. Present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, W. W. Go3s4ge, J. Midwood, F. Heyes, J. Taylor. J. Hourihton, S. Sadler. R. Cook, W. T. Husband, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (ea- gineer), T. Higginson (surveyor),

div.head: POLLUTION OF NETHERBY BROOK.
div.p: THE POLLUTION OF NETHERBY BROOK.

The following letter was received from the clerk of Little Woolton Local Board :—Referring to your letter of the 4th instant, which was laid before this Board at its meeting, held yesterdty, lam directed to inform you that the In- spector of Nuisances of this Ilvird reported to the meeting that the foul condition of the Netherby Brook was caused by sewage from the Huyton-with•Roby district, and also that the duyton-with-Roby Local Board have been re- quested by the Board to take immediate steps to effectually abate the anisance."—The clerk to the Huy- ton-with-Roby Local Board wrote en the 11th inst. with reference to the sewage farm :—" This Board has received a report from their analytical chemist, and a resolution has been passed to carry out his recommendations, which he states will prevent any nuisance whatever."—The Chair- man said these letters were so far satisfactory, but the matter ehould net be allowerl to drop by the Board for one moment. The Beard should be continually on the alert to see whether the nuisance was abated. There had been two or three ways pointed out by which these nuisances could he abated by the Huvton-with-Roby Local Board. Whether the Huyton- Board intended te adopt one of these systems or not was a question the Widnes Board ought to watch most carefully.

div.head: GAS AND ICATER.-INTERESTING ITEMS,
div.p: GAS AND ICATER.-INTERESTING ITEMS,

The Engineer reported tc the the and Water Committee that the waste of water in Simm's Cross 'district had been reduced about four gallon pee head; the present total supply is at the rate of 7,14 gallons per head, MG of which is waste. He recommended that a six inch meter should be fixed at the bottom of Peelhouse-lane, • which would check the supply to the whole of the east portion of the township, including Appleton, Halton View, Crow Wood, Warrington-road, and LugedAle districts. The mean rainfall for the month was 1.77 inches, and the water in stock on August 25th was 10,408,749 gallons. The illu- minating power of the gas during the past month had averaged 17.05 candles was recommended that a waste water meter be fixed in Albert-road, near Peelhouse-lane It was also recommended that•the charge for water for baths he discentinned from the 30th met, and that the charge for water closets in dweiling-houses be not enforced from the same date in the case o! closets fitted with a two gallon flushing cistern. It was further recommended that no ten- der for tar be accepted, but that the tar be used for firing Purposes ; that the trice of gas be reduced from let July 31 per 1,000 feet. and that a gas stove exhibition be held and a series of lectures en cooking given.—The minutes were paseed on the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. W. W. Gossage.

div.head: PRIVATE IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: PRIVATE IMPROVEMENTS.

Tha Highway Committee recommended that the tenders on schedule of prices of Mr. F. Chadwick be accented for the fo'lowin streets :—Viaduct-street £789 7s, Irwell-stre.t £1,017 61, West-street £1,083 ss. Parsons.ge-road £420 18s, and James-street £651 se; total, £3.945 Is. It was also recommend,cl that the tenders of Cocks and Smith for the followinz streets be accented :—Wallington-s.-reet £563 12s 01, Victoria-street £614, Margaret-street £33t 18s 7d, Farrant-street £2Bl 9s. New-street £266 13s 6d, Ellison- street £322 15s 7d, Lea-street £207 5, Fisher- street £243 193 9d. and Brynn-street £125 104 id; total, £2,961 4s. These were accepted in each case, subject to the sureties being satisfactory.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Sadler.

HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer of Health reported to the Health Committee that during August there were 92 births and 72 deaths, representing rates respectively 40.14 and 3141 per 1,000. Of the deaths 43 occurred amongst children under one year. and 14 amongst children between one and fire Years. Zymotic diseases caused 18 deaths. The Nuisance Inspector reported that 10 deaths were from diarrheet. and two from whooping cough. It was recommended that the Health Committee be empowered in future to take proceed- ings on behalf of tho Board for the abatement af all nuis- ances requiring prompt attmtion.—Dr. O'Keeffe in the ! adoption of the minutes said the deaths seemed to exceed what they had usually in Widnes, and the rate was enormous indeed. If, however, they took from them the number of children who had died under one year, and between one and five years, the death rate was reduced, and brought the sanitary condition of Widnes to a very healthy position.
THE INFECTIOUS DISFASES HOSPITAL.
Dr. Page, of the iOC-ii-1 Government Board, forwarded

plans to the Local Board, and advised that the administra- tive block or a caretaker's cottage should Ve added to the Infectious Diseases Hosoital.—Dr. O'Keeffe said Dr. Page did not at all approve of the Board's ,intention to remove the wooden hut from the Old small pox hospital, and cause the caretaker or-nurse to live in it. Dr. Page advised that the administrative block or a cottage should be erected. There would be very 'little difference in the price for the erection of either of these buildings, bat it was for the Board to decide.—Mr. Carey said he should oppose the building of the administrative block or the cottage.—Dr. O'Kseffe said if the Board wished to ignore the recommendation of Dr. Page he was perfectly satisfied.—lt was ultimately decided that the Health Committee should submit a more explicit and definite recommendation at the next meeting. THE INSPECTION OF COW SHEDS, &C

Dr. O'Keeffa said under the new regulations ef the Local Government Board power was now vested in the Widnes Local Board to examine cow sheds, dairie,, and milkshops, and under the direction of the Health Committee the clerk had drawn up regulations with a very great deal of care and trouble after correspondence with many sanitary authori- ties in this portion of Lancashire and other counties in Eng- land. They were proposed that day for the approval of the Board, and he had no doubt, if thoroughly carried out, they would be for the benefit of those who kept C-31,1 sheds, dairies, &c, and for the benefit of the inhaoitants generally. The regulagions were approved.

div.head: SAYING.
div.p: A SAYING.

On the recommendation of the Health Committee, it was decided that application be made to the Local Government Board to sanction Mr. Cooper's appointment'as medical officer of health for the following 12 months, that the Lon- don Board be asked for a moiety of the salaries of that officer and of the sanitary inspector.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The minutes of the Finance Committee, adopted, on the motion of Mr. Handley, contained a recommendation that two loans of £6OO each. at 3i per cent for five years be ac- cepted. The Local Government Board sanctioned the bor- rowing of £7,644 for seven years for private street improve- ments. It was resolved that six months' notice be given to , Lancashire and Earnshaw terminating the lease of the present offices. Accounts amounting to £7,117 6s 10d were passed for payment. The General Purposes Committee submitted the following minute :—Priblic Offices: Letters from architects, 17th July, enclosing tracing !thawing new doorway connecting engine-room and waiting-room: 7th September, enclosing tracing shewing arrangemenrxfor fire escape and hose drying, also statin4 that tbe en2int-roorn can be warmed with hot water pipes from library service for £5 and 11th August, ackin4 to be &Lowed te in- cur RR ex ra expense of £4O, afterwards reduced to .f:23, for a dado of be;rer wood and an improved ceiling in the board- room.—Recornmended, that the new doorway, the arrange- ments for fire applianc4s, and the extras of -£5 and £2O, be approved.—Mr. Carey explained that it was intended that the dado should be of yellow pine painted, and several mem- bers of the committee considered that that would Make the Board-room, which was to be used for the School Board and for general public purposes, look very common indeed. It i was therefore thought better to have these extras recom- mended by the architect. The dado would now be a mix- ture of Walnut and oak.—The minute was adopted.

div.head: COAT OF ARMS AND MOTTO.
div.p: THE COAT OF ARMS AND MOTTO.

• From the minutes of the General Purposes Coaomittee it appeared that Sir James Pieter' had been consulted as to the coat of arms arid motto for the town. Sir James suggested that the coat of arms should be a shield—half to be. from 'the Duchy coat of Irma, and ;he other, half "Bees," with a suitable motto. It was recommended that this suggestion be adopted, and that the motto should to "Industry, valour, and fortitude."—Mr. Carey moved the adoption of the mi- nutes, and a tracing of the coat of arms was handed round to the members. In reply to questions, Mr. Carey said -Sir James suggested three mottoi. The first was" Hine odor at saaitas"—hence fragrance and health. (Laughter.) The second was "Jadustria ditat "—industry egriches ; and the third "Industrie virtue et fortitudo "—industry, valour, and fortitude.—Dr. O'Keeffe said the first would be pecu- liarly appropriate to Widnes—(laughter)—but he thought the second was the best, and he moved an amendment that the second be adopted.—Mr. Carey said he should cartainly object to the first. It was only laughing at us —The Chair- man ; The first was only proposed in a joke.—Dr. O'Keeffe said he had thought of suggesting " Floriat semper "—may it always flourish.—Mr. Carey : A very good seatiment,"doc- tor.—The motto "Industry enriches" was then adopted.— Mr. Husband described‘he liens on the coat of arms as more like rampant torn cats—(lauglkter)--,and moved that the matter be referred back so that the members might con- sider the matter.—Mr. Heyes kchnired the li,ns. They ware "on the smile." (Laughter.)—Mr. Husband's motion was not seconded, and the coat of arms was therefore adopted.— On the proposition of Mr. Carey, seconded by Dr. O'Keeffe, cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Sir James Picton for the pains and trouble be had taken in the matter. There was no other business.

div.head: FARN WORTH AGRICULTURAL . SOCIETY.
div.p: FARN WORTH AGRICULTURAL . SOCIETY.
ANNUAL SHOW.

The annual show of the Farn worth Agricultural Society was held at the show field, Farnworth on Thursday. For 22 years the society has existed with varying good and bad fortune, but ever maintaining its position as an organisation intended, and ins great measure securing ita aim to aid the tenant farmers in die!' stock raising purimits. Two years ago, through a succession of bad seasons, the society was burdened with a debt of £3OO, but the committee, of which Mr. Wm. Longton, Eccleeton Grange. Prescot, is the chairman, and Mr. James Warburton, Dallam, and Mr. Thos Baker, Bold, are rice-chairmen, bravely battled for the good of the society, and Usti year the annual exhibition is expected to wipe off the debt of about £lOO which now remains. In all itsaspects Thursday's show was one of the most success- ful ever held by the society. The entries showed an en- couraging increase, the exhibits were numerous, and the spectators, who paid for entrance, were numbered in thou- sands. The annexed comparative table of the entries will be read with interest : • 1881 1882 1883 1884 18'5 188% Cattle _B5 _3O

Farm and Garden Produce In the early morning the witti was bitterly cold and the attendance up to one o'clock was considerably bslow the average. After that hoar the clerks at the turnstiles were kept busily at work, and the field presented a veryinimated spectacle. The principal attraction of the afternoon was the jumping of the horses, and thousands lined the enclo- sure. whilst the stands were well filled. In the contest for horses 15-2 hands and upwards, the competition was very keen. Better all-round jumping had never been seen on the Farnworth field, and seldom at any show of much greater pretensions has it been surpassed. Very few mistakes were made, and the leaping of a bay be- longing to Mr. Wm. Dodsworth, Nottingham. excited nniver- , eal admiration. The animal, ridden by a boy about 14 years of age, cleared the hurdles very cleanly, and on each occa- sion the water jump was performed in grand style. It was fully expected that it would be awarded the first prize, and a shout of astonishment arose when the coveted red card was handed to the rider of a light grey belonging to-Mr. J. G. Sykes. of Poulton-le-Fylde. This animal had, however, performed capitally, but not with the same dash and style as the third prize winner. The black mare belonging to Mr. Gilbert Helsel!, of Halewood. ran the prize winners very close, but was very unlucky in its last round. In the ales for the best horse under 15-2 hands, the leaping was not of the some excellency, and early on a serious scc,cleht occurred. When attempting the first hurdle, the jockey of I a beautiful dark brown mare, "Little Queen," belonging to the Stand Stud Company, was thrown. He alighted partly on his head and shoulder, whilst the horse rolled on its side happily clear of its rider. It was thought the jockey had his neck broken, so awkward was the fall, but an examina- tion by Der. McDonnell and Neil revealed the fact that no bones were broken, and that the injuries, although serious, were not dangerous- He had, however, received a shock that will prevent him from riding for many a day. Later, a horse leaped the rails amongst the crowd, but no person was injured. With regard to the other classes of horses, the mares with foals were of an inferior character ; but the three year olds were of a very superior class, and the competitiora was very keen. Lord A. Cecil took honours with his bay Crocus. The two year olds in the opinion of competent judges were fit to appear at any show. The competition amongst one year olds was very limit,d, but the animals shown were worthy of note. The team horses were an admirable lot, and better animals were never exhibited at Farnworth. In 1884 and 1885, owing to the prevalence of swine fever, pigs could not he exhile'ted, but the district being free from disease at present there was a very good show of these animals. The middls and small breed were very good, but in the class for the best boar the prize was withheld, none of the ani- mals exhibited being deemed wo,thr of a pize As usual, the dogs were numerous, and of line breed, are' emelt a collection of animals can seldom be seen. In 6,158 there were some eolendid specirresne, awl tee judess +rad a most difficult task in awarding the prenri,r lewoure. The cattle showed a great improvement upon Any or erieus year, and induced cornmenderione from He memos good judges. The excellency of the animals may be tali,ll from tee fact that a Pair of dairy cows belonging to Messrs. James and Walter Birch, which were placed first at Chester last week, had here to be content with a less honour. The Preeident, the Hon. Lord Lionel C-cil, oreside,l at the luncheon. which took place in a tent on the show ground at one o'clock, the caterer being the proprietor of the Griffin Inn, Farnworth. The President was supported by the Rev. George Bond, vicar of Fa.rnworth ' • the Rev. J. E. Lawton, curate of Garston ; and Messrs. Robert Davies, of Warring. ton; William Longton, Eccleston Grange, Prescot (chair- man of the Committee of Management); Mr. James War- burton, one of the vice-chairmen; Mr. W. F. Earle, Mr. Charles Sherwin, of Altrinchana ; Mr. T. Hedgecock, Widnes; Mr. Thomas Baker, of Bold; Mr. Richard Hedgecock, Huyton ; Mr. T. leenwright, and Mr. Griffith!,. of Hale.
After the usual loyal toasts, the CII&IRMAN proposed " The clergy and ministers of all denominations." _ _

• The Rev. G BOND, in responding, said he was very glad. indeed to return thanks once more on behalf of the cletgy. He trusted that measures would be taken shortly to ensure, if possible, the greater prosperity of the landed int:a-est,. whirii had been lately so distressed. (Applause.)

. , Th., CHAIRMAN said the next toast was " Succ-ss to the Farnwerth Agricultural Society." (Applause.) He con- sider,al himself someahat of a judge of what agricultural societies should he, as be had had a great deal to do with them in his farm in Scotland. He was a tenant farmer there, as they perhaps all knew, and, of course, they found that these local shaws did an immense amount of good to the stock in the country. (Applause.) They improved the stack all thraugh the country, and without them they would not be able to get such good specimens. At tl.e same time they required an immense amount of worklng up, as he had no donbt Mr. Longton, the Chairman of the Committee of Management, could tell them but they weie certainly worth the trouble. (Ap- plause.) He supposed that a few years ago this society was in low water, but he was glad to hear, that it was now more likely to pick up. Another advantage of taese local shows, as Mr. Bond had pointed out, was that they brought landlord and tenant together to discu.s matters and make friends. In these times that was a most important molter, though he was quite sure that in Lincishire there was al- ways a good feeling between landlord and tenant, and the only way of keeping it ep was to continue shows like the present. (Applause). Mr. LoNo.roN had great pleasure in responding to the toast which had been so ably proposed litr their noble friend the chairmao, because he knew that Lord Cecil did so from his heart and with the best possible feeling. This was a local agricultural society, as most of them knew, and was supported by really practical small forrnele. The support they were receiving that day from their friends, and Dar. t'cularly from the chairman, acted as a stimulus to them, and enabled the commf.ttee to work with redoubled energy —with the energy which it was necessary for all Eng- lishman to put forth if they wished to have a glorious issue. ' (Applause,) The health of the president was given by Mr. Robert Davies, and responded to by the chairman.—Mr. James I Warburton propased the health of th.. judge.—Mi. Charles ISherwin, of Altrincham, respandel. He said the show was an erztNmely good one, as far as the dairy stock was con- cerned, a class be bad had under his care. (AWause.)

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE
_ WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Alderman Davies, Councillor Greening,

and Mr. John Fairclough. NAGLIGItNT FUSTIAN Curruus.—Margaret Gibbons was charged on a warrant with absenting her3elf from work as an apprentice to Mr. Platt, on the lUt'a February. The sum of 5s was asked for as nominal compensation. De- fendant was ordered to pay that amount, with costs, at 6d a week. an te return to work. Similar oraers were made upon Ellen McGinn and Elizabeth Ann Wordsworth. DRUNEENNESS.—James Codey was fined lOs and costs, or 14 days' hard 'labour, for being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street on Saturday night.—Margaret Fleming was charged with being drunk and disorderly at the pollee sta- tion. She went to the police station and demanded that she should he locked up. She behaved in a very disorderly manner. Tr,e magistrates sent her to prtson for a month.— John Cusack, for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., on Sunday morning, was fined 5s and costs.—John Mullen, charged with being drunk and disorderly on Pinner's-brow, on the 4th inst. was fined 103 and costs —Thomas Gor- man was charged with being drank and disorderly in Winwick-street, on the 4th inst. He was tined 5s and costs. —Margaret O'Brien and Annie Daley, young girls, were each sent to prison for a month for drunkenness and dis- orderly conduct in Horsern trket-street, on the 14th inst.— For being drunk and disorderly in Old-road, Latchford, on the sth inst, Mary Burns WAS fined 5s and costs.—James Farrell was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Arnolds-yard, Haydock-street, on Saturday night, with assaulting Mary Thompson, and with damaging the door of a house to the amount of 23 6d. The magistrates fined him 5s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, and ordered him to pay 23 64 to defray the damage. SUSPECTED.—Richtrd Mellor, a tramp, was charged with being on the premises of the Union Workhouse between midnight and one o'clock on Sunday morning, with intent to commit a felony. The Bench said that they had some doubts as to the sanity of the prisoner, but would commit him for seven days to orison, where his state of mind would ne inquired into. THRMATS.—Robert Barns was summoned for using threats to his father, Patrick Burns, on the 7th inst. He was ordered to he bound over, himself in 10 and one surety in £5, to keep the peace for six months, or go to prison for 14 '!.ays- A NUISANCE.—Sarah Percival, who did not appear, was summoned for allowing a nuisance to exist en the premises, 12, Friars-green. Inspector Norman proved the case. The Bench ordered that the work be done in seven days, and that defendant pay the costs. DISTURBING THS PRACE.—Patrick Macdonald was sum- moned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Buckley-street, on the sth inst. He was ordered to find a surety of £5, and to be bound over himself in £lO, to keep the peace for six months, the alternative was seven days' imprisonment. MISCELIEF.—Frank Dyer, a respectably dressed boy, pleaded guilty to ringing. a door bell at St. Mary's-street, Latchford, on the 9th inst, to the annoyance of the resi- dents. The Bench ordered him to pay 3s 6d, including costs.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—Thomas Walmslev, sweep, Tur- ner's-square, WAS summoned by Mr. George Riley, for not sending his child Thomas regularly to school. It was the eigth time he bad been summoned. The Bench inflicted a fine of ss, including costs. W RDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Jahn Fairclough. UNKANNESS

Da.,.—Samuel Cawley, an elderly man, who said that he came from Northwich, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Butterrnarket-street, on the pre- vious evening. He was discharged on promising to leave the town.

THIMSDAY.—Before Major Litton. DRUNKRNNESS.— George Brown, charged with being drunk And disorderly in Eorsemarket-street on the previous day, was dismissed on promising to leave the town. DusitaTiow.—James Sullivan, charged with deserting from the Fusiliers at Salford, was remanded to Strangeways. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Dr. Gornall. _ .

DRUNIKENNESS.—Margaret Riley was fined lOs and costs for being drunk in Scotland-road on the previous evening. —Margaret Rigby, an elderly woman, was charged with be- ing drunk and disorderly in Guardian-street on the previous night. From the evidence it appeared that she was very violent and abusive. The magistrates discharged her on condition that she went to the Workhouse. SLEEPING Our.—Bridget Lally wag committed to prison for a month for sleeping out in a field off Battersby-lane, without vieibie means of subsistence.
_ WIFE ASSAULT.—John Longshaw was summoned by his wife, Agnes, for assAulting her on the 14th inst. The Bench ordered him to find two sureties in £lO each to keep the peace for six months.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDA.Y.—Before Mr. P. Stubs. DnuNgemerEss.—William and Eliza Cresswell, were each fined 5s and coats for being drunk and disorderly on the 14th ult., at Penketh, and Williara Carrington was simi. larly fined for being drunk at Penketh on the 11th inst.— Patrick Donoghue and George Cosgrove were each fined 53 and costs for being drunk in the highway at Newton.—John Jones, for being drunk and disorderly at Winwick-road, on Sunday. WA3 fined 5s and costs.—Thomas Wroth well was charged with being drusk and disorderly at Burtonwood on the 2-d inst. He was fined 5s and Costs. STEALING CU CUMBERS. —Gilbert Warburton and Thomas Heesorn, boy,e, were each ordered to be imprisoned for one day for stealing three cucumbers at Poditon on the 12th Sept., the property of William Warhurton. Da rem ON LICENSED PREMISES AT EARI.ESTOWN.— Patrick Donoghue, collier, was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, for being drunk on the licensed premises of Mr. Lythgoe, the Prince of Wales Inn, Earles- town, on the 14th ult. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH. William Melling was fined 53 and costs for riding a bicycle on a footpath, at Poulton, on the 27th July. ilmnwAy OFFENCES.—John Gilfadder was fined is and costa for not having proper control of a horse, of which he was in charge, and John Cartledge was fined a like amount - for driving furiously. CHARGE OF STEALING A JAcsiirr.—Charles Holden was remanded on bail on a charge of stLaling a cardigan jacket, value 7s, from a field at Orford, on the previous afternoon. Mr. P. Davies detenied, and said that the defendant had no intention of stealing the jacket.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs, W. Long, T. P. Norris, H. Stanton, and C. Lister. DuuNrcENNEss.—Peter Harrison, for having been drunk and disorderly at Lymm on the 4th inst., was fined 5s and costs 53 6d.—Paul Grant and his wife, Elizabeth Grant, were charged with having committed a like offence on the 12th inst. at Lvmm, and were each fined 5s and costs, 8s Gd each. —Mary Brazendale, drunk and disorderly at Lymm on the 14th inst, was ordered to pay costs, 4s 6d.—James Rourke, of High Leigh, drunk at Lymm on the 18th ult, was fined 5s and costs, 83 6d.—William Braeendale, drunk at Heatley on the 21st ult, 5s and costs.—Thomas Demp- sey, drunk at Lymrn on the sth inst, ordered to pay costs, 4s 61—Patrick Kirby, drunk at Lymm on the 12th nest, ordered to pay costs, 43 6d. SwINE FEVER.—Samuel C. Cooper, farmer, West Derby, was charged with having caused three pigs to be unlawfully moved into a circle declared to be infected with swine fever. It was stated that a servant of the defendant was seen conveying three pigs in a cart at tiigh Leigh on the . 21st ult, the district having been declared an infected cir- cle. Defendant said the pigs were being removed from his farm at West Derby to Rushton, in Staffordshire, and he was unaware that they had to pass through an infected district.—The magistrates ordered defendant to pay the costs. A CARLESS DRlVER.—Michael Tully was charged with having been asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart at Thelwall, and was ordered to pay 23 6d costs. NEGLECTED CHILDREN.—Thomas Lee, a labourer, was charged with not sending three of his chilldren regularly to school. It was stated that the defendant was a farm labourer, and had been left a widower between two and three years ago. Whilst he was at work there was no one left in charge of the children, who were found sleeping in a pig- stye one night, and on another occasion they were taken home at twelve o'clock at night, and could not then get in. The Bench adioarned the case for a month in order to give defendant a chance of looking better after the children, and Mr. Moore, the school attendance officer, was instructed that if defendant did not avail himself of this opportunity to surnenontiim under the Vagrancy Act, when he would prob- ably be sent to gaol. ALLEGED ASSAULT.--Joseph Hurst, labourer, Sandy-lane, Lymm, was charged with having assaulted Matthew Hol- croft, gamekeeper, on the ithSeptember.—Complainant said that on the night of the itia inst. he met the defendant and another man in Sandy-lane, and defendant accused him of having thrown him out of work., and afterwards struk and knocked h7:tl djiVfl ~ , 1.-J•nuant, on the otter hand, asserted that tile complainant struck him a blow on the head with a loaded stick and knocked him down.—Both

complainant and defendant were bound over in £lO to keep THE STATE OF IRELAND. the peace for six months. DAMAOBS TO CROPS.—Six lads, named John Eccleston,Two police constables were fired on by moonlighters at , George Eccleston, Frank Lord, Harry Lord, Isaac Bell, and Robertstown. county Waterford, on Monday night. The shots William Clare. were charged with having done wilful dam- did not take effect, and the assailants escaped. age to the growing crop of turnips, the pear trees, &c., of General Buller, with Colonel Turner and County-inspec- e Mr. J. E. Peters. It was stated by Sergt. Harrington that a tor Whelan, left Kilke on Monday for Milltown-Malbay, great deal of Ennistymon, and Lindeonvarna. The peasantry take little 4amaee had been done to crops, &c., in Lymtn. —On the parents of the lads promising to chastise them interest in the general's movements. they were discharged. Mrs O'Flaherty, of London, has offers I her estate in the townland of Ballincarry, near Longford, for sale to the ten- ants, a great number of whom have come to terms with her, and have agreed to give If 3 years' purchase at the old rent, as none of the tenants have had judicial rent fixed under the Land Act. ' A report from County Clare states that several landlords have just made substantial reductions from the judicial rents fixed after the passing of the Land Act of 1881, with the result that the tenants are paying. In one or two cases the concession made represents a reduction of 40 per cent. on the original rent. The arrival at Galway of the man arrested for participa- tion in the diststrbance which followed on the arrest of Father Fahy et Woodford led to some riotous proceedings, in the course of which several constables and townspeople were seriously hurt. An attack was also made on the gaol. On Wednesday so great was the excitement in the town that business was almost suspended. So many raids were reported in Tralee on Monday that they need noi be detailed separately. There were two burn- ings on Sunday night near Castleisland. The houses of Maurice Brick and Timothy Divane, large farmers, about three miles east of Tralee, were entered and arms and money taken. Farther raids are reported from Kilmoyly. As far as can be judged, all were the work of one organisa- tion.

The presence of Miss Gardiner's emergency man Cuffs at ' the chapel of Belcarra, on Saturday, created much sensa- tion. About a dozen women, wives of recently evicted ten- ants, dragged him out of the chapel and drove him some distance away, but the curate, who is president of the parish branch of the National League, afterwards admitted Cuffs and his bodyguard to the sacristy while mass was going on. The locality is much excited. Mr. J. M`Carthy, M.P., speaking in Liverpool on Wednes- day evening, said he was not sorry at the result of the elec- tions, as he believed that when Englishmen became more educated upon the Mel question a larger and better measure of Home Rale would be obtained. The present Government were not long since actively engaged in preparing to brieg Home Rule forward, and he should not be surprised if Ithe party brought in a comprehensive measure on the sub- ject. At a National League demonstration at Midleton, on Monday, to protest against the action of Lvd Midleton in prohibiting monthly fairs, resolutions were passed condemn- ing the appointment of General Buller to overawe a defence- less and impoverished peasantry in Kerry, and urging the Government to accept Mr. Parnell's bill, as, owing to the bad harvest it would be impossible to pay an unjust rent, especially in face of the present low pricer. The meeting was attended by several thousand persons from Cork, Yong- hal, and Queenstown. A farmer named Thomas Greene was fired at on Saturday evening as he was returning home from Ennis, and was five miles from the town. He received the full charge of shot ' in the back, shoulder, and right ar.n, and is considered to have had a narrow escape of his life. It appears that Greene took the graaings of a Toureen farm, from which a family named Hynes bad been evicted, and which is now in the pesseetsion of the Bank of Ireland. The Hynes family received compensation. but the farm 3ontinues to be boy- cotted. Greens continues to be in a promising way towards recovery. Five men, named Meaney, Carney, and Winer- ney, and two brothers named Halpin, who were ariested on suspicion in connection with the crime, were taken before Mr. Killkelly, R.M., at Boris Jail on Monday, on charges of being comma.' in the crime. They were remanded for a week. IMPRISONMENT OP AN IRISH PRIEM". Father Fahy, a Roman Catholic curate, who, at the Woodford petty sessions, county Galway, on Monday, was ordered to find sureties or go to gaol for six months for threatening Mr. Lewis, a local landlord, who recently carried out some evictions, has elected to go to prison. On Monday night he was accom- modated at the police barracks, the weather being too in- clement to convey him to the gaol, as he is suffering teem a bronchial attack. During the evening bands paraded the streets and serenaded. The proceedings in connection with the pollee court investigation were of the most remarkable nature. Father Faby was capried on the shoulders of the people to the court. His prosecutor, who, wherever be goes, is carefully protected by police, gave evidence that the accused visited Mei and told him if ha went on with the evictions his house would be blown up before six months were overeand his life taken, and he thought it was his (Mae priest's) duty to denounce him from the altar. Witness ordeced him from his house. Last December an attempt was made to blow up his house, and be believed Father Fatly would procure some one to do it again. He was in dread and fear of him. On the magistrates aunouncing their intention to bind him over, Father Fehr asked and obtained per mission to retire from the court to consult his clerical brethren, and on returning he said he would accept the alternatiae of six months' im- prisonment.—On his arrival at Galway on Tuesday Father Fehr was met by about 4,000 persons, whe rescued him from the pollee. Father Fahy entreated the people to hand him over to the authorities. This they finally consented to do, but instead of handing him over to the police they themselves escorted him to gaol.
