Mr. Joseph Chamberlain on Wednesday had an interview with Chief-Superintendent Farndale, at Birmingham, and, it is said, arranged for police protection during his holidays abroad. He leaves England on the 25th inst.

THE TITHE AGITATION.—The Rector of Llandyrnog, in whose parish the anti-tithe agitation began, has offered to allow a reduction of 10 per cent, being the same abatement as the neighbouring landlords have made. Before the dis- pute became widespread the farmers had agreed to a com- promise of this nature, but there appears now to be some probability of their holding out for a reduction of 25 per cent.

WRECKS AND Loss OF LlFE.—Three Clyde ships—Cape Horn, Charles Connell. and Berwick Law—which left East Indian poi ts for the Channel in February or March last are now so long overdue that they have been given up as lost, with all (an board. A foilrth ship—an Italian barque, which sailed from Java in Febrrary for Greenock—is also looked upon as lost, no news of the vessel having been received since her departure These four ships carried valuable cargoea of sugar and rice,' and the total pecuniary loss, which will fall largely on Glasgow underwriters, is between £120,000 and £130,000. Unfortunately, also, there has been a considerable sacrifice of human life, as the combined crews numbered, all told, above a hundred persons. The Girvan, another long overdue Clyde ship, unexpectedly ar- rived at Falmouth a fortnight ago, after all hopes of her safety had almost ceased to be entertained. She left Ran- goon within a few days of the Cuarles Connell. and en- countered near Mauritius a cyclone which is believed to have overwhelmed the Missing vessels. A. Bath paper says : While the English climate at times causes great suffering, it can be avoided by using proper means. Hr. H. 3. Masters, chemist, 12, Argyle-street, writes: For the relief of rheumatism and of severe and long standing cases of muscular rheumatism, I find St, Jac- WI Oil particu- larly adapted, and one of the leading members of the medical profession of this city ft equently recommends it to his patients, —Bold by all druggists at 23 6d a bottle, or by post 2s 9d. from the Charles A. Vogeler Company, sole proprietors, 45 Farringdon-road, London.
GENERAL NEWS.

Through the collapse of a section of the Marine Colliery, near Scranton, Pennylvania, seven persons were killed. A boat, in which two men were mackerel fishing, was up- set by a squall off Douglas, Isle of man, on Tuesday, and one was drowned.

The Rev. W. Berry, vicar of of Bruntingthorpe, Leicester, was on Monday found dead at the foot of a haystack in a field. It is supposed he expired in a fit. At Yewsley, a number of children where playing with matches in their bedroom, when the nightdress of a little boy becawie ignited, and he was burned to death.
At the Old Bailey, London, on Tuesday, George Walby was senteneed to eight months' hard labour for selling in- decent 13,)0k5. The prisoner had offered them to boys at Eton.
The committee of the Philacielphia City Council ap- pointed to investigate the charges of corruption against the Mayor (Mr. Smith) has reported in favour of an impeach- ment.
• Upon the (aria of an evicted tenant named Flahier, near Listowel. now in charge of the police and a cAretaker, four acres of coru were cut on Monday night and successfully carried off.
Another terrible crime from Paris is reported. In the Montmartre quarter Jaems Derval, a shopman, stranzled his mistress, Marguerite Buisson. The murderer jumped from the room window and was killed.

Greit excitement has been occasioned at Chatham by the receipt of an Admiralty order directing that workmen are to be employed night and day in hastening the completion of those 'vessels which are required for immediate active ser- vice.

An extraordinary attempt to commit suicide was made by a tinplate worker in Clerkenwell, on Monday. He poured a large quantity of benzoline over is body, and then set fire to it. When found he was in a mass of flames, and his re- covery is considered doubtful.

Lord Folkestone has, on behalf of the Government, put a blocking notice against Mr. Parnell' s Tenants' Relief (Ire- land) Bill. At Balton. on Thursday, James Hope wile lcoilmitted to prison for seven days, for the third time, for refusing to give evidence in a case of wife desertion. Another shock of earthquake was experienced at Charles- ton at a quarter past two on Wednesday morning. The shock was only a slight one, but sufficient to cause a return of.nervous terror to the citizens. The St. Leger was won on Wednesday by the Duke of Westminster's " Ormonde," by four lengths ; Mr. Manton's St. Mirin being second, and Mr. Jenning's Exmoor third. Time, 3 minutes and 211 seconds. A BOY POISONED.—A shocking case of poisoning is re- ported from Tredegar. A lad named Clark, aged 14, em- ployed as a hauler by the Tredegar Iron Company, noticed a bottle in a workmen's cabin on the cinder tip. Thinking ,it contained ginger-beer he drank a portion. His screams brought workmen to the spot, and it was then discovered he had drunk a quantity of nitro-glycerine. He died'in three hours.

Mr. Chamberlain will leave England at the end of the present pr the beginning of next waek for the Continent. He has intimated to his political friends that he will not return until the end of the year. The right hon. gentleman will be accompanied by Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P. ARMAMENTS FOR MERCHANT CRUISERS—The Admiralty have issued orders that armaments for merchant ships are to be maintained in readiness at the dockyards. They are to be capable of being fitted on at a few boars' notice should circumstances at any time necessitate the arming of the mercantile marine. POACHING EXTRAORDINARY.—The Builtb magistrates have fined Rd. Rees, of Treortsy, £l5 and costs for illegally taking fish. The defendant put into the brook Clettoir, a tributary of the Wye, Elb. of chloride of lime, and was afterwards found by a policeman standing in the stream with a bag containing 271 b. of trout and salmon, the water for 400 yards above him being literally covered with dead and dying fish. A SAVAGE Hawxnu.—William Jepp, a hawker, was re- manded at Croydon, on Saturday, charsed with feloniously cutting and wounding James Bateman. The prisoner pro- duced a pair of scissors, alleging that be had killed men and womee by wholesale in America. He then stabbed Bateman in the eye. The wounded man fell, and was at once con-

veyed to the hospital. Medical evidence was given that the prosecutor was not out of danger. RAILWAY MYSTIIMY NBAR CHBVIE.—On sunday, a young man named Hopkins was admitted to the Crewe Railway Hospital suffering from frightful injuries. Hopkins was travelling from Liverpool to Swansea on Saturday at said-

night, and either was thrown out of the carriage or fell out when the train was passing Wrenbury. Tw3 trains passed over him before he was discovered. It is believ‘d hardly possible that be fell into that position, and the supposition is that he either jumped out of the carriage er was thrown out.

COLLAPSE OF A BRIDGE.—A large portion of the Albert Bridge, one of the bridges over the river Laizan at Belfast, fell in on Wednesday night with a great crash. The structure is a complete ruin, and the bed of the river is blocked up. Early next morning the body of a watchman named Matthews, in the employ of the corporation, was found among the debris, and removed te the morgue. THE REVISION COURTS. The Revising Barrister at Barrow (Mr. John Devey) on Wednesday disallowed the Conservative objections, 32 in number, on the ground that the notices were not posted in sufficient time.—At the Ash- ton Revision Coul, on Wednesday, the Conservatives objec- ted to the claim of a man named -galthouse, urging that his recent bankruptcy had disqualified him. 'I he Barristel. held that a bankrupt was not necessarily a "criminal, alien, or lunatic "—which were the grounds of legal incapacity to vote—and allowed the claim. THE LORD•LIEUTENANT AND THE CITY OF DUBLIN.—At a !meting of the Dublin City Council on Thursday Sir George Owens moved the adoption of an address of welcome to the Marquis of Londonderry on the occasion of his State entry into the City. In seconding the motion Mr. Sexton said he thought that no Lord Lieutenant who had ever come to Ireland would so little represent the Government as the Lord Lieutenant who was now coming over. Mr. Dennehy moved an amendment, that the Council should decline to take any part in welcoming the representative of a Govern- ment opposed to Home Rule, and this amendment was car- ried by 27 votes to six. THREATENING TO MURDER CHILDREN.—At Chester, on Tuesday, Ellen Smith, widow, 25 years of age, was charged j with threatening to murder her four children. The prisoner gave herself up, saving that she wished to give herself up or she would murder her four children, whom she had ' deserted in the streets. She belonged to Philadelphia, and I same to this country seven years ago. Her husband died shortly afterwards. She lipid been three years in the Birken- head Workhouse, and since she had been wandering about the streets with her children, and she had now become so desperate that she gave herself up for fear of murdering her children. The children were afterwards picked up in the streets. Prisoner was remanded for a week. THE WELSH EISTEDDFOD.—The Royal National Welsh Eisteddfod was opened under favourable circumstances at Carnarven on Tuesday. In the choral contest the Birken- head choir obtained the second prize of £2O, Wrexham taking the first. On Wednesday, Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., delivered an address. Prizes were awarded for Welsh and' English essays, poetry, singing, instrumental music, paint- ing, Jrc. A prize of -£25 for a choral competition of male voices was awarded to the Glentane Glee Society from Swansea. Thursday was Chair Day, and the ancient cere- mony of chairing the chief bard, together with a choral competition for a first prize of £4O and a second of twelve guineas, again induced a large attendance of visitors. Mr. J. H. Puleeton, M.P., presided, and adjudications followed his address. ROYAL MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL., AND NORTH LANCA- SHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.-011 Saturday the show was favoured with fine weather, The programme for the day included the judging of foals and young hareem for prizes given by the Chester and Wirral Farmers' Club at 9-30, parades of hunters at 11, prize cattle at noon, and prize horses at one o'clock. There were 12,000 spectators on the ground during the day, whicn VMS a considerable deorease on the number passing the gates on the previous day.. The number of persons who visited the show was ia the aggregate 4.4,000. lii 1873, when the show was last held at Chester, the anaount taken was—at the Rates, £1,800; and st the stand, £344 141; so that there is a slight falling off in the receipts upon this occesien as compared with 1873. The show officials are, however, thoroughly satisfied, and pro- nounce the show a decided success. MR. GLASTONE.—At Hawarden Castle the best amounts aro received of the state of Mr. Gladstone's health. A Lon- don correspondent says the right hon, gentleman has tele- graphed to Mr. John Morley that he will be home on Sun- day. As soon as peesible after his return there will be some interesting proceedings at Hawarden. A deputation from the Cork Town Council, consisting of the Mayor and Town Clerk, will wait on the ex-Premier to present him with the freedom of the city of Cork. The authorities in several other Irish towns have expressed a wish to follow suit. An address from the ladies of Ireland is also to be presented to Mr. Gladstone. The Mayor of Cork is in communica- tion with the promoters of the movement for presenting the address from Irishwomen, with a view to arranging that all the deputations shall visit Hawarden on the same day.

Tay TITHE QUESTION.—Mr. T. Lewis, M.P., addressing a meeting of fanners at Anglesey, on Saturday. urged that the payment of tithes should be made compulsory by the landowners, and not by tenants, the bulk of whom in Wales being Nonconformists, strongly objected to pay directly towards the stipend of a clergyman whose services they never attended. The tithe war in Wales would tend te in- tensify the differences already existing between the Church and lissenters in the Principality, and would hasten dises- tablishment and disendowment. • This POISONING OF A WEDDINS PARTY. A discovery has been made which is likely to elucidate the mysterious poisoning of a wedding party at Carlisle last month. Of the 19 wedding guests and servants, nearly all suffered more or lees from tie effects of poison, and the bride died in Edin- burgh. After various theories had been propounded, the ' ham need was suspected ef containing bacilli, and on Mon- day night Dr. Barnes, of Carlisle. who has had charge of the investigation, received an intimation from Dr. Walker, city analyst, that be lied discovered on several occasions a bacillus in portions of the ham. RUNAWAY RAILWAY CARRIAGES. A singular accident oczurred on Saturday at Brockholes Junction, near Hud- dersfield. The noon train from Huddersfield to Holinfirth had brought twe third-class carriages to Broekholes for use ' on the Claytcn West branch live. On being detached these carriages started bask in the direction of Iludderefield, gathering way as they descended a somewhat steep incline. The only passenger in tie carriages got out without injury. All attempts to atop the carriages failed, and they dashed I through Henley Station at a high rate of speed, but .it Berry Brow they were turned into a siding, and there ran in to some waggons doing considerable damage. WHOLESALE THEFT OF SE-SEP.—A large number of sheep are pastured on the open commons of the Bast Fells in Cumberland, and at a periodical counting it was found that several hundred of them were missing. Information was r given to the pollee, who discovered that a few days age 56 , sheep were sold at itexham Auction Mart, about 20 miles- distant, which have been identified as some of the missing property. The man who it is alleged entered the sheep . for the sale gave a name and address which aroussd no suspicion. He was paid the amount realised directly the sheep were sold. There is no trace as yet of any of the others. Aw ELECTTLIC VOYAGES ACROSS THE ENGLISH CHANNEL.— The small launch Vette, which is propelled by the electric current, left Dover in Monday morning on a voyage across the Channel. A great deal of interest concentrated in the event on account of the novelty of the trip and the scientific nature of the experiment which was to be made. The hull of the Volta is 37 feet long, and nearly 7 feet beam, built of galvanised steal plates. She has a very light appearance in the water. The yacht arrived in Calais in 3h. 51m. She left on her return voyage to the English coast at 3-15 time and arrived safely at Dover, after having accomplished the journey to Calais and back, 50 miles, with her accumulators charged only once. . ~..„ TORY BIGOTRY AND ROMAN CATHOLIC-S.-I.lle directors of the Scottish Protestant Alliance have been. summoned to meet this week to consider Lord Randolph Churchill's reply to their remonstrance against the appointment of a Roman Catholic as a Secretary of State. Meanwhile the Rev. J. ' Paton, minister of St. Paul's, Glasgow, and a director of the Alliance, has written to his lordship as follows :—" You have penned an insolent reply to a respectful public docu- ment. You are now a Cabinet Minister, but I observe with astonishment and regret that you have not laid aside those weapons of abase and scorn with which you tomahawked your way to power. You seem to think it not unworthy of a Minister to the Queen to describe a body of representative men as senseless and irrational for daring to differ from you . on a matter of public policy. It is a national calamity when men pitchforked into a high position are destitute of , decent manners. It is one thing to tear oppoqents and growl over them like the bulldog of politics; it is quite ' another to be a British statesman." Mr. Paton, after this preface, argues that the Alliance founded their pro- test on the same grounds as exclude Papists from the Throne. SAD DROWNING FATALITIES.—A coble, containing four men, went from Seabam Harbour on Saturday morning for preliminary practice prior to the regatta in the afternoon, ' when a strong gust of wind caught the boat. She went over on her side and sank. Assistance was rendered by several pilot boats, but two of the men were drowned. The cliffs and the docks were lined with people, and a scene of great excitement Was presented.—The English steamer Hector ar- rived at Grand Canary a few weeks ago, She had on board ' a young gentleman named Harris, belonging to Norwich. Mr Harris, along With the third engineer of the vessel, and another of the crew, took the ship's boat and went for a sail. . A day or two afterwards the ship's boat was found on the southern part of the island with no occupants, and none of , them have since been heard of.—as the Peel fishing boat Choibe was returning to Douglas Harbour from fishing on Saturday morning, the master, John Joughin, was washed overboard and was drowned within sight of a number of persons. No effort could be made to save him, as the small boat had been lest during the night owing to the rough sea. The deceased was 55 years of age, and belonged to Peel. ILLEGAL MARRIAGE CEREMONY.—A CLERGYMAN SENT FOR TRIAL.—The Whitehaven magistrates on Monday heard two charges preferred by the Treasury against the Rev. John Henry Latrobe Bateman, vicar of Haile, Cumberland. The first charge was of solemnising matrimony between Robert ' Little, aged 18 years, and Mary Jane Cockbain without li- cense ot certificate, and without due publication of banns, and without the consent of Little's parents, he being a mi- nor. The second charge was of inserting, causing, or per- mitting to be inserted in a register of marriages kept for the parish of Haile a false entry relating to the marriage on the 9th May last.—Mr. Hodgson prosecuted and Mr. Pickering defended —Evidence was given that the couple who were married bad formerly been in the rev, gentleman's service. In May it came to tne knowledge of Little'a parents, who reside in Egremont, that he was ahont to be married. The mother of the youth told Mr.Bateman that if he married her son, "She would give him trouble if she could." Mr.Bate- man told her he would not marry her son. On the Bth May —the day before the marriage—Mr. Bateman again saw Mrs. Little. She said she was as much gigainst the marriage as ' ever, and told him not to dare to marry her sen, adding that she would as soon see her son shot as married at his age. Notwithstanding this, Mr. Bateman married the couple on the following day. He asked Mrs. Little to forgive him, as be was hurried, and the same night he went to see William Little, the father, saying he had come to apologise. The matter was reported to the Bishop of Carlisle, and in due course the present proceedings were instituted. Evidence was given that neither of the parties married resided out of Egremont for over three months prior to the marriage, and several clergymen at Egremont gave evidence that the b Inns of marriage were never published ; whilst the parish clerk at Haile Church proved that the berms had not been • published there.—The defendant was committed for trial at the Cumberland Aesizes on the first charge, and bail was , accepted, defendant in £2OO and two sureties of £ICO each. The second charge was adieurnecl on a legal point. •

THE AMERICA CUP YACHT CONTEST.—The second race sin the America Cup contest began on Saturday morning from New York. The Mayflower (American) started at 11k. 22tnin. 25sec., and the Galatea (English) at 11b. 24tnin. 55aec. The wind was west-north-west, blowing at the rate of 15 miles an hour, and the weather was fair. The course was 20 miles to leeward from the Scotland Lightship and back. The yachts kept close together at the start, neither seeming to get any advantage, but after a short dis- tance had been sailed the Mayflower slowly drew away, and at 11-48 was a quarter of a mile ahead. At 12-17 six miles of the course had been traversed, the Mayflower being then nearly a mile ahead. The Mayflower crossed the winning line at 613. 13min. 35 sec. The Galatea was then three and a half miles astern, and finished at 6-46. The weather was clear threughout the race, which was witnessed by a large number of persons both ashore and afloat. GALE IN SCOTLAND.—Tbe severe gale that raged•from the south-west over the north and west seaboard of Scot- land on Thursday and Friday was followed on Saturday by a tremendous downpour of rain, which lasted all day, caus- ing great damage to growing crops, and doing more des- truction than the wind had done. On Saturday the sea was so boisterous that the ferry-boat did not venture out from Broadford to meet the Clydesdale, and the steamer was just about to steam onto! the Bay, when a boat was observed coming out from the island Scalps, with passengers for the steamer. She was struggling in the storm, ard those on board the Clydesdale expected to see her founder every moment. The craft had nine pas- sengers on board, and was overloaded in such a sea. Ropes were thrown from the Clydesdale, and in the scramble to seize them the boat swamped, and the nine oc- cupants were thrown into the surging sea. A boat was launched from the Clydesdale, and rescued six of the drowning passengers. Two others were saved by ropes thrown from the steamer, but one, Charles McLeod, was drowned, having from exhaustion been unable to retain his hold of the rope thrown to him. EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPE OF AN ALLEGED MURDERER. —On Wednesday afternoon James Murphy, the alleged murdereer of Police-constable Austwick, at Dodworth, es- caped from three experienced police officers under remark- able circumstances. Since the murder on the 31st July no trace of the murderer hen been found until Wednesday afternoon, when Superintendent Kane, Detective-inspector Ramsden, and Inspector Stansfield, of Leeds, went to the house of the murderer's sister-in-law at Barough Village, near Barnsley. They entered the house, and while two of them talked to the sister-in-law Ramsden went upstairs. As he opened the bedroom door the murderer sprung through the window into the garden below. The inspector had seized Murphy by the collar, but was unable to retain his hold. He followed him to the window, and Murphy turned round and pointed a gun at him. The detective drew back for an instant, and Murphy, who was shoeless, bounded away across the fields and disappeared. A staff of police officers with two blood hounds were speedily on his track, but up till a late hour on Wednesday night the murderer was still at large. Murphy's sister-in-law and her husband were arrestel and conveyed to Barnsley. An examination of the cottage from which he escaped shows the daring nature of the adventure, the window of the bedroom being only twenty-two inches wide, half of which only opens. There is every evidence that Murphy has repeatedly visited his sister-in-law's cottage during night, it being capitally adapted and easy of approach from the adjacent fields. Ad- joining the cottage is a Wesleyan chapel, where, it is be- lieved, he secreted himself. . LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL AND THE PROTESTANT ALLIANCE.—At the request of the directors of the Scottish Protestant Alliance, their honorary secretary, the Rev. Jas. Kerr, Glasgow has replied to Lord Randolph Churchill's recent letter. In vindicating the position assumed by his directors in relation to Roman Catholics and the Govern- ment of the country, Mr. Kerr recapitulates the leading statements contained in the resolution commented on, and' in support of these statements refers to or quotes from Encyclicals of Popes Gregory XVI, Pius IX, and Leo X, the Vatican degrees of 1870, and declarations by Cardinal Man- nino, Mr. Gladstone, and Lord Denbigh. In conclusion he characterises the sentiments in 'his lordship's letter as an indirect attack upon the Protestantism of the Throne ; and maintains that in this controversy the members of the alliance are the true friends, and the noble lord the foe of ,civil and religious liberty. Lord Randolph has acknow- ledged the receipt of the views of the directors of the Scot- tish Protestant Alliance on his reply to the resolution pro• testing against the appointment of a Roman Catholic to the office of Home ;Aecretary, and expressed his regret that he has not time to follow the directors on the field of acute polemical theology to which they invite him. Lord Ran- dolph reasserts the opinion he expressed in his former let- ter, and suggests that the views of the directors if practi- cally pushed to a logical conclusion would involve the repeal of all those Acts of Parliament which have removed the political disabilities formerly imposed on Roman Catholics, and the re-enactment of all those pease/ laws against our Roman Catholic fellow-subjects which the wart majority of the British people are anxious to forget. Public Analysts have sUbmitten CADlriay's Coati to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing h eosverage, Beware o! Imltationa. Advt.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Batora Mr. J. Brunner and Major C. W. Hazle-
burst.

DRUNICENNESS.—Harry Bootb, of Rock Savage, was fined 5s and costs 115 Gd fer being drunk. For a like of- fence Abraham Kilgress was fined 103 and costs 14s 6d. Elizab.th Johnson, for being drunk and disorderly was fined 103 and costs 5s 6d. FilusHED win( DoGs Now.—Elizabeth Burton, dealer in haberdashery in Devonshire-square, was charged with per- mitting her dog to be at large in contravention of an order made by the justices.—P.C. Barker proved that the dog was , hot under control in Devonshire-equars on the 9th inst.— The defendant said the dog had been fastened to the table leg with a chain, but it became unfastened, and whilst she was serving a customer "out he went." She had finished I with dogs now, they were a great trouble to a person. A fine of Is, and costs 9s 6,1, was imposed. A YOUNG TutßF.—Thomas John Oliver, 13 years of age. was charged with steeling two glass ornaments, worth 2d, from the shop of James Lea, of High-street. The boy pleaded guilty, and as he had 13-en previously convicted, and his borne surroundings were not of the beet, he was sen- tenced to 21 days' imprisonment, and five years in a refor- matory schonl.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

TRUIISDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall (chairman) and F. H. Gossage. DRITNS AND REFUSING TO QUlT.—Thomag Clarlev, labourer, was charged with having been drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Arch Hotel, Widnes, on the 7th August. and, on the evidence of P.C. Thompson, was fined 10s and costs.

- ILLEGALLY Pawmerd.—Alice Lyons. widow, and small shopkeeper, Appleton, was summoned by William Mort, who said he was formerly a shopkeeper and farmer, for illegally pawning a number of goods, value £2, which be- longed to him.—Mr. W. T. Husband appeared for the defen- dant.—lt was alleged by complainant that he and his two children had been lodging with defendant for some time. On the 4th August she locked the house door upon him. On the Sunday following he sent to the house for the goods, which were worth £lO, but she would not give them up. He also sent her 6s for his lodgings. She had since pawned the goods at Mr. Charles Niel's for 165, without asking his permission.—Mr. Husband argued that the case was really one for a civil court. Com- plainant owed defendant £3 17s 11d, and she had a land- lady's right to retain the goods until the sum was Raid. There had been no felonious intent.--Several witnesses proved that complainant swore and used abusive language towards the defendant, and it was in consequence of that she locked the door on him.—The Bench considered that defendant had no right to pawn the clothes, and she was fined 5s and costs, and ordered to pay 16$, the value of the goods.—Mr. Hall said the defendant had her remedy as to anything owing by Mort in a civil court. -BREACH OF THE PEACE.—David Winders, for creating a breach of the peace on the 3rd inst. was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in the sum of £lO and one surety of £5, or go to prison for seven days. NEIGHBOURS' QUARRELS.—Elizabeth Williams was sum. mooed by Mary Lee for having assaulted and beaten her on the 10h September.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for two months, herself in £lO and one surety of £5, or seven days in default. WIFE ASSAULT --Thomas Turton was summoned by his wife, Ellen, for having beaten her on the 10th SeptetoLer.— Complainant went to a certain person's house, where her husband was, and asked him to come home. It was after ten o'clock, and she thought it was time he was at home. When he sew her he caught hold of her by the throat,while a woman who was there with him beat him about the head. When they got out of the house he struck her in the eye and mouth, and called her bad names.—Defendant said it was very seldom that his wife was sober when he came home. Sometimes he never saw her for 24 hours, and the children were neglected. It was under provocation, he said, that he struck her. Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO, and one surety of £5, or seven days. A CLOTHES BURNER. William Brewn, labourer, was summoned by Catherine Welsh for having burned three shirts and several other things, which belonged to her hus- band. It was alleged that complainant asked defendant's wife to wash the clothes for her on the let September which she consented to do. When the defendant came' home, however, and found the clothes in the house, he put them into the boiler fire. Defendant, who said the things had no right in his house, and they should have asked his consent to pat them there, was fined 108 and costs, the cost of the clothes, 153 DJ, in all 3.15, or one month in default.

CLAIM BY A WIDNES BOOTMAKER.—Frauk H oiling- wortb, clogger, of Earlestown, was summoned by Mr. Thos. Hall, bootmaker, of Waterloo-road, who claimed £3 from him for wrongfully leaving his work on the 16th August. Mr. Knowles was for the complainant, and Mr. Browne for the defence.—lt appeared that an agreement was entered in- to by Mr. Hall and the defendant on the sth July, 1885, for the -latter to work for the complainant for two years, at the sum of 153 a week. After the first week's emplcyment Mr. Hall gave the defendant 21, and said he would repeat it every week if he would work well and conduct himself with propriety. On the Ist Jandary, 1886, Mr. Hall did not give the defendant the 2s, but said he would keep it for him, and if he conducted him- self properly would buy him some clothes and some boots. On the 16th of August defendant went into the shop and asked for the money, meaning the money for the clothes, but Mr. Hall refused to give it to him. The defen- dant then went away from work, and had never been back, in consequence of which Mr. Hall had been put to consider- able expense.—The defendant put in a counter claim of £3 6s, the money which the complainant said he would keep for the defendant.—The Bench overruled the counter claim, and made an order on the defendant to pay £2. He was given a month in which to pay. DISMISSED —William Turton, joiner at Messrs. Mus- pratt's. was summoned by his wife, Alice, under the Mar- ried Women's Maintenance Act, to show cause why he should not maintain her. Mr. Knowles was for com- plainant, and Mr. Swift for the defence. After the case had gone on for a short time it was withdrawn, defendant promising to give his wife 7s 63 a week, which she accepted. SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Edward Roberts, Martin Rourke, Thomas Omens, and John Brannon were each fined 6d, and 43 6.1 costs, for not sending their children regularly to school.

div.p: OUR LOND(pç LETTEI,:.

LoYnoN, THURSDAY. As Lord Randolph Churchill ,sits upon the Trea- sury bench fretting and fuming under the obstruc- tion of the Irish members, his mind must be visited by many reminiscences, It is at the most two years since his place was at the corner seat below the gangway opposite, in convenient contiguity, to his old friend Tim Healy, and within hail of Mr. Harrington, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, Mr. Biggar, and the rest. When Lord Randolph was in his place, and in the humour, it was hard lines for a Minister in charge of a bill, or eager to make progress with the Estimates. Now the tables are turned. The Irish members are as persistent as ever in obstructive tactics; bit!, it is Lord Randolph who suffers. It has been. given to few men to possess in equal degree this measure of experience. To be one year the life and soul of obstructive tactics, and in the next be responsible for the conduct of affairs and anxious, above all things, to advance public busi- ness, is an unequalled Parliamentary experience. Lord Randolph is not able to bear the situation with philosophic calm. He is naturally of an im- patient, imperious disposition, and a man of phleg- matic temperament might well be moved by the constant iteration in Irish obstruction. It is curi- ous to note how n the present circumstances the veterans of the old guard stand aside and watch i while the work s done by eager recruits. Mr. Par- nell is never in his place. Tim Healey finds it more profitable to look after briefs in Ireland than to sit in the House of Commons. Mr. Sexton cannot al- ways resist the opportunity of making a speech, and occasionally Mr. T. I'. O'Connor shouts defiance at the Treasury Bench. But for the most part the work is done by men whose names are not familiar to the newspaper reader, obscure nominees of Mr. Parnell, at the last General Election. When the Speaker is in the chair, he makes short work of these gentlemen, who have not yet had time and opportunity to acquire the ingenuity necessary to condact the campaign of obstruction. They are always tumbling into irrelevancy, and the Speaker swiftly sweeps down upon them, ordering them to resume their seats. Mr. Courtney has been driven to this latter resource once or twice. But there is fuller scope for obstruction in committee where the license of conversationalists is wider, and the authority of the chairman less grave. It is still hoped that the round of dreary work may be brought to a close this week, and that the prorogation may take place on Saturday week. The necessity of dealing with Mr. Parnell's bill might, if a conciliatory spirit prevailed, be made to work in with the exigencies of the Appropriation Bill. Eight days are required for the elaboration of the Appropriation Bill, counting the day on which Supply is finished. But in the absence of obstruc- tion, or of a serious intention to debate the policy of the Government, the varied stages of the Appropria- tion Bill are merely formal, and the time of the House could be given up to debate on Mr. Parnell's bill. It is hoped that this will be the case. As for the bill itself, its fate is certain. It will be found impossible to carry it through the House of Com- mons, and if it were otherwise the Lords might be counted upon to make short work of it when it reached them. The Government must inevitably deal with the Home 7 Rule question, and they will do so as nearly as possible upon the lines of Mr. Glad- stone's measure. But they, fairly enough, ask for time to elaborate their scheme. It would be absurd and impossible to, think of legislating on the matter at this time of the year. They will come back in- vigorated and refreshed in the spring, and then we may see the Home Rule question settled, probably in some' such manner as the Redistribution Bill was carried. In the meantime Mr. Parnell's bill will be useful as a kind of trial balloon. It will show which way the wind blows, and with what force. The Liberal party remains at sixes and sevens, and is no nearer reconciliation than it was when Parliament met. For the most part the Dissentient Liberals have executed a strategical retreat before the approach of Mr. Parnell's Bill, which is very embarassing for them.. Men like Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Collings, and Mr. Caine could not vote against such a•measure, nor could they in view of their compact with the Conservatives vote for it. They have accordingly with one consent gone on their holiday. As for the Gladstonians they have been left in a somewhat awkward predicament, owing to the absence of their chief. There have been stories told during the week of communications passing between Mr. Gladstone and Mr. John Morley, pointing to the former's return on a particular day. I have the best means of knowing that this state- ment is absolutely without foundation. At this present time of writing Mr. Morley and Sir William Harcourt do not know on what. duy Mr. Gladstone will return, or what are his views with. respect to Mr. Parnell's A communication is expected this evening. But hitherto nothing has been known, and in the absence of such information nothing could be done. The other statement about the Liberal chiefs: sending out an urgent whip in support of Mr. Parnell's Bill is consequently equally without foundation.

The statement that the Queen has been actively moving in behalf of Prince Alexander of Battenbers has been somewhat timidly contradicted. It possi- bly is not true, but certainly a contrary belief . widely spread and exists in usually well informed quarters. I have heard from an intimate supporter i of the Government that Lord Salisbury s seriously embarrassed by the warm advocacy Her Majesty displays for the cause of her daughter's brother-in- law. After the Cabinet Council on Saturday, Lord Iddesleigh unexpectedly set off for Balmoral, his mission i being, according to report n the House of Commons, to reason with the Queen on the delicate situation. There is no doubt that Her Majesty has sent, an invitation to Prince Alexander to visit this country—a demonstration of personal friendliness, designed as a counterblast to the snubbing which the Prince has received from Russia and Germany. No one would envy poor Lord Iddesleigh his mission. But it is hi s fate, whether as peer or baronet, to be' sacrificed on the alter of public duty. It begins to grow dbubtful whether the present generation will see a life of Lord Beaconsfield. Lord Rowton, to whom, the task has been committed, speaks of its accomplishment with a disheartening vagueness. Lord Rowton has never displayed any special fitness for the work. Good biographers are among the rarest finds in the literary field. It may turn out that Lord Rowton is one; but at present he is at least wholly unsuspected. I fancy he is a little appalled at the enormiN of his task. I was very much struck a year ago by the tone in which he spoke of the boxes bequeathed to his care. He had not then written a single' line of the work, and doubt. whether he is any more forward to-day. Lord Beaconsfield was woefully unmethodical in dealing with his correspondence. He kept nearly every scrap of paper- sent to him, but his manner of : .dealing -with them was embarrassingly simple:. He just thew them into a box, when the box was full i locked t, and commenced to stock another. Lord Rowton sits in despair amid these unnumbered boxes, and the world is waiting for the book. The announcement that Lord Henry Lennox has left behind him materials for a biography greatly flutters the political and social world. Fitz- forty years Lord Henry lived in the inner sanctuary both of politics and society. He was on intimate terms with everybody worth knowing, went everywhere and saw everything. If he has with a free pen noted men and events as they have passed before • him, we shall have an interesting work. Lord Henry was at one time particularly intimate with Mr. Disraeli, who employed him in many confiden- tial negotiations. The fashion of keeping diaries I has greatly spread since Greville's Memoirs were published. Amongst the men of the' day who are known to be "taking notes "is Lord, Derby. Ills diary is said to be minutely and faithfully written up. Some day, if we live long enough, we shall know all 'about the proceedings which led to his retirement from the Beaconsfield Cabinet in 1878. The Lord Mayor has already realised that lie made a mistake when lie volunteered to open a Mansion House Fund for the sufferers by the Charleston earthquake. Tie has received some money, but it is almost exclusively contributed by Greek residents in London,and is specifically directed' to be expended for tho relief of sufferers by the earthquake in Greece. The English people are not accustomed to confine their charity to home objects. But it unfortunately happened that at the time the Lord Mayor made his appeal on behalf of the citi- zens' of the United States, our own colony of St.. Yin- cent was subject to a similar calamity, and thou- sands Of people were homeless. If there was to be , a.Mansion House Fund started it was instinctively felt that our fellow subjects in poverty-stricken St. Vincent had a call before the citizens of the great and wealthy foreign State. The Lord Mayor has now harked back, and to-day announces that Ile will receive subscriptions for the sufferers at St. Vincent. But there is too much reason to fear that the whole thing will prove a fiasco. It is a pity that the counsel of the American Minister here was not taken in the first instance, and the kindly offer refused by the American Government.

div.p: Landon is filling and iliptying. The end of fiat week will see the commencement of many hard- earned holidays. I had no idea till this year how many people and how many classes of people are dependent on the sitting of Parliament. On° naturally thinks only of the members, and they al* easily counted or accounted for. But when Parlia- ment is still sitting Downing-street retains a poPu- lation that generally migrates in August. These birds of passage, belated by the cussedness of a general election, will commence their flight in a. few days. The South Coast watering places will be very full, and Wales, which has been, very einpili through September, though crowded in August, wu commence to reap a second harvest. Already, however/. people are pouring into England from the Contin- ent, and the universal report is of a bad seaserk Hamburg has had but two-thirds—in fact, not Me' thirds—of its average attendance. The Swiss hotels' have been Foorly patronised, but there has been a quite unaccountable concourse of English visiter,iB to the- Black Forest. This tract in Germany anu. the Ardennes district in Belgium have been crowded beyond precedent, and apparently Nvith` out cause. The Great Eastern Railway has cer- tainly been pushing the district round about the Spa and Luxemburg, and that venerable watering place seems to have recovered a little of its fternler splendour.

-It is curious to see how Belgium is taking thp benefit of the social feud between Germany an France. The: Germans who want sea air all for Ostende, where they can talk bad French with: out crossing over the rival frontier, and the Frenc," who have to take waters and are not advaiiceu enough for Royat, go to Spa. International.jeale.aaY has been fiercer this year than it has been slfle! the peace of Berlin. Its ferocity seems contaglon and fashionable. Twenty years have not enabl.et. the Danes to forget Sadowa. I see in the Danlsu... capital the opera house produces this week ner's Tannha user. The singers are all Danes, excePu , the tenor. It was necessary to send for a German:4 The selected Tannhaiiser could not,sino• Danish, auu'_ is not allowed to sing German. As a—concession TA' national prejudice he delivers his songs and sen- tences in English.

div.head: CHASE AFTER LONDON THIEVES
div.p: A CHASE AFTER LONDON THIEVES
AT WARRINGTON.

At the Warrington Occasional Court on TaesdaY afternoon, before Mr. P. Stubs and Mr. J. Marson, two London youths named James Portlock and John Atherton, were charged with committing a robbery at the shop of Isaac Saunders, of Lower Whitley', near Warrinffton• Mrs. Saunders said that at halt 5' past one o clock on the afternoon of the August she was in the kitchen of her house, wh!ch communicates by a door with a provisioll shop she kept. Hearing the chinking °' money, she went into the shop and saw prisoner Atherton leaving the shop. On the counter was-tile till lrawer empty, with the exception of four hair' pennies. She had left it about a minute previonslY containing ten or eleven shillings in silver and cop- per, chiefly the latter, She called out, "Stop thief' you have got my money ! " and followed Atherton mto the road, where close to the shop Was Portlock, who appeared to her to be olle of Atherton's confederates. Alter half an hours pursuit Atherton was might in a field by a young man named Henry Richardson. The other prisoner was caught by several others who had joined in Oleo pursuit. On the 6th inst a parcel containing 5s 91" in copp r and a cup, which had also been .0300 from the drawer, was thrown into the house by some person who ran away. He is believed to be third man who had eluded his pursuers. Prisoner 3 were committed for trial at Knatsford Seselons.

div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF

GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, Gibson, Blackhurst, Jolley, Jones, WoOdt? Isherwood, Clarke, Eckersley, W. Houghton, J• Houghton,Wright, Heaton, Strange, Swinton, Owen, Humphries W. Long (ex-officio) •, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). THE SCHOOL COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Padgate Industrial Schools Commit' tee etated that on the recommendation of the Superintendent the committee agreed that an advertisement should be 'sent to the "Army Gazette" announcing that eight or ten boys in excellent health, and well instructed in musical instill' ments, and who have passed the necessary school standardsf await employment, and also that other boys are available for useful employment. The children were reported to be all in excellent health, and the hospital to be closed. it was recommended that the wages of Mrs. Lindsay be in- creased to the rate of £l5 per annum, her children having ceased to be chargeable. A report of Messrs. Greening and Woods, noon the desirableness of buying the necessary machinery and requisites for shoe making, &c., was read, the cost whereof would be about £45, Messrs. Greening and Woods were thanked for their report and services, the sub' jeot being deferred for consideration until the next meeting of the cornmittee.—On the motion of the CHAIRMADTP seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were confirmed. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEI The committee reported that fees had been allowed in 65 eases, 25 of which were new and 40 old.—On the motion of Mr. GREANING, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, the minutes were confirmed.

VACCINATION. The CLERK said that he was in receipt of a letter froul Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer. :Newton, which stated that according te the report in the newspaper it had been repro': sented at the previous 'meeting of the Guardians that he heel made a blender or mistake in connection with a summone that had been issued in respect of non-vaccination. Mr' Cooper, however, pointed out that after an adjournment the case again came before the court, and it was found that s mistake had not been made, and the person was ordered to have his child vaccinated within 21 days, and to pay costs —The CLERK also read a letter from the Local Government Board stating that that Board, under the circumstances . mentioned in a letter from the Clerk to them, would offer no objection to Mr. George Holford retaining for the pre' sent the office of vaccination officer to the Warrington .‘ Union.

div.head: DR. JACK'S APPOINTMENT.
div.p: DR. JACK'S APPOINTMENT.

In reference to the proposed appointment of Dr. Jack as medical officer of No. 1 district the Local Government Board wrote to say that the resolution passed by the Guar- dians did not set forth the reason, which in the opinion of the Board r.ndered it necessary to appoint a person not re siding in the district. They therefore requested that a special minute should be made and entered in the usual re- cord of their proceedings, setting forth those reasons, and that a copy of it should be forwarded to the Local Govern- ment Board for their consideration.—The CLERK therefore suggested that a motion be passed temporarily reappointing Dr. Jack till the 25th December, subjEct to the approval of the Local Government Board, and asking the Local Gov' ernment Board to approve of the payment of Dr. Jack to the end of the present quarter.—Mr. JoLLEY moved, and Mr. BLACKIIIIRST seconded a proposal to that effect. The latter gentleman asked if that would terminate the appoint" ment of Dr. Jack.—The CLERK said it would, but he would by re-appointed and before the period of re-appointment Gs' pired they might expect that Dr. Jack would have secured a house in the district. He (the Clerk) knew he was trying to get one.—Mr. BLACKRIIRST : But if be does not the BP' pointment will terminate.—The CLERK: Yes. RE-APPOINTMENT OF DR. SEPRTON.,

Mr. GREENING, moved: "That inasmuch as Mr,.R. Sepb. ton has for some years past satisfactorily.filled the office ?f medical officer for the No. 3 district of the Union, and 1318 present residence and surgery, although situ Ate ont of the district, are accessible and convenient to the Union patients', and there being no duly qualified medical man resident within the district, he bp re-appointed medical officer for that district for a further period of three years, terminating on the 29th day of September, 1889, at the annaal salary of £3C4 subject to the approval of the Local Government Beard."—Mr.,llEA.Tox seconded, and the CUAIRMAN sur" ported the proposal, which was agreed to. .

div.head: WIT AND RUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND RUMOUR.

1 "Yes, sir," said White," c.perience makes fools wise." "Think so ?" said Black; "then you've never had any experience." Extract from a leader in an Irish paper: "So long as Ireland was silent under her wrongs, England was deaf to her cries." When you hear a man say "I will risk my honour that this is true," you can generally make up your mind that his honour is not paying 'a very heavy dividend. A lady who was a member of a class studying art con- cluded a recitation on Benjamin Haydon by stating that "toward the close of his life he committed suicide." "There is a great amount of cruelty to dumb things," says an exchange, and we must admit this is true. Notwithstanding civilisation, eggs are "beaten," cream is "whipped," wheat is "thrashed," and postage stamps are "licked." OUT OF FASHION.—Fond Mamma: Why I thought you and little Flossy Brown were great friends.—Little Miss Fashion: So we are; but you would'nt have me play with a little girl who dresses her doll in last year's fashions, would you, mamma? WHAT SHE MARRIED Fon.—Second husband, to wife: Are you as fond of me as you were of your first hus- band, dear ?—Wife: Yes, indeed; and, if you were to die, John, I would be just as fond of my third. I'm not a woman to marry for anything but love. Employer: I am very suspicious of young men nowa- days. • You can't tell how they are going to turn out. Why, in six months they know a good deal more about your business than you do yourself, and want to manage it entirely !—Applicant for position: I can assure you, sir, that, if you will engage me, I will devote as little time as possible to your business. REAL FARMYARD MILK.—The following conversation occurred in the French language; it loses, we fear, none of its significance by being turned into English— "My good woman, have you only that one cow ?" "Yes, sir, only this one." "How much milk a day does she give ?" "Ten quarts." "And how much of it do you sell ?" "Fifty quarts ever morning." Printers have much to endure. A morning paper that had sub-edited a cheap "ad." received the following lucid complaint: "Pleas insurt the abuve as it is roate down, not alter it as it ware last weak pleas." This is how it was " roate " : "A respectbl woman age 47 as good plane cook trustwurthey to eldy or small lamely good refferenc. adress," &c. A well-known aurist was called in by a medical practitioner to see one of his patients, an old lady who was suffering from deafness. After several tests which appeared unsuccessful, the aurist said to the medical ' man, "The old girl is as deaf as a post !" "Only with one ear, Mr. X.," said the old lady quietly; "and I wish you, good morning, and shall not require your services again." Scene—Wayside Northern hotel; dramictis persona—a party of wheelmen, several of whom had put up at this hostelry for the night a few weeks previously; time— morning, when about to settle bills. Spokesman for party: "Why, how's this? You have gone up thirty per cent. on the prices you gave when we stopped here before !" Hotel proprietor: "Yes, I know it; I hadn't seen you feed then." "If we want to get at the genuine, unadulterated man," says a scientific writer, "we must go back, not for 250,000 winters alone, but perhaps for two or three million years, into the dim past of the tertiary ages." Some of our readers may be anxious to "get at" the genuine, primitive man, but we advise them not to go back so many years into the dim past to do so. The probabilities are that they will find the man dead any- way. " oi,m tired av workin' like a nagur. Oi wush I was dead, so I do,' remarked Tim M‘Gadden to his father, down at the docks. "Oh, oh, ye do, eh? That's like ye, ye lazy fellow. Wishin' ye wuz dead, and spendin' the rist av yer days in a foine coffin, and yer father workin' sixteen hours a day to support yer lazy carcase; bad luck to ye." "Bobby," said the school teacher, "why did you take Frank's slate?" "Didn't take it," said Bobby, doggedly. "Bobby," said the teacher, severely, "I saw you." "No, you didn't!" yelled Bobby, "cause you were down- stairs when I took it !" The teacher saw that Bobby had caught her fibbing, so she did not punish him for the same thing. A TOUCHING INSTANCE.—A touching instance of in- sect instinct has just been sent to us, says an exchange. The writer says :—" I found a cockroach struggling in a bowl of water. I took half a peanut shell for a boat. I put him into it, gave him two wooden toothpicks for oars and left him. The next morning I visited him, and he had put a piece of white cotton thread on one of the toothpicks, and set the toothpick on end as a signal of distress. He had a hair on the other toothpick, and there that cockroach sat a fishing. The cockroach, ex- hausted, had fallen asleep. The sight melted me to tears. I had never to chew leather to get a soul; I was born with one. I took that cockroach out, gave him a spoonful of gruel, and left. That animal never forgot my kindness, and now my house is chock-full of cock- roaches." Next! A SHREWD WIFE.—The wife of a Detroit speculator went East a few days ago to visit friends in the Mohawk Valley of New York. In due time he received a letter from her announcing her safe arrival, and adding, "I am going to show you that a woman knows how to speculate as well as a man. Apples are much cheaper here than in Detroit, and I am going to buy and ship a car-load on speculation." The thermometer was at zero, and the man pranced around like a crazy steer. She could not be reached by telegraph, and the letter he sent in reply had not been gone two hours when he received a second, which said, "Inclosed you will find the ship- ping bill of the car-load of apples. Don't sell one of them at less than 2 dollars a barrel, and don't never say again that women don't know how to turn a dollar to account." Yesterday the man went down to look at the car. Every apple was, of course, frozen as hard as a stone, and when the freight agent asked, "What '---' fool shipped you apples in this sort of weather?" it seemed to be a great satisfaction to reply, "My wife, sir—my wife I" A man was moving about in a car on a new Dakota railroad when the conductor came through. "Can you tell me," said the restless one, with a show of sarcasm, "whether this car is on the track or not?" "Sir," re- plied the conductor, putting his hand into his pocket, "here is a volume of the rules and regulations on this road." "But what do I want of it r "Look it over, and see if you can find any rule saying that I must spend my time running alongside of the train reporting its position to the passengers. See if there is anything in that volume that compels me to go humping myself along on the prairie and yelling through the windows, 'Fore wheels off now!' or ' Hind trucks dragging on the ties!' or 'Gentlemen, the baggage-car has just rolled into the ditch!' or 'Passengers will please remain seated while we turn off here and scoot across the prairie after a jack rabbit!' Look over them rules, sir, and see if you can find any of them directions. If you don't, in future please take your own observations on the wheels." ' EN

A VICTIM TO DELIRIUM TB. ENS. 1 At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Wednesday, be- fore Colonel Gamble and Bfr. William Pilkington, Samuel Wilson, described as of unsettled residence, was charged with haying been drunk and incapable in Church-street, Whadle, early that morning. On being placed in the dock, the prisoner, who was evi- dently a man of good education, but was only poorly dressed, exclaimed "Excuse me, I want to see a doctor." The Deputy Magistrates' Clerk: You are charged with being drunk this morning.—The prisoner (excitedly): I am not drunk this morning, sir. lam suffering from delirium tremens.—Pointing around the court, the prisoner continued : I can see them all round me now, sir. Punish me, shoot me if you like. Do anything to me.—The De- puty Magistrates' Clerk : Keep quiet for a short while.— Prisoner (cooling down) : Yes, sir.—P.C. Hodson then gave evidence that at ten minutes past one that morning he found the prisoner lying helplessly drunk in Church-street. As he was a stranger to the town witness had to lock him up for safety.—lhe prisoner (walling about the dock) : Here, will you let me go. I have never been confined in my life before.—Colonel Gamble: Have you any quee- tines to ask the officer ?—Prisoner : None at all, sir; his evidence is perfectly true, sir.—Colonel Gamble : Have you anything to say ?—Prisoner : I have no money to pay a tine, sir. I shall get employment if you will let me free, sir, to look for it. I am suffering from delerium tremens, but will walk them off.—Mr. Pilkington, J.P. : Where do you come froin ?—Prisoner : Tile last place I was in work at was Victoria Theatre, Newport, Monmouthshire. lam a scene painter. I have lost my wife; I have lost my home Do you see, sir? I have been on the drink for a good long time now, air, very nearly ten weeks.—The Chairman :Have you anyone who knows you here ?—Prisoner : Yes, sir, Mr. Wallace Reville, of the Theatre Royal, knows me here, but I don't want to apply to him. I want te walk the drink off if I possibly can. (Patheticelly) Will you give me a chance, sir? Don't send me to prison as a felon, I was never in a dock 6efore. I have been a soldier, sir, and I would rather be shot at than put in a place like this. If you would only allow ins to go free I would get employ- ment in Manchester, and would walk there to-day.—ln re- ply to the Bench, Inepector Kei.ehley said there was nothing known about the prisoner, and the prisoner said, Leen walk this off, if you will allow me. If you send me to prison yoa will sign my death warrant.—Tne Chairman : You will have to pay a fine of se, and costs 7s 6d. 12s 61 in all, or go to prison for seven days We hope you will go to prison. It will be the best thing for you, and you will be taken care of for a week—Prisoner: I wish to - see a doctor, sir.—ln- snector Keighley eaid the police would atterel to that, and the prisoner was removed.

div.p: THE EXAMINEi?, SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 18, 1886- THE ADVENTUUS OF A NIGHT. I t-

By B. B. Near to the highway from W— to B— not very far from a small quiet village, there stands a square red-brick house called " The Rectory." Trees overgrowing its front, fields stretching on every hand as far as the eye can see, a death-like stillness hanging over the whole place, give the spot the melancholy aspect of a ghost-haunted solitude. It has been said that a man either committed suicide, or was murdered there, and that his spirit frequently returns in the night to the place of the deed. However that may be, the passers by after dusk are few indeed, and none but market carters —whose duties obligate them—will go that way. • The parson whose good luck it is to have fallen into the living of this Rectory, is a pious little old ' man, with a short grey beard, bald head, soft voice, and stammering tongue. It is .his lot to possess a wife and an invalided daughter. He employs two female servants and one male servant; but how long each has held his or her remunerature post, and what are their respective duties, I cannot say. Suffice it that I say they all board and sleep at the Rectory. At about half-past ten, on a particular night in the month of December, the wind was howling, the rain was coming down in torrents, the trees swayed to and fro, slates blew off the roof of the the house, and filled the people inside with appre- hension. The parson and his wife and daughter sat thinking in the drawing-room, the female servants sat in the kitchen reading ritualistic stories of the blessed martyrs, the male servant—whom we will call Phillip—was retiring to bed. He had lighted his candle, gone 'upstairs, undressed, was about to get into bed, when--oh, horror! what could it be? —he touched a man's leg! Terrified and paralysed, for a moment he stood there. Then partly recover- ing himself, undressed as he was, he rushed down• stairs, across the hall, into the presence of the family. What was the matter? What did he mean? What had brought him there in that condition? Phillip could not explain; he was breathless; his eyes were starting from their sockets ; be fainted. The servants were sent for to bring water. They brought some. It was applied liberally and plentifully to Phillip's face' and under its cooling influence he soon recovered to tell his story. He had seen a burglar under his bed; he had touched his face; he thought he had had hold of his hand and felt a revolver; his hand had moved. He then screamed and fainted again. Again water was applied. All was excitement and bewilderment. The par- son paced about with hurried footsteps; gave orders and countermanded them. He ordered Phillip to go for a policeman; no—Phillip was undressed. He would dislodge the burglar himself. Phillip must bring the required weapons: Phillip was dressing in one of the parson's thrown-off suits and could not come. The parson must arm himself, and Phillip must do the slime; they would go together and pitch the man out. Where was the parson's revol- ver? No one could tell; but after about a quarter of an hour's excited, hurried, search, it was found. By that time Phillip had got on the knee breeches and long frock coat. Ile armed himself' with an axe, the parson charged the revolver, and, trembling and shaking, upstairs they went, kicked at the room door, shouted, and stood there. Shortly, their fears told them that they heard something move, and they scampered off downstairs again expecting to find the burglar after them. They stopped in the hall, breathless and pale. The parson's wife, daughter, and servants rushed out of the house and would not come in. The parson and Phillip went alter them. The daughter went in hysterics and nothing would quiet her. What -must now be done? Phillip must go to the village for the policeman, and send some men up to watch until he should ar- rive. After much persuasion, Phillip set out, carefully looking on each side of the road afraid lest some one. might be hidden behind the bushes. Coming to a part where the road leads over a railway, and is raised to an embankment, faced on each side by wooden rails,a white cow rose up in a field at his right hand and sent him in cold shivers. A little further on a stump to a gate leading into a field looked like a man and frightened him. Then the echo of his footsteps behind him persuaded him that some•one was coming, and set him running for his very life. He had no sooner ceased than the wind blowing among some trees at his left caused him to imagine that some one was there, and he ran again. Passing through the village without hat, in the parson's long coat and knee breeches, what few people were still out laughed at him, but he took no notice, and still hurried on. At last he arrived at the policeman's, but Only to be told that the policeman was not in. He then aroused all the neighbours and sent them round the village crying that the Rectory was attacked. He took two men with him, set out in further search, and advised all the rest to make off as speedily as possible to the scene of action. Arriving there in dozens, they were set to watch at the gates and all round passagesdoleorsof h tte se, and staredohaonudfromthegar up t h den, at d he windows for a movement inside, half fearing that a . pistol-shot might proceed from one of them. But no movement was perceived. Inside all was silent ' and still. Outside all was bustle and stir. The parson was running about in terror; his wife and daughter were declaring that the house was haunted, and protesting they would never enter it again; the servants stood trembling near to the main entrance, sheltering from the rain under some . trees. Nor would any of them be consoled. Meanwhile, Phillip and his companions had tra- versed the whole village, had searched every cor- ner, but no policeman could they find. It was now past midnight. They were giving up the search and thinking of retracing their footsteps, when up r came the identical man. In agitated and nervous ! tones Phillip tolgl him his business. The policeman looked surprised, but, with a confident and know- ing nod, said he would put the matter straight. Arriving at the Rectory, they found everybody in a state of bewilderment and dismay. The police- man, immediately setting to work, stripped himself of all unnecessary encumbrances, procured a ligh- ted candle, asked for some of themen to follow him, went quietly upstairs, pushed open the room door and entered. Finding a pair of feet protruding from under the bed, he handed the light to one of his gallant confederates, seized hold of the breeches gave a savage jerk and • flew on his back at the other end of the room. His hat with its crown knocked in bounced in one direction, his truncheon broke a hand-bowl in another, his head sounded its contents against the wall, and no doubt his in- juries in other quarters were no less severe. But, undaunted, ready again for action, he sprung to his feet, was pouncing on his victim a second time, when he discovered him to have no head. This for the moment startled hi'm—" Surely he had not pulled his head off," he thought. On further ex- amination, however, he found that the neck mas only made of a broom handle. It was all a hoax; the body was a dummy. The constable's expecta- tions dropped, and his ardour turned to disgust.. • His confederates laughed, and leaving the body ther6, they all went downstairs together. He told the parson what they had found. The parson went 1 in a rage, said he was determined to get to the root of the matter, and make an example of the perpe- trators. Meanwhile the laughing villagers had dis- persed, and the parson and the rest soon retired to bed: Thus the matter ended. The only harm done was that it kept the whole village out of bed till about two in the morning, and got the whole lot wet through with rain in the attempt to catch a burglar.

A STIPENDIIRY MAGISTRATB. Sir,—Of late I have noticed one -or two references made in "The Examiner" to the business of the borough court being delayed by the difficulty to procure magistrates to ad- judicate upon the cAses down for hearing. In my opinion the beat part of the police court is the outside, but I can still sympathise with professional men whose time is in this way wasted, and also with the prisoners, some of whom must be dreadfully anxious to know what is going to be done with them. Surely there are plenty borough J.P.'s to attend properly to their duties, and it is to be hoped, now that three more have been added to the number, that they will do so in the future. But, after all, perhaps the best remedy would be in the appointment of a qualified stipen- diarv.—Yours, dze., Warrington, September, 1886. FAIR PLAY.

div.head: OUR "ED#CATIONISTS."
div.p: OUR "ED#CATIONISTS."

Sir,—" A School Board," said Mr. Beamont at the founda- tion stone laying in Hamilton-street last week, "is worse than a property tax." These few words give us an insight into the real origin of by far the larger part of the hostility that is entertained against School Boards. It is, of course, the proper thing at ceremonials like that of Hamilton- street to say that all this hostility is due to pious detestation of modes of educatiou not distinctly religious, but were a School Beard not "worse,' or rather equivalent to "a pro- perty tax," we should see precious few foundation stone lay- ings of voluntary schools. The ardour of a lot of these gentlemen for education is wonderfully like that of the slave for cotton picking or sugar boiling. In the one case it is stimulated by a sight of the taskmaster's whip, and in the other by the fear of the tax-gatherer's visit. When the motives are often so sordid, would it not be better if there were less sanctimoniousness ?—Yours, _
'LOOKER ON.
THE NEW CHAPEL FOR STOCKTON HEATH.

Sir,—An ordinary reader, on perusing your report of the laying of fonadation stones of a new chapel at Stockton Heath, would imagine that this was to be the first Bethel whose object is to illumine the spiritual darkness of a hitherto benighted village. At any rate, such was the im- pression made upon me when I read the report, and I could not help thinking that if anyone else took the same view they had get a decidedly erroneous impression of the situa- tion. The fact is, this is not by any means the first Dissent- ing congregation that-has gathered for worship in this vil- lage, and there is now, and has been long exieting, a chapel that will accommodate all the Nonconformists in the neigh- bourhood. In its day this chapel, known as Providence Chapel, has done good service to the locality, and until very recently sufficed for the spiritual needs of the Noncon- formist villagers. But some of the leaders of the new movement, who then worshipped there, commenced to pro- mulgate doctrines which they knew were entirely at vari- ance with the constitution of the church, and when they were beaten, after an attempt to gain the mastery of the situation, they betook themselves to that haven of refuge— the old Barn. And now, not content with deserting the place which had formerly given them shelter and afforded them a sphere of usefulness, they seek to ignore the exist- ence of the former congregation, and loudly proclaim themselves—or rather get neighbouring ministers to do it for them—the pioneers of Nonconformity in Stockton Heath. Sir, to my mind, this action is all the more un- worthy remembering, as the leaders of the movement must remember, that the worshippers of Providence Chapel never avail themselves of any opportunity to advertise them- selves. It would have been far better if these men of light and leading bad stated the plain facts to these who came to speak for them, and it would have been a graceful act on their part to have acknowledged the assistance of the church which gave them succour. However, they probably took the course tbev did to gain the sympathy of those at a distance, as they must know that those who are aware of all the circumstances think there is no necessity for a new Chapel in such a small place. It is to be hoped that when the new building is ready for opening, the leaders of the church will fiee:n it necessary to give a "plain, unvar- nished " account of its origin, and that in all HONESTY.

Stockton Heath, September 13, ISB3. • HOW WE ARRANGE MATTERS. Sir,—Realing over your report of the meeting of the Town Ceuncil, I eVa2 a little interested in the discussion following the reading ef the minutes of the Sanitary Com- mittee. It seems to be mere matter of form for a committee to submit its minutes for confirmation to the General Council. D:scuesion rarely elicits information ; whatever project is submitted diecnesien at once becomes one-shied, and the chairman of the committee assumes that there is a want of confidence, and surrounds himself with a lot of dignified rubbish which at once excludes legitimate discus- sion. I am led to make these remarks in consequence of something—l know not what—that seemed to be left un- said touching the inefficiency of the woks, that may henceforth be known as the "Longford Folly." Alderman Burgess spoke, I think truly, when he said that " It was not a question of Owen Warner; there was something more behind it. It had not come out thal night, but one night it would come out." Now, what is this 41 something" ttlat has to "come out ?" Is it possible that the majority of the Town Council has come to the conclu- sion that in erecting such large and elaborate sanatoria' works at Longford, they have not best consulted the conve- nience of farmers living away in Cheshire ? or away at Poulton, Fearnhead. and other outlying places far away from Longford ? It may be possible that the Council half regret that they have not given the farmers an oppor- tunity of conveniently acquiring manure, and at the same time saving the town's rates, by establishing at the four quarters of the town modest yet sufficient works for all re- quired purposes. There can be no doubt of one thing, and tbat is that Councillor Roberts was right in saying "the Sanitary Committee was on its trial at the present time." Why he did not go further and say with Ceuncillor Dixon that a " nurse "'was Warted at Longford I cannot say. Your readers will, like myself, no doubt keep their eyes on Councillor Dixon, now that he has confessed to being "under the impression when be saw the word ' engineer ' that a mistake had been made; be thought it ought to have been the appointment of a nurse, just to nurse the machinery until a certain time got over." Why Mr. Owen Warner did not at once receive his dismissal I cannot comprehend. Here. was a nurse wanted; and who so fit for the poet as the gen- tleman who had discovered the great Longford secret? By the transferring of Mr. Councillor Dixon to the salubrious district of Longford, several points would have been gained. First, the mind of Alderman Burgess would have been set at rest, and he would no longer have been expecting the "some- thing" which be says he is " prepared to meet." Second, Councillor W. Pierpoint's "poor opinion of the machinery" at the depot, and its requiting "a man who did not know very much about it" would have been fully met, sad we should have had the satisfaction of knowing that the "receipts for manure at Longford were less in amount each year." What a lot of blessings the town would have received from this single appointment; but the greatest of all would have been—but stay, Mr. Editor, let us have Councillor Dixon's own words—" He also understood that Warner be- longed to a firm in Nottingham, and be thouaht the Sooner the knct between that firm and Warrington was cat the better." so I think, if the "knot" implies that we must not only buy machinery that wants nursing, butthat we must import a "nurse." I have heard a few strong remarks made anent this appoir ttrent It seems stranne that a man should be advised by the corntrittee, of which Mr. Councillor Bar- ker was one," to eend ip his resignation," and immediately after the same committe si.ould euddrnly fin a out that it was "requisite that an engineer should be appointed," and at once appointed, "a show man," at 455. per week. Coun- cillor Roberts was mistaken in saying that they had

"swallowed a camel and were now straining at a gnat ; " it was the camel with the extra hump that they were straining at, and very right too. No doubt the whole of the Council were satisfied that an efficient engineer or "nurse," as the case may be, could not have been found in Warrington, and tbev did right to import one frcm Nottingham. Engineers in Warrington may have a chance of learning something. I should also advise the hospital matron to keep her eyes open. Perhaps at the next meeting of the Council Coun- cillor Bolton's question will be answerod—" Why Warner had been discharged."
