FATAL FIGHT AT EARLI4,STOWN• SHOCKING DEATH OF A WOMAN.

On Thursday a great deal of excitement was oc- casioned in many parts of Earlestown by a report that a woman named Smith, residing in Legh-street, had that morning died from violence, and that a young man named Campbell had been apprehended on a charge of causing her death. Inquiries have proved that a certain degree of truth attached to the rumour. The deceased is a woman named Han- nah Smith, 39 years of age, who had cohabited with a collier named William Campbell, at 181, Legh- street. Campbell is a widower, and along with his son William, a young man of about 21 years of age, was employed as a collier at the Ram Pit, Haydock, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Company. The son did not live at his father's house, however, but lodged in the same street. On the night of last Friday Campbell and his son were drinking in the Oddfellows' Arms, Legh-street, and the father went home about eleven o'clock. A short time afterwards his son visited his • father's house, and the parties j had some words. In order to settle the quarrel the , father and son retired to the street, where they I fought, and during the struggle they fell on the , floor together. Several persons were near at the j time, and one of the spectators was the woman Smith. The young man, Campbell, suddenly left his father, it is stated, and going to the end of the house picked up a brick, weighing about Sibs., and violently threw it, as he informed the police, at his father. The missile missed that individual, how- ever, but struck the woman Smith on the left side, knocking her to the floor. She was seriously njured and was picked up, carried into the house, and put to bed. Dr. Mounsey was immediately sent for and that gentleman shortly afterwards attended. He continued to treat her daily for the injury, but she rapidly grew worse and expired about half-past eight on Thursday morning. In the absence of a post mortem examination, Dr. Mounsey can assign no cause for the death except the injury whicli she had received from the brick. Shortly after the death of the injured woman the police apprehended the young man Campbell, on a charge of causing the death of the woman and, pending the coroner's inquest, he will be kept in custody. It appears that the deceased woman was attended by Dr. Mounsey about 15 months ago, and she was treated for a sore throat, but since then up to receiving the injury, she had not been medically attended. It is stated that the prisoner was not on the best of terms with his father's paramour. All the parties came from Mowcop, near Hanley, Staffordshire, some two or three years ago. Prisoner's mother died abotit ten years since, but the father married a second time, his second wife dying some two years ago. At Newton-le-Willows Town Hall, on Friday. Camila"( -vas charged with causing the death of Hanm h 3 nith. Pending the coroner's inquest, the prisoner Wa ; remanded.

THE MILITARY.

The Liberals objected to the name of Major Ham- ilton, Orford Barracks, being retained on the regis- ter.—Mr. Roberts : What is your official position in connectiodwith the militia regiment ?—Major Hamilton: I am not connected with that regi- ment. lam connected with the Liverpool regimen- tal depot. —Mr. Roberts: You occupy quarters at Orford Barracks ?—Major Hamilton : Yes.—Mr. Roberts : Has the regiment been away during the past year for training?—Major Hamilton: It is not a militia regiment, I do not go up for training.—Mr. Roberts: Have not the officers and men connected with the regiment been away at Aitcar for shooting practice ?—Mr. Nicholson : The question is whether this gentleman has been away. Mr. Roberts; Have you been at Altcar this year?—Major Hamil- -1 ton : No.—Mr. Roberts: Have you been anywhere from your quarters in connection with your duties during the past twelve months?—Major Hamilton : No.—The Revising Barrister: That would not be ' the difficulty. He might be accidentally away.— Mr. Roberts : I want to ascertain whether he was away in connection with his regimental duties.— Major Hamilton: No.—The Revising Barrister over- ruled the objection. Major Ritchie, Orford Barracks, was similarly objected to. Major Ritchie, replying to Mr. Roberts, said that he had been away from his quarters to Altcar from 28th of May to the Bth of June. During that time he had no right to return without leave from the commanding officer, and without obtain- ing a pass.—Mr. Roberts: That is the ground of our objection. When there is &breaking of the tenancy the claim cannot be sustained. Major Ritchie was unable to return, except as a matter of courtesy, and consequently he had no right to have ihis name , inserted on the register.—Mr. Nicholson: As a mat- ter of fact, you were not 21 days absent P—Major Ritchie: I was not.—Mr. Nicholson: When you ap- ply for leave of absence you obtain it on reasonable grounds ?—Major Ritchie: Always. When I was at Altcar I slept in a tent, and had no other quarters.— Mr. Roberts submitted that Major Ritchie had not occupied his quarters continuously, and that his occupation had been broken. —The Barrister asked Mr. Roberts if he would argue, because a.doorkeeper left his post for a few minutes, he would lose his vote.—Mr. Roberts said there was a difference in that case as contrasted with that of Major Ritchie. The claimant could not return to his quarters with- out leave.—The Barrister: You say that the autho- rities could interfere ?—Mr. Roberts: According to Major Ritchie's own evidence.—The Barrister: You say he is prohibited by special power from going to those rooms ?—Mr. Roberts: Exactly.—The Bar- rister said he would withhold his decision.

. Quarter-master Hawes was also objected to by the Liberals. In answer to Mr. Roberts he said he had been at Altcar during the year. He could not have left Altcar without leave of absence, but he could have leave of absence without saying where he was going to.—Mr. Roberts: Remember you are on your oath.—Mr. Nicholson protested against cautions of this kind being given by Mr. Roberts. ' —Mr. Roberts said the revising barrister wouldlcall him to order if necessary.—Mr. Nicholson'objected to a gentleman and an officer being reminded in that way that he was on his'oath.—Mr. Roberts said he should ask the Revising Barrister to protect him from Mr. Nicholson's interference.—Mr. Roberts (to Quarter-master Hawes): Supposing you were ap- plying for 48 hours' absence, would you, in making the application, tell the Colonel where you were go- ing to.—Quarter-master Hawes: I might tell, him I was going to Warrington.—Mr. Roberts: Would not that leave be to go to Warrington.—Quarter-master Hawes: Certainly. In answer to Mr. Roberts he said he could not stop away longer than the time permission was given for.—The Revising Barris,ter decided that this case must be reserved with the previous one. The vote of Sergeant John Catchpole, of Orford Barracks, was likewise objected to by the Liberals. In reply to Mr. Roberts the claimant said he had been at Altcar, and whilst there he had been twice away on leave of absence. He could not claim leave of absence as a privilege, but he had never been refused leave. He had known cases in which private soldiers had been refused leave of absence. He had been at Altcar nineteen :days.—Mr. Nichol- son said his contention was that this temporary ab- sence did not affect the residence at Orford. The men were sent to Altcar simply because there was a better range there to shoot at than at Orford.— Questioned by Mr. Nicholson, Sergeant:Catchpole said there was no reason why they should stop at Altcar except the difficulty of getting home at nights. He had no duties to perform at night while at Altcar. The Revising Barrister said that lie could not see any evidence •to substantiate this case.—Mr. Nicholson said that there were only one or two of the soldiers' claims different to the present one.—Mr. Roberts mentioned that these cases were allowed last year. The Liberals appealed, but this question of; absence" was not mentioned by them, and the votes:were allowed.—The claim was dis- allowed,.

Sergefint-Major William Byrne's vote was ob- jected to by the Liberals. In answer to questions, he said he:lived in a house in Battersby-lane. He was connected with the Liverpool Regiment of Militia, and this Year he had been at Altcar for twenty-five days training. He came to Warring- ton on the day of the Parliamentary election with- out leave, as the regulations said they could'come up without leave to vote. He was also at home, with leave, on the 10th and 17th July. He hadra wife and children, and lived in a house outside the barracks.—The Revising Officer said the point in the service franchise did not arise in that case, and he allowed the vote.—Sergeant-Major Byrne then applied that expenses might be allowed him.—Mr. Roberts: Have you lost anything? -- Sergeant- Major Byrne: I have 104 my day, I have lost my dinner, and I have lost my breakfast. (Laughter.) —The Revising Barrister: Mr. Byrne you state your case very effectively; let us hope you won't lose your dinner altogether. We will allow 2s to- wards getting your dinner.—The cases of a number of other non-commissioned officers were dealt with, and in the case of those who lived in houses out of the barracks the vote was allowed, but the claims of those living in barrack and who had broken their occupation by going to Altcar for certain periods, were disallowed.

THE REV. IL BROWN'S VOTE.—The Rev. 1.1. Brown claimed as a lodger at 18, Parker-street, and was objected to by the Liberals. In answer to Mr. Roberts, Mr. Brown said there was another lodger in the house, the rent of which was £l6 a year.— Mr. Roberts submitted that a house of which the gross rental was only £l6, could not show £2O a year value for unfurnished rooms to qualify two lodgers.—Mr. Nicholson said the question was whether the rooms Mr. Brown occupied were worth £lO a year or 4s. per week.—The Revising Barrister said they had got clear evidence that the rent was £l6, and that there were two lodgers, which did not allow,Elo for each.—Mr. Nicholson submitted that lodgings had a value irrespective of the value of the house.—The Revising Barrister: I want authority for that.—Mr. Nicholson: Ido not think there is any authority.—The Revising Barrister; I have always felt a difficulty in these cases, but the law has prescribed £lO a year as being the value.—Mr. Nicholson asked if the Revising Barrister meant that unless the rental of a house was £2O a year or upwards he did not consider it would qualify two lodgers? —The Revising Barrister said he could not allow two votes on that house, and if the house was not £lO he could not grant one vote.—Mr. Nicholson: You are not asked to grant two.—Mr. Roberts: It is immaterial : there is another lodger. —ln answer to further questions, Mr. Brown said that he had the front room for his own use, and the back bedroom, which he selected;in preference , to the front bedroom. The otherlodger had not a separate sitting-room. lie (Mr. Brown) paid 10s. a , week for the use of these rooms, and paid extra for washing, fire, and light.—Mr. Roberts again sub- mitted that there was not sufficient value to show a beneficial occupation of £lO a year.—The Revising Barrister said they 1141 to place against that what the rooms fetched; it might be from fanciful con- siderations.—Mr, Roberts submitted that it was not the fancy prices of these rooms that ought to be taken into account, but their market value.--The claim was allowed.

LODGINGS IN A PUBLIC-HOITSE.—In this case the lodger vote of Mr. Peters, Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latchford, was objected to on behalf of the Liberals.—Mr. Roberts: Are not all the rooms on the ground floor at the Cheshire Cheese public

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY 9 SEPT EMBER 18 1886 • THE REVISION AT WARRINGTON. On Wednesday Mr. J. T. Foard, barrister-at-law commenced the revision of the list of voters for the Parliamentary borough of Warrington, and the hearing of claims and objection, at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street. Mr. Henry Roberts (Liberal agent) appeared on behalf of the Liberal party, and Mr. Nicholson, with Mr. llampson (Conservative agent) attended on behalf of the Conservatives. The num- ber of occupiers' claims was put down at 489, and the lodgers' new claims at 508, whilst the occupiers' objections numbered 489, and the lodger objections 287. Considerable interest was manifested in the proceedings

rooms ?—Mr. Peters: I have a room on the ground floor. That is not a public room. It is brought into use for Public-house purposes if I do not object. In answer to a further question, he said that if Mr. Ireland, the landlord, under pressure of business, wanted to use the room he could do so. He had a bedroom upstairs, one of five not used for public purposes. He had no interest in the business, and paid 8s 6d a week for the rooms, boarding himself. —Mr. Roberts submitted that where a person had ' only one room in a public-house it was not of suffi- cient value to allow him a vote.—The Revising Bar- rister: I think it is a doubtful and suspicious case, but he has proved sufficient to establish his right. FINES AND THE VOTE. —The Conservatives ob- jected to the name of Michael Griffin. 3, Bay Horse- yard, remaining on the register. In answer to Mr. Nicholson, Griffin denied that he had been in prison during the last twelve or eighteen months.—Mr. Nicholson: Have you been brought before the magistrates ?—Griffin : Yes, many a time. (Laugh- ter.)—ln answer to further questions, he said that on the last occasion he was brought before the magistrates it was for taking two or three cauli- flowers. He was fined Os 6d, and his master paid the money for him.—The Revising Barrister allowed the vote.

freshed his memory that morning from books.—Mr.Roberts: Why were you dismissed from the force ?—Witness • For a reason that I am not going to tell you. The witness further declined to answer the question, and the Revising Barrister said the question might be permissible if it became a question of oath against oath, and character against character.— Police-constable Chantler was then called on, he said he assisted to take Mulkearn to the gaol. He was tined 5s and costs, but the defendant refused to pay and he said he would sooner go to gaol.-111r. Roberts submitted that fact did not disqualify his vote, as th• man had the opportunity uny time of coming home by paying the fine.—The Revising Barrister said that was 80, and the vote would be allowed.— Mr. Roberts said all the trouble would have been saved if the other side had obtained a note from the Chief Con- stable, bat they preferred to call a man who had been dis- missed from the force.

A QUESTIONABLE LODGER —The vote of Isaac Pickton, on the list as a lodger with his sister, in Wilderspool-road, was objected to by the Liberals. It was stated by Mr. Nicholson that Pickton nad been on the register for some years, and the house was rated at £2B —Mr. Roberts said there was already ens lodger on the list for the same house. —Mr. Nicholson said the first mentioned case was a new claim, but Pickton had been on the list for years.—ln reply to Mr. Nicholson, Pickton stated that he had made an arrangemeet with his sister, Who kept the house, to pay her 103 per week for a room and bedroom. His Sister did not use the, rooms ; they were kept solely for him. The furni- ture in the two rooms belonged to him. He paid his sister every week, and he never paid her less than lOs per week. In reply to Mr. Roberts, Pickton admitted giving his sister a pound or two occasionally. His sister was the tenant of the house.—Mr. Nichaleon : How many other lodgers be- sides yourself are there in the house 7—Mr. Pickton : Two. —Are yours the best rooms in the house, or are they not.— Mr. Pickton : Mine are the best rooms —ln reply to the Revising Barrister, Mr. Pickton said his sister had a room to herself, and she took her meals alone. He also took his meals alone in his own rooms. He would swear he had his meals by himself —Mr. Roberts asked if the furniture be- longed to Mr. Pickton, how tie came to claim for "furnished apartments ? "—Mr. Pickton said he had bought some of the furniture, and part of the furniture belonged to leis sister. The property belonged to his sister, and was worth £l3OO or £7OO, and it was the best furnished house in War- rington. (Laughter.) Even the Mayor of Warrington had no rooms like it. (Renewed laughter.)—The Revising Bar- rister ultimately allowed the vote.—Mr. Roberts said he had a witness who formerly lodged there to prove that Mr. Pick- ton regularly had his meals with his sister.—The Revising Barrister said he was strongly of opinion that Mr. Pickton was not telling the truth with a strict regard to his oath, but at the same time he was bound to take his evidence as sworn.—Mr. Roberts said he thought he was justified in objecting to the vote; and the Revising .Barrister declined to allow costs.

A CullaTE's CLAIM—no Rev. J. A. Drummond, curate at the Parish Church. claimed to be placed on the list as an necupier.—Mr. Roberts objPcted to this claim, On` the ground that Mr. Drummond could not properly be described as an occupier, and mentioned that the gardener and his wife also lived on the same premises.—In answer to a question, Mr. Drummond said that during the time he had been in hi, present residence there had been several curates appointed, but they did not occupy the rooms. The furniture belonged to the rector.—The Revising Barrister was of opinion that Mr. Drummond could not be put on as an occ,ipier : and Mr. Nicholson then asked that the Revising Barrister might rxercise his power to alter the qualification t`-) that of a lodger. The Revising Barrister said he should consider his power to do his, and wou!d Nave the matter over till day (SatureNy).

bullet. A mob unsuccessfully tried to lynch the man who shot at Bratiano. They next attacked the offices of two newspapers which had denounced M. Bratiano, and de- stroyed the windows, docuMents, and furniture.

A " TECHNICAL Inaa."—Frank Hesketh claimed as a lodger in a house in Battermarket-street, and was objected to by the Liberals. In answer to questions, he said the rent of the house he lived in was £l2, and he and his brother lived in it. There was a woman came occasionally to cook for them. He paid Us. Bd. a week for his two rooms, but some of the furniture was his own. His brother had a right to come into his room 'as a brother." His brother was a partner in the firm of Thomas Hesketh and Sons.—Mr. Roberts: Are you, partner in the concern ? Claimant declined to answer.—Mr. Roberts: Answer me or not, as vou like: are you or are you not a partner in the firm of Thomas Hesketh and Son ?—Claimant: Well, that is rather a technical idea. I will not tell you. He (the claimant) was in the employ of the firm, and the brother he lived with was a member of the firm. In answer to the Revising Barrister, he said there were seven rooms in the house, and the Barrister asked how they could make £lO vales out of two rooms when the seven were 0017 £l2. The claim was not allowed. .

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. ITOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at 4 o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. Sanaa', replying to Mr. Mallork, said the store of Martini Henri rifles was not sufficient to enable them to issue them to volunteers.—The Roma SECRETARY, replying to H. Campbell, said his attention had been drawn to the starernent that the member for west Birmingham (Mr. Chamberlain) had made arrangements with the chief of the Birmingham police for an inspector to accompani him on his visit to the continent. He had no, authority over Birmingham police. He had made inquiries and found the statement of facts in the- paragraph were inaccurate. iss to whether there was. danger of attack on Mr. Chamberlain while visiting the continent he declined on public grounds to give any answer.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, replying to Mr. W. Redmond, said Sir H. Wolff was still engaged in Egypt by the Government in carrying out with Mukhter Pasha the general organisation of Egyptian administration. His recommendations were now under the consideration of the Government, Sir H. Wolff was paid £5,000 per year. I THE CouRSH OP EUSINESS.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, replying to Mr. John Morley, said if Supply t was concluded that night the report would be received next day and the Appropriation Bill read the first time. If that I was done the Government proposed to take Mr. Parnell's • Bill on Monday. rr Supply was not finished to-night they would have to make special demands on members to-dap- to bring it to a close. SUPPLY.—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates. On the vote for the Consta- bulary of Ireland, Mr. GILHOOLY pointed out the advis- ability of suspending evictions during the winter.—Mr. ; KENNY wished to know the reason police were drafted into districts where there was no danger of disturbance.—Mr. DEASY complained ef the extra police sent to Mayo, and Mr. P. PowER said the way to resist extra taxation for ad- • dittional police was to strike against the county rate.— '• Other Irish members spoke in the same strain, but sr Michael Hicks-Beach defended the vote, which was finally i passed. On the vote for National Gallery Sir G. CAMPBELL pro- posed to reduce the vote three hundred pounds, as a protest against the purchase of the Blenheim pictures.—After some discussion the amendment was withdrawn and the vote agreed to, as was the vote for the National Portrait Gallery. The House was afterwards occupied with a discussion arising out of the vote for public education in Scotland. [LEFT SITTINGii

A " BONA-FIDE " LoDpun.—Charles James Houghton, who was on the list 29 a lodger with his parents at 73, Lovely-lane, was objected to by the Liberate. He said he had the exclusive use of two rooms, a sitting room, ar d a bedroom, but the Revising Barrister decided that the vote, should not be allowed.-,.-Claimant: I am struck off, then, sir.—The Revising Barrister : Yes.—Claimant : I am a bona jid,o lodger for all that. (Laughter.) The Court will be resumed this (Saturday) morning.
CRlCZET.—Australians, first innings, 194; South of Eng. land, 126 for seven wickets.
The steam yacht Glenelg was run into and sunk by the steamer Claine at Greenock on Friday afternoon. The crew were saved.

The race for the Doncaster.Cap was run on Friday with the following result :—The Bard 1, St. Michael 2, Stone Clink 3 ; four ran. The condition of Mrs. Drew, wife of the Rev. Harry Drew and daughter:of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, is causing the family at Hawarden serious apprehension. The King of Portugal arrives in London on Friday after- noon on a few days visit. Buckingham Palace has been placed at his Majesty's disposal during his stay. On Thursday and 'again on Friday morning severe frost prevailed over the northern counties of Scotland, and ve- getation of all kinds has received a check. Potatoes have suffered most.
The police have received evidence implicating a farm servant in the supposed murder of John 11411, near Ellinya- binch. Notwithstanding the vigilance of the police, Hall has not yet been found.

A Cabinet Council was held at half-past two o'clock on Friday afternoon at the Foreign Office, Lord Salisbury pre- siding. The Cabinet sat for just over an hour, when most of the Ministers went to their respective offices. On Friday morning a man named Robert Palmier Winch, a tradesman, of North-street, Westminster, aged 54 years. while bathing in the sea at Margate was seized with a fit and drowned. He had gone to Margute to attend his father's funeral. . _

MR. PARNELL'S LAND BILL.—Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P., has issued the following whin to Gladstonian Liberals and Unionist Liberals alike :—"Your attendance is particularly requested in the House of Commons on Monday, September 20, when the second reading of the Tenants' Relief (Ire- land) Bill will be moved." It is expected that Mr. Gladstone will be present on Monday evening and take part in the. debate.

ARREST OF MURPHY, THE! MURDERER.—On Friday morn- ing, Murphy, the murderer of Police-constable Austwick, at Dodworth, was apprehended after a desperate struggle and murderous attack on three police-officers. At half-pat eleven o'clock Murphy was taken before Mr. Thomas Norton and other magistrates, and remanded for eight days on a charge of murdering Anstwick. The case has created great excitement in the district.

THE CHOLERA IN ITALY. Rom?, FRIDAY.—The cholera returns for the last 24 hours are as follow :—Torre Dell Annurziata four cases, two deaths; Putignana six cases, five deaths; San Marco in Latnis five cases, one death ; Manfredonia three cases, one death; Padua seven cases, two deaths ; Ravenna four cases, three deaths: Rovigo eight cases, one death; Taranto 16 cases, six deaths. CYCLONES IN THE UNITED STATES. NEW YORE, FEIDAY.—The States of Indiana and Illinois and South Eastern Michigan have been visited by cyclones, and much damage has been done at Indianopolis, Detroit, Terrehante, and the surrounding country. The town of Montezuma, in Illinois, and Helton, in Michigan, are reported to have been partially destroyed and some lives lost. TROOPS IN BURMAH STRICKF:N WITH CHOLERA:

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.
The court was resumed on Thursday morning, Mr. Foard again presiding. The Liberals were again represented by Mr. H. Roberts and the Conservatives by Mr. E. J. Nichol- son.

AN AnRANGENIENT.—James Maxwell Muir claimed as a lodger. The claim was objected to by the Liberals, and it was stated by claimant's father, who appeared on his behalf, that he paid be. Gcl. per week for his lodgings and 9s. 61 for his board. Witness made that arrangement purposely with his son in order to secure his vote. Mr. Roberts said the vestion was whether there had been a bona fide arrange- ment and not a mere colourable arrangement to secure a vote.—The Revising Barrister thought it was a colourable arrangement, but he could not go behind the agreement.— The vote was allowed.

A MANAGER'S VOTE.—The vote of James George Carr, 7, St. James'-street, was objected to by the Liberals.—ln answer to Mr. Roberts. Mr. Carr said that he was manager for Edgar Valentine Morton. Five and seven, St. James'. street, were separate places, bet there was internal com- munication between the two. Mr. Morton had no residence at No. 5 now and had not slept there during the past 12 months. Mr. Morton used to sleep there, but he does not now.—The claim was allowed, but as it was stated that Mr. Morton had also been on the register in respect of the same premises, his name was struck off. Too YOUNG —Charles Travers claimed as a lodger at 28. Parker-street, but was objected to by the Conservatives. —ln answer to a question, Mr. Travere said he was 21 years of age in August last, and Mr. Nicholson said their objection was that the claimant had not been 21 in the qualifying year and the claim was disallowed on this ground. COLONEL GREENALL'S Vcern.—A vote was claimed on behalf of Colonel Greenall, in respect of a room in the Volunteer premises in Bath-street. The Liberals objected. Sergeant-Major Fennelly, who appeared on behalf of Col. Greenall, said he believed Colonel Greenell lived in Lon- don.—Mr. Roberts : Has he any other residence than the Carlton Club ?—Sergeant-Major Fennelly : I expect so. —l,lr. Roberts : DO you know whether he has or sot ? Sergeant-Major Fennelly : Not exactly ; he has another house but I forget where it is.—Mr. Robbrts : He has .another house where his servants and Mrs Greenall live. Sergeant-Major Feanelly : I cannot tell you that exactly.--e- Mr. Roberts: As a matter of fact do you know that he has another house besides the Carlton Club F—Sergeant-Major Fennelly : Yes. He added that the premises claimed for were the headquarters of the Warrington Volunteers. There were two other families resident on the same premises, and there was one room reserved entirely and exclusively for Colonel Greenall.—ln reply to the Revising Barrister, Mr. Nicholson said he maintained that -in this case it was an actual inhabitancy. Colonel Greenall was down here con- stantly and for a considerable time.—The Revisieg Barris- ter said that there must be a distinct inhabitancy by him- self and "for his own part and for no other purpose," and he did not see how they could possibly suggest that in this case.—Mr. Nicholson said he did with deference contend the.t it was a fit inhabitancy.—The Revising Barrister : I 'must give you the chance of raising the point ; I must de- cide against you. The vote was not allowed. A MI.TAKEN IDENTITY—The Claim of Hugh Harper. 33, Town Hill, was objected to by the Conservatives, but it was found on inquiry that they had mistaken the father for the eon, and the vote was accordingly allowed. EMPLOYER AND EMPLOYED.—Henry Jackson, 31, Irlam- street, claimed as an occupier, but was objected to by the Liberals. In reply to Mr. Roberts, he said tie occupied the whole of the premises excepting the shop. Mr. Unsworth had no rooms there, and he got his meals at home at Pad- gate, except on Saturdays, when be is at the suop. He had never slept on the premises during the last twelve months, but there was a bed for him to, use if lee liked.—Mr. Roberts argued that this reservation deprived the claimant of the right.—Tbe Revising B=rrister thought that the case was similar to that of a coachman living over a stable, and' in which the proprietor might go and sleep on the pre- mises.—Mr. Roberts submitted that the cases were not analogous. The coachman under the circumstances referred to would occupy premises distinct from those of-the master. —The Revising Barrister remarked that the employer had never exercised his right in the present case; if he had done so that would have been a question.—The vote was allowed.

A RETICENT LODGER.—Robert Daiateth, claimed as a lodger with his father in Sankey-street, and was objected to by the Liberals. He paid, he said, 53 a week for his rooms, but declined to say how much he paid for board and lodg- ings.—The Revising Barrister ruled that it was a proper question. and as the claimant still declined to impart the desired information the vote was not allowed.

VETERAN CLAINANTS.-Mr. Samuel Barlow appeared on behalf of his father, Samuel Barlow, sen., who claimed as a lodger, the claim having objected to by the Conservatives. Mr. Barlow said that his father was 78 years of age, and lived with his sister at 92, School-brow. He paid 10s a week for the use of his rooms, and about 20s a week for his board, attendance, dx. The vote was allowed.—Mr. Barlow, also appeared on behalf of his father-in-law, the Rev. Jas. Clelland, who, it was stated, was 84 years of age, and lived as a lodger with Mr. Barlow. The claim was, how- ever, not allowed. A Snowmates VOTE.—A man named Chadwick claimed to be put on tile list as the occupier of a house in Lythgoes- lane. It was stated that the claimant was the keeper of a shooting gallery, and that he left home about Good Friday, and returnned home in November. The vote was allowed. A PRECOCIOUS ASPIRINT.-A young man named Arthur James Allen claimed in respect of lodgings at 7,Lovely-lane. He was objected to by the Liberals, and in reply to Mr. Roberts said he would not be 21 till next month. This ad- mission, of course, disposed of any chance he had of becom- ing a voter. _ _ _

A BLANK DElllAL.—Joseph Devonport, late of 23,School- brow, was objecte4 to by the Liberals. Mr. Roberts: Have you been in the county court recently for a matter.—Mr. -Deyonport : What has that to do with yon.—Mr. Nichof- son thought that before such a question were asked there should be some connection between it and the matter in band.—Mr. Roberts said he would show that there was some connection.—Mr. Roberts then asked the claimant if he bad sworn in the county court that one or other of the hotpes 23. or 24, Scheol-brow, was not in his name.—Mr. Devon- port: No, and you have no right ts ask me such a ques- tion.—The vote was allowed.

AN EASILY KNOWN FACE.—William Richardson, of 16, Hardy-street, whose face was covered with a dense coating of coal dust, was objected to, but his vote was allowed'. He then claimed expenses, and said that he had to attend at the court on the previous day.—The Revising Barrister: I don't remember seeing your face, and I think I should have recognised vou again. (Laughter.)—Richardson did not reply to this, and the barrister remarked that he sup- posed he had been there In the shade of the evening. (Laughter.) Richardson then mentioned that he worked in a coil-yard, and he was allowed 25 6d expenses. ATTEMPTED MANtFACTTIRE OF VOTES.—Towards the end of the sitting on Thursday a considerable number of Conservative lodger claims and Liberal objections to lodger voters came before the court and were successively struck of, owing to insufficient rental of the houses. The Revising Barrister remarked that if these had been allowed there would have been a manufacture of votes, a wholesale manu- facture, and not merely a manufacture in detail.—Mr. Hamp- son (Conservative agent) said that claims of this kind had been allowed last year and the year before.—The Revising Barrister said he was not dealing with last year. He did not intend to help anybody to manufacture votes. What the law allowed he would of course allow, and he would lean to the side of giving a vote, but he tould not allow a general manufacture of votes in the teeth of the law.

The revision of voters for the Warrinizton Parliamentary borough list of voters'was resumed on Friday forenoon, be- fore Mr. Foard. The Liberals were again represented by Mr. H. Roberts. and the Conservatives by Mr. E. J. Nicholson and Mr. John Hampson (Conservative registration agent). A QUESTION OF IMPRISONMENT.—Tbe name of Michael Mulkearn was objected to by the Conservatives on the ground that he had been in prison during the past twelie months. Claimant said he had not been in prison for more than 15 months. Mr. Nicholson thereupon asked for an adjournment of thecase, to enable him to commenicate with the Chief Constable. If claimant's statement was found to be correct he would consent to pay the costs.—Mulkesrn consented to await the arrival of a messenger from the police station, but shortly afterwards he informed tho Re- vising Barrister that he had been fined ss.—Mr. Nicholson said they would wait until the messenger from the police office returned.—The case came up about an hour later, and the question was whether he had been In prison during the qualifying year.—Mr. Nicholson thee called Joseph Nield, late assistant police clerk, at the police office, whereupon Mulkearn called out: "His evidence is not fit to tie believed."—Mr. Roberts: It is not, sir. In the first place he is net an officer of the police court.—Nield was then sworn. He said be was at present out of employment. He knew the man Mulkearn, who was sent to prison for drunkenness in January this year.—Mulkearta : I Paid the fine.—ln reply to Mr. Roberts, the witness said Mul- kearn had the option of paying a fine. He (witness) was not employed at the police office now. He had been die- missed.—Mr. Roberts: What for P—Witness : That is not material.—ln reply to further questions, witness said he and Constable Chantler removed the man, to prison. He had re-

Many deaths have occurred among the troops. At one Diane held by twenty-five men of the second battalion of the Liverpool Regiment eight cases and six deaths occurred in twenty.four hours. ATTEMPT TO MURDER A PREMIER. BUCHAREST, FRIDAy.—An attempt to assassinate M. BrAlan°, the Roumanian Premier, was perpetrated yester- day:evening. M. Bratiano had just come from a Cabinet Council, and was going home, accompanied by a deputy, M. Robesco, when, as they reached a street near the Premier's house, a man came forward and fired a revolver at the Minister. The shot missed M. Bratiano, but hit M.Robesco in the loin, fortunately inflicting only a slight wound, as M. ! Robesco was wearing a metallic bandage, which turned the.

A SEarous OFFENCII.—On Wednesday at the Lymm Police Court, Henry Hatton, a labourer, aged 24, was char- ged with having committed an unnatural offence at High Leigh on the 15th ult. and was committed for trial to the Assizes.

CONGRBGATIONAL CIiIIRCH ANNIVERSARY.—The anniver- sary services in connection with the above place of worship were held on Sunday. At the morning and evening service a sermon was preached by the Rev. R. G. Leigh, of Hope Chapel, Salford. In the afternoon a special musical service was held, when the oratorio, "Christ and his soldiers," was given by the choir, under the leadership of Mr. Jas. Astley. The soprano and contralto solos were admirably rendered by Miss E Holt, Miss Stone, and Miss E. Moston, Mr. T. Spar- ling and Mr. A. Ellison giving the bass and tenor solos. There was an accompaniment of violins, cornets, violincellos and flutes. At each of the services there was a crowded at- tendance, especially in the afternoon, and the collections, which will be devoted to the use of the-Sunday school, amounted to a little over £2O.

A STrarGaLts WITTE POAXIIIEIt9 AT RAINFOYAs,----PefOre Colonel Gamble and Mr. William Pilkington, at the SE. Helens Town HAP,,, on Wednesday, Alfred Lund, a collier, was charged with assaulting P.S. Smith at Painford, On the previous afternoon. Police Sergeant Smith stated that he met the prisoner and anether man in Owen's-lane, and noticing something bulky in Lnnd's pocket, he asked him what he had got there. The prisoner replied that the', were apples, and when he (witness) went to search the bulky pocket the two men set upon him. The prisoner kicked him on the shins, struck him several ties, end threw him into a ditch. A struggle followed, and Land, drew a knife, but ultimately ran away. Witness and another officer gave chase, and after running a miS they found him concealed in some ferns at Moss Bank. In hie possession they found a net used for taking game. It had stubble entangled in it, and had evidently been recently in use. Prisoner said the officer nearly strangled hint with the muffler he wore round his neek, and he (Lund) dror the knife to cut the neckerchief. He was fined 4...,15 costs.

S. Ass' CHURCIL—On Sunday the annual charity sermons were preached by the Very Rev. Gerard Woollett, Father Rector of St. Anne's, Sutton. Solemn high mass was celebrated in the morning at 10-30 by the Revs. Canon Holden, deacon, and Father Smith, sub-deacon; and there was the Benediction in the evening. There was a fair con- gregation, and the collection, which was in aid of the mis- sion and day school, wAs a good average. T.fte choir was aided en the occasion by singers from St. Anne's. TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION—There was again a well- attended meeting of the above on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. E. S. Eccles. An address of great interest was given by the Rev. J. W. Walker, 8.A., describ- ing life in New Zealand, and his experience of a recent visit. The chairman addressed the meeting briefly, and a musical entertainment followed, in which Miss Simpson played a solo on the pianoforte, Messrs. H. and P. Capper gave songs, Dr. E. Capper a reading, and Master Makiuson recitations. New members were enrolled at the close.
FRODSFIAIII.

CHOIR TRIP.—The annual choir trip in connection with Kingsley Church took place on Thureday•week, when the party, which numbered, including the vicar (the Rev. A. P. Reynolds) and the organist (Mr. F. Cocker),) about 24. left Frodsham by an early train en route for Liverpool. After a short ramble in the city, the company visited the Exhibi- tion, where the rest of the day was spent in enjoying the ample attractions of the place. All arrived safely at Frod- sham Station by 10-40 p.m. The day's arrangements (owing to the absence of the churchwardens) were under- taken by the vicar.

"SHAM FIGHT" BY FRODSHABI VOLUNTEERS.-011 Sat- urday evening the Frodsham Volunteer Corps made their annual visit to Fos Hill, near Frodsham, the seat of Mr. James Reynolds. The company left their headquarters about five o'clock, under the command of Captain Harris- son, te the strains of martial music, each man carrying 20 rounds of ammunition. An enemy, consisting of a detach- ment under Lieutenant T. Ashton, were stationed on the wooded heights near the mansion, and the remainder did their best to withstand the strategic movements of the enemy, who took advantage of every available cover, assailing the gallant defenders at two points, and a conflict ensued at close quarters. Captain Harrisson directed the attack, and was ably assisted by Sergeant Evans. The rnanceavres were watched with much interest, and at the close the officers and men were entertained by Mr. Reynolds, who made a short speech. Captain Harrisson also delivered a abort address.

THE EAELESTOWN COFFEE PALACE COMPANY.—The directors of the Earlestown Coffee Palace Compan 7 held a meeting at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-place, Earles- town, on Wednesday evening. Mr. Joseph Cordingly, pre- sident, occupied the chair, and there was a full attendance. Several matters of business connected with the improvement of the Coffee Palace, and with the view of making it sti:l more attractive to the public, were discussed. GOOD TEMPLAEY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earl estown Lodge of Good Templara was held on Monday evening, under the presidency of Brother J. Macdonald, W.C.T. There was a fair attendance. After several items of lodge busiuess had .been transacted the. evening's pro- gramme, 'Sharp Practice and Harmony," was proceeded with. Several questions were introduced for discussion, and the proceedings were interspersed with selections of music.

MuNiarAL MATTErts.—The Mayor of St. Helens (Alderman Mcßryde), gave a private banquet to a number of leading gentlemen on Thursday night. In connection with the Council there are two vaeant aldermanic chairs, viz., for West Sutton by the death of Mr. H. Baxter ; and for Eccleston, by the bankruptcy of Alderman Johnson. The retiring councillors this year are Lieutenant-Colcnel W. W. Pilkington, W. Langton D. McKechnie, Jas. Fisher, J. C. Gamble, and R. A. Gaskell. THE MIDNIGHT STRUGGLE AT NEWTON.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and W. F. Gooch, Thomas John Gosl in, employed as a striker at Vulcan Foundry, was charged on remand with being drunk and disorderly on the previous Saturday night, and also with assaulting P.C. Spencer.—The office.r stated that he found the prisoner lying drunk and asleep on the footpath, and when he awoke him the prisoner struck and kicked him several times. During the struggle prisoner broke his (P.C. Spencer's) whistle chain, and threw the whistle away.—The prisoner said on the Saturday afternoon in question he had been prize firing at Highfield Moss with the local volunteers, and after the shooting the whole of the volunteers retired to the Pied Bull Hotel, where they drank out of the prize cue that had been won. He had a little more than was good for him, and he did not remember anything about his subsequent conduct.—The Bench im- posed a fine of 5s and cost for the drunkenness, and 10a and costs for the assault., THE MARRIED WOKEN'S MAINTENANCE A CT.—At the St. Helens Town Hall on Friday, John Crane was charged with haying deserted and neglected to maintain his wife, Ellen.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Ellen Crane stated that she and defendant had been married a year and nine months. He had deserted her twice, the first time be- ing in last December. ,On the 28th of August her husband came home drunk and asked for his tea. She told him it was supper time, and also told him what she had for his supper. He then, tumbled her over a chair, and removed the clock and some clothes to be brother's. She then went to bed, but defendant returned between one and two o'clock in the morning and burst the'cloor open, arid was going to take all the food that was in the house away with him, but she prevented/ him from doing so. He earuck her between the shoulder& with a loaf of bread. He then rushed at her with an armchair. He went out, and she did not see any- thing more of him until the previous Tuesday morning. Her husband had told her ahat he would not maintain her. He worked at Messrs. Pilkington's. Complainant added that the woman with whom she was living would not have her husband in the house.—Defendant said his wife was never sober, and he produced a bundle of pa,wntickets. He also , said she had been guilty of immoral conduct with other men. She had upon one occasion laid his head open with the fire irons.—Comflainant said she only did that once, and she was fined for it.—The Chairman asked the defendant if he could not make her an offer and live separately.—The defendant said he would not maintain leer.—The Chairman: You are bound to support her, and if you will not make some offer you will be compelled to maintain her.—Defend- ant said he would be compelled then, bat he would leave the country firstaaalae raagietra,tea made an order for as. a 1 week.

WARRINGTON UNlON.—Persons willing to CON- TRACT for the supply of any of the undermentioned articles from Michaelmas to Lady Day next, to be delivered free of expense at the Warrington Union Workhouse, or at the Industrial Schools, Padgate, at such times and in such quanti- ties as the Board of Guardians shall direct, are requested to send In TENDERS, properly sealed, endorsed, and free of expense, addressed to the Clerk to the Guardians,before four o'clock p.m. on Tuesday, the 28th day of September in-tent. The following are the articles for which tenders are required : Groceries and Provisions Coal and Slack Beef and Mutton • Shoes and Clogs Fish Glazing Milk Brushes Flour and Meal • Coffins Loaves of Bread Best Oakum Rope for picking Good Cheese Best Penmaenmawr Stone Beer and Porter for Breaking Purposes. Wines and Spirits Leather Straw and Potatoes Wood for cutting into Fire- Drapery, &c. wood • Suits of Clothes Carbolic Soap Samples of any of the above may be seen en application to the Master of the Workhouse. The Coal and Black supplied must be to the satisfaction of the House and Schools Com- mittee. The Pit and quality of Coal must be named in the Tender. Forms of tender and full particulars as to the prob- able quantities of each artlcla required may be obtained at the Clerk's Office, The Guardians also invite Tenders for Printing and Station- ery, from Michaelmas 1886, to ichaelmas, 1887. All goods mode- this head must be equal to sample to be seen at the Clerk's Office, where also forms of Tender, &c., mar be ob- tained. Goods required from Poor Law Publishers will be ob- tained through the Stationery contractor, Each tender must be made upon the prescribed form, and properly enclosed and endorsed with the name of the article tendered for. Each contractor must be prepared (if required) to enter into security for the due performance of his contract. The Guardians do not bind themselves to aceept.the lowest or any tender. All contract accounts will be paid quarterly.— By order, JAMES CLOWES SUTTON, • Clerk to the Guardians. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, September 16th, 1886.
